review_note: C applies to channel-associated execution failures, not every syntax/client failure; F is specifically the documented legacy SBT1.1 Additional information format. ACF is the intended contextual key.

mnemonic.anchor: A, C and F are the intended diagnostic statements, with C understood for channel-associated execution failures.

text: Which two are true about block media recovery? (Choose two.)

options.text: The data file containing the block being recovered remains online.
To use it, Flashback Database must be enabled.
A block being recovered is not accessible.
It can be performed on noncorrupt blocks.
The target database for which one or more blocks are to be recovered must be in the OPEN state.
It cannot repair logical corruption.

explanation:
A and C are the two unqualified supported statements in the supplied wording. The old selection of B was wrong, and the question has been changed from three choices to two rather than replacing it with another absolute claim contradicted by current 19c documentation.

Option A is true because block media recovery limits the recovery scope to selected blocks while the datafile can remain online. Option C is true because the corrupt blocks being recovered remain unavailable until their recovery finishes. Other good blocks in the file can remain usable.

Option B is false because Flashback Database is optional. If enabled and usable, its logs can provide good block images, but backups and other supported sources can also be used. Option D is false because the documented operation recovers blocks marked corrupt, not arbitrary good blocks. Option E is false because the target may be mounted or open with a current control file and must satisfy the ARCHIVELOG requirement.

Option F is too absolute. Oracle says block media recovery may not repair all logical block corruptions; that is different from saying it can never help any logical corruption. Interblock logical inconsistencies often require another recovery technique.

Begin with diagnosis, for example:
```sql
SELECT file#, block#, corruption_type FROM v$database_block_corruption;
```
Validate the corruption classification, available good images and redo chain before choosing block recovery. A block-level technique does not recover a missing entire datafile, and a successful physical checksum check does not prove every relationship between table and index blocks is logically correct.
original_text: Which three are true about block media recovery? (Choose three.)

sources.title: Block media recovery scope and prerequisites
Only corrupt blocks, mounted/open target and optional flashback search

review_note: Only A/C are unequivocal; F says cannot repair logical corruption, while current 19c docs say may not repair ALL logical corruptions. The choose-three count was corrected to two.

mnemonic.anchor: A and C are the two unqualified supported statements in the supplied wording.

text: In which two situations can you use Database Upgrade Assistant? (Choose two.)

options.text: when the operating system (OS) needs to be changed as part of the upgrade
when a character set conversion is required during the upgrade
when multiple pluggable databases in a container database have to be upgraded in a specific sequence
when the target and source database are on the same platform
when the hardware platform needs to be changed as part of the upgrade

explanation:
Option C is correct: DBUA supports prioritizing PDB upgrades. Its PDB selection page has a priority column, so applications can be upgraded in planned batches after the root and seed. Priority is a dependency and scheduling tool; it does not permit upgrading an older root after its dependent PDBs.

Option D is correct for the supported same-platform upgrade scenario. DBUA changes the database dictionary to the target software release and runs prerequisite checks, upgrade scripts and post-upgrade processing. A supported source release and a correctly installed target Oracle home are still required.

Option A and Option E describe a platform migration. An operating-system or hardware-platform change can require transport, export/import, replication, or another migration design. DBUA is not the mechanism that converts database files to a different platform or endian format. Replacing a machine with another compatible host is an operational move, not evidence that DBUA itself performs cross-platform conversion.

Option B is incorrect: a database character-set migration is a separate operation. Upgrading software does not automatically convert application data to a new database character set.

For example, assign the finance PDB priority 1 and reporting PDB priority 2 in DBUA, after testing both applications in the target home. Check component status and invalid objects afterward:
```sql
SELECT comp_id, version, status FROM dba_registry;
```
Treat priority, platform compatibility, character-set suitability and recoverability as separate parts of the upgrade plan. A successful dictionary upgrade alone does not prove application compatibility.

sources.title: DBUA PDB priorities and upgrade workflow

mnemonic.anchor: DBUA supports prioritizing PDB upgrades.

text: Which two are true about the Program Global Area (PGA) and its management in an Oracle database instance? (Choose two.)

options.text: The private SQL area (UGA) is located in the System Global Area (SGA) when using dedicated servers.
PGA_AGGREGATE_LIMIT is a hard limit on the PGA size for any one session.
The entire PGA is located in the System Global Area (SGA) when using shared servers.
Sorts and Hash Joins use PGA memory.
The private SQL area (UGA) is located in the System Global Area (SGA) when using shared servers.

explanation:
Option D is correct: sorts and hash joins use SQL work areas managed as PGA memory. When a work area cannot fit within its allocation, the operation may spill to temporary segments, increasing I/O. This is why a large sort can consume both PGA and temporary tablespace without either being the same storage resource.

Option E is correct: in shared-server mode, session state, including the UGA/private SQL session information, must remain accessible when different shared server processes handle successive calls. The UGA is therefore in the SGA, normally the large pool when configured, otherwise the shared pool.

Option A reverses the dedicated-server arrangement. A dedicated server retains the session UGA in its PGA; it does not put that session memory into the SGA merely because it contains SQL information.

Option C overstates the shared-server rule. The UGA moves to shared memory; each process still needs process-private PGA memory. The entire PGA does not become part of the SGA.

Option B confuses an aggregate instance/PDB safeguard with a per-session limit. `PGA_AGGREGATE_LIMIT` governs aggregate PGA usage, with documented enforcement and exemptions. A single session does not receive that entire value as its personal guaranteed or absolute allocation.

For diagnosis, inspect aggregate work-area demand separately from session memory:
```sql
SELECT name, value FROM v$pgastat
WHERE name IN ('total PGA allocated','over allocation count');
```
Increasing an aggregate target is useful only after checking concurrent workload, available physical RAM and temporary I/O pressure.

sources.title: PGA, UGA, shared server and aggregate PGA management

keywords: private SQL area (UGA) is located in the System Global Area (SGA) when using shared servers
mnemonic.anchor: sorts and hash joins use SQL work areas managed as PGA memory.

text: Which two are true about creating RMAN backups for an Oracle container database? (Choose two.)

options.text: Online Redo Log backups can be created while connected to the root container.
Control file backups can be created while connected to the root container.
The BACKUP TABLESPACE command can back up a PDB tablespace even if RMAN is connected to CDB$ROOT.
Archived Redo Log backups can be created while connected to an application root CDB.
Control file backups can be created while connected to a nonroot container.

explanation:
Option B is correct. The control file belongs to the entire CDB, and an RMAN target connection to `CDB$ROOT` can back it up. It contains shared physical database metadata rather than a separate control file for every PDB.

Option C is correct. A root connection can select a PDB tablespace by qualifying its name with the PDB name. The connection scope and the backup selection are separate: connecting to the root does not force every backup to contain the whole CDB.

Option A is incorrect because RMAN does not back up online redo log members using its ordinary backup commands. Protect online redo with multiplexing and an appropriate storage design; archive the redo and back up archived logs for media recovery.

Option D is incorrect. An application root is still a PDB-level container, not `CDB$ROOT`. Archived redo logs cover the CDB and are backed up through the CDB-root target connection. Calling an application root an application-root CDB does not confer physical-CDB privileges.

Option E is incorrect. A direct nonroot PDB target connection cannot back up the CDB control file. Use the root for such CDB-wide operations.

For example, from an appropriately privileged root RMAN connection:
```text
BACKUP CURRENT CONTROLFILE;
BACKUP TABLESPACE salespdb:users;
```
The second command selects only that PDB's `USERS` tablespace. Confirm the actual tablespace and PDB names and ensure the backup strategy also captures required archived redo; a tablespace backup alone is not a complete recovery strategy.

sources.title: RMAN CDB/PDB target connection scope and tablespace backups

keywords: Control file backups can be created while connected to the root container
mnemonic.anchor: The control file belongs to the entire CDB, and an RMAN target connection to `CDB$ROOT` can back it up.

text: Which three are true about Automatic Workload Repository (AWR) snapshots? (Choose three.)

options.text: They are generated if STATISTICS_LEVEL is set to TYPICAL.
They are generated if STATISTICS_LEVEL is set to ALL.
They are always created automatically.
They are always created manually.
They can be retained forever.
They are generated if STATISTICS_LEVEL is set to BASIC.

explanation:
Option A and Option B are correct for ordinary automatic snapshot collection: `STATISTICS_LEVEL=TYPICAL` or `ALL` enables the statistics needed by AWR. `ALL` gathers additional statistics; it is not a prerequisite for the basic AWR repository. The normal default is `TYPICAL`.

Option E is correct. AWR retention can be configured as unlimited. This is a retention setting, not a statement that an ordinary default repository keeps all snapshots forever. Explicit baselines can also protect selected snapshots beyond normal retention. Unlimited retention requires a realistic SYSAUX capacity plan.

Option C is incorrect because manual snapshots are supported. Option D is incorrect because scheduled automatic snapshots are supported. Neither exclusive description covers both methods.

Option F is incorrect as a claim about normal automatic collection: `BASIC` disables the self-managing statistics required by the automatic AWR workflow. Oracle permits manual snapshot creation with BASIC, but the resulting data can be incomplete. That exception should not be confused with enabling the ordinary automated collection mechanism.

A practical investigation can bracket a representative workload with manual snapshots:
```sql
EXEC DBMS_WORKLOAD_REPOSITORY.CREATE_SNAPSHOT;
-- Run the representative workload.
EXEC DBMS_WORKLOAD_REPOSITORY.CREATE_SNAPSHOT;
```
Compare an interval that actually contains the problem, rather than an arbitrary whole-day average. Query `DBA_HIST_WR_CONTROL` to inspect configured interval and retention, and account for the required Oracle management-pack entitlement before using licensed diagnostic features. Changing retention does not repair a collection gap that has already occurred.

sources.title: AWR collection levels, snapshots, retention and baselines

mnemonic.anchor: Option A and Option B are correct for ordinary automatic snapshot collection: `STATISTICS_LEVEL=TYPICAL` or `ALL` enables the statistics needed by AWR.

text:
You must transport the UNIVERSITY tablespace from one database to another. The UNIVERSITY tablespace is currently open read/write. The source and destination platforms have different endian formats.

Examine this list of actions:

1. Make the UNIVERSITY tablespace read-only on the source system.
2. Export the UNIVERSITY tablespace metadata using EXPDP.
3. Convert the UNIVERSITY tablespace data files to the destination platform format using RMAN on the source system.
4. Copy the UNIVERSITY tablespace data files to the destination system.
5. Copy the Data Pump dump set to the destination system.
6. Convert the UNIVERSITY tablespace data files to the destination platform format using RMAN on the destination system.
7. Import the UNIVERSITY tablespace metadata using IMPDP.
8. Make the UNIVERSITY tablespace read/write on the destination system.

Which is the minimum number of actions required, in the correct order, to transport the UNIVERSITY tablespace?
explanation:
Option C gives the required minimum sequence: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8. This is the conventional transportable-tablespace workflow using Data Pump metadata and physical tablespace datafiles, with endian conversion performed on the source.

First make the source tablespace read-only so its contents remain stable. Export its metadata, convert the physical datafiles to the destination format with RMAN, and transfer both the converted files and the Data Pump dump set. Import the metadata on the destination, specifying the transported files, then make the destination tablespace read/write. Conversion is required because the source and destination endian formats differ.

Option A omits conversion. Its metadata export/import steps are present, but they do not convert physical data blocks. Option B performs destination-side conversion, which is a valid general approach, but its particular sequence omits copying the metadata dump set, step 5. Option D converts on both systems; one appropriate conversion is enough, so that sequence is not minimal. Option E omits the initial read-only transition and the final requested read/write state, so it is not the complete listed workflow.

Before any transfer, validate self-containment:
```sql
EXEC DBMS_TTS.TRANSPORT_SET_CHECK('UNIVERSITY',TRUE);
SELECT * FROM transport_set_violations;
```
Resolve dependencies on objects outside the transport set and verify destination compatibility. Data Pump metadata and physical files serve different purposes: a dump file alone is not the tablespace data, and copied datafiles alone do not register its objects in the destination dictionary.

text: Which three are true about using Database Resource Manager in an Oracle multitenant environment? (Choose three.)

options.text: A PDB-level resource plan can limit session PGA memory.
A CDB-level resource plan can limit PDB CPU utilization.
A CDB-level resource plan can limit session CPU utilization.
PDB-level resource plans can limit uncommitted UNDO per consumer group.
A CDB-level resource plan can limit PDB UNDO use.
A CDB-level resource plan is mandatory when using PDB-level resource plans.

explanation:
Option A is correct. A PDB resource plan manages workload inside the PDB, including a per-session PGA limit through its consumer-group directives. That control is distinct from an aggregate PDB initialization-parameter limit.

Option B is correct. A CDB resource plan allocates resources between PDBs and can cap a PDB's CPU utilization. Shares distribute resources when tenants compete; a utilization limit is a ceiling, not a guarantee that an idle PDB consumes that percentage.

Option D is correct. Within a PDB, a consumer-group directive can limit uncommitted undo consumption using the applicable undo-pool control. This protects against a workload retaining excessive transactional undo before commit or rollback.

Option C confuses scopes: a CDB plan manages PDB-level CPU competition, while session/consumer-group policies belong inside a PDB. Option E similarly attributes a PDB-wide undo control to the wrong plan level. Do not infer such a control merely because CDB resource plans include other tenant-level limits. Option F is incorrect: a PDB-level plan does not universally require an active CDB-level plan; the two layers have different responsibilities.

For example, protect an interactive tenant from a reporting tenant with CDB shares and CPU ceilings, then separate interactive and batch consumers inside the reporting PDB. Inspect the active plan from the appropriate container:
```sql
SELECT name, is_top_plan FROM v$rsrc_plan;
```
Test the plan under real contention. A quiet development system may never activate the scheduling behavior that matters when several PDBs simultaneously demand CPU or undo resources.

sources.title: CDB and PDB Resource Manager scopes

mnemonic.anchor: A PDB resource plan manages workload inside the PDB, including a per-session PGA limit through its consumer-group directives.

text: How do you configure a CDB for local undo mode?

options.text: Open the CDB instance in upgrade mode. In CDB$ROOT, execute ALTER DATABASE LOCAL UNDO ON, and then restart the CDB instance.
Open the CDB instance in restricted mode. In CDB$ROOT, execute ALTER DATABASE LOCAL UNDO ON, and create an UNDO tablespace in each PDB, then restart the CDB instance.
Open the CDB instance in restricted mode. In CDB$ROOT, drop the UNDO tablespace. Execute ALTER DATABASE LOCAL UNDO ON in each PDB, and then restart the CDB instance.
Open the CDB instance in read-only mode. In CDB$ROOT, execute ALTER DATABASE LOCAL UNDO ON, and then change the CDB to read/write mode.
Open the CDB instance in upgrade mode. In each PDB, execute ALTER DATABASE LOCAL UNDO ON, create an UNDO tablespace, and then restart the CDB instance.

text: Which three are true about using an RMAN Recovery Catalog with a pluggable database (PDB) target connection in Oracle Database 19c and later releases? (Choose three.)

options.text: The base catalog owner must give the Virtual Private Catalog access to metadata for one or more PDBs.
The base catalog must be enabled for Virtual Private Catalog use.
The target PDB must be registered in a base catalog.
The base catalog must be used by RMAN when performing point-in-time recovery for the PDB registered in the Virtual Private Catalog.
The target PDB must be registered in a Virtual Private Catalog.
The target PDB must be registered in both the base catalog and the Virtual Private Catalog.

explanation:
Option A and Option B describe the delegation model. A virtual private catalog is a restricted view of recovery metadata held in a base recovery catalog. The base owner enables the required virtual-catalog/VPD infrastructure and grants the virtual owner access to the appropriate PDB metadata. A tenant does not acquire unrestricted catalog ownership merely by connecting to its PDB.

Option C is the intended answer if registered means that the target's recovery metadata is present in the base catalog, normally through the registered CDB and catalog synchronization. Its wording is imprecise: do not invent a separate `REGISTER PDB` command. RMAN database registration, catalog ownership and PDB metadata visibility are separate concepts.

Option D is incorrect. The purpose of granting a virtual catalog access is to let the delegated administrator perform supported operations using that catalog; there is no universal requirement to switch to the base owner's credentials for every PDB point-in-time recovery.

Option E and Option F incorrectly describe the virtual catalog as an independent second repository requiring duplicate PDB registration. Delegation filters metadata in the base repository; it does not make two physical copies with two independent PDB registrations.

A typical base-owner delegation includes:
```text
GRANT CATALOG FOR PLUGGABLE DATABASE salespdb TO sales_backup;
```
Use the exact syntax and privileges appropriate to the registered CDB and catalog version. Then test the virtual owner with `LIST BACKUP` against its PDB and verify that unrelated PDB metadata remains inaccessible. The provisional key preserves the intended architecture while explicitly qualifying the loose registration terminology.

sources.title: Recovery catalogs, virtual private catalogs and PDB metadata access
Granting virtual catalog access for a PDB

review_note: C is retained as intended base-catalog metadata registration, not a separate REGISTER PDB command; VPC is a metadata visibility layer, not a second physical registration.

keywords: target PDB must be registered in a base catalog
mnemonic.anchor: Option A and Option B describe the delegation model.

text: Which three activities are possible for PDBs? (Choose three.)

options.text: converting an application PDB to a regular PDB
converting an application PDB to an application root
converting an application seed to an application PDB
converting an application PDB to an application seed
converting a regular PDB to an application PDB
converting an application container into another application container in a different CDB
converting an application container into another application container in the same CDB

explanation:
The intended key is Option B, Option C and Option E, but the word converting is insufficiently precise to establish a unique three-choice answer. Oracle documents several creation, cloning, unplugging and plugging workflows; these are not all in-place changes of a PDB's role.

Option B can describe creating an application root from an existing PDB through an appropriate creation/plugging workflow. Option C is supported by unplugging an application seed and using it to create an application PDB. Option E describes integrating a regular PDB into an application container, including the required conversion script and synchronization considerations.

Option A should not be understood as an unrestricted inverse operation: application-common object dependencies and metadata ownership prevent treating an application PDB as an arbitrary independent regular PDB without a migration design. However, that does not prohibit every possible data migration into a regular PDB.

Option D is problematic as a distractor because Oracle explicitly supports creating an application seed by cloning an application PDB. If converting includes cloning, as other choices implicitly do, D cannot simply be labelled impossible. Option F and Option G similarly blur moving/recreating an application root/container with changing an individual PDB role. Moving a root requires handling its seed and member PDB relationships; it is not a one-command conversion of the entire hierarchy.

For a real operation, inventory the roles first:
```sql
SELECT pdb_name, application_root, application_pdb, application_seed
FROM dba_pdbs;
```
Choose a documented workflow for the exact source and destination roles. The retained key is provisional; the original broad wording needs clarification before it can serve as an unambiguous scored question.

sources.title: Application root/seed creation and cloning an application PDB into a seed
Regular PDB integration and application-container administration

review_note: The stem mixes in-place conversion with cloning/plugging. D is also supportable as creating a seed by cloning an application PDB; BCE is retained only as the intended provisional key.

mnemonic.anchor: The intended key is Option B, Option C and Option E, but the word converting is insufficiently precise to establish a unique three-choice answer.

text: Which three are true about actions that can or cannot be performed by users with the SYSBACKUP privilege? (Choose three.)

options.text: They can view data from any data dictionary view or dynamic performance view.
They cannot create restore points.
They cannot drop tablespaces.
They can create any table.
They can drop any tablespace.
They can view data from any user-defined tables.

explanation:
Option A, Option D and Option E match Oracle's documented `SYSBACKUP` administrative privilege set. It includes dictionary/fixed-view access, `CREATE ANY TABLE`, and `DROP TABLESPACE`. The last two capabilities are powerful recovery-administration operations; SYSBACKUP is not a read-only monitoring privilege.

Option B is incorrect because the privilege permits creating restore points, including the supported guaranteed restore-point operation. Option C is the inverse of a documented privilege: dropping a tablespace is permitted. Option F is incorrect because SYSBACKUP does not grant arbitrary access to the contents of every user-defined application table. Metadata visibility and recovery capability are different from general business-data query authority.

Distinguish the administrative privilege from a username or an ordinary role. A connection using `AS SYSBACKUP` enters the backup-administration security context. An account could separately have additional privileges when connected normally, but those extra grants do not define the SYSBACKUP privilege itself. Equally, the ability to back up physical files does not turn a backup-administration SQL session into an unrestricted application reader.

For example, connect RMAN using a designated backup administrator:
```text
rman target 'backup_admin@cdb_service AS SYSBACKUP'
```
Use the appropriate password file or operating-system authentication configuration, and verify container scope before CDB/PDB operations. Grant application SELECT privileges separately only when that account actually needs them. Also distinguish `DROP TABLESPACE`, which is in this administrative privilege set, from an invented blanket `DROP ANY TABLE` entitlement. Precise privilege names matter when evaluating these options and designing least-privilege operational accounts.

sources.title: SYSBACKUP administrative privilege capabilities and separation of duties

mnemonic.anchor: Option A, Option D and Option E match Oracle's documented `SYSBACKUP` administrative privilege set.

text: Which three are true about RMAN archival backups with the RESTORE POINT clause? (Choose three.)

options.text: All archive logs are retained after an archival backup is taken, until the next archival backup is taken of the same database.
The SPFILE is included in the archival backup.
They are never considered obsolete by RMAN.
Archive logs are retained if they are necessary to allow the database to be recovered to a consistent state when an archival backup is restored.
The ARCHIVAL attribute for a backup overrides the RMAN retention policy.
They can optionally be written to a fast recovery area (FRA).
Use of a recovery catalog is always required to support the creation and use of archival backups.

explanation:
Option B is correct: an archival `BACKUP ... KEEP` operation includes the SPFILE when the database is using one, together with the other files needed for the self-contained archival recovery goal. Option D is correct: the required archived redo is retained so that restoring the archival backup can recover it to a consistent state associated with the operation. This is a bounded recovery requirement, not indefinite retention of every subsequent log.

Option E is correct. The KEEP attribute exempts that archival backup from the ordinary configured retention policy for its specified KEEP lifetime. `KEEP UNTIL TIME` has an expiration; `KEEP FOREVER` is the indefinite variant.

Option A is incorrect because it invents a dependency on the next archival backup and retains far more logs than the documented consistency requirement. Option C is incorrect because a finite KEEP period eventually expires. Option F is incorrect: KEEP backups cannot be written into the fast recovery area. An explicit long-term destination outside that managed recovery area is required. Option G is incorrect because a recovery catalog is required for `KEEP FOREVER`, not for every finite KEEP backup.

For example, an archival backup to an external disk destination can use:
```text
BACKUP DATABASE FORMAT '/archive/annual_%U'
  KEEP UNTIL TIME 'SYSDATE+365' RESTORE POINT annual_archive;
```
The restore point names the recovery target; it does not replace the physical backup files. Preserve the associated metadata and encryption credentials, and test restore/recovery rather than assuming a KEEP label guarantees that an old storage device will remain readable.

sources.title: Archival KEEP backups and restore points
KEEP restrictions, retention and required archived redo

mnemonic.anchor: KEEP` operation includes the SPFILE when the database is using one, together with the other files needed for the self-contained archival recovery goal.

text:
Your container database, CDB1, is in local undo mode.

You successfully execute this command while connected to CDB1:

```text
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 -
ADMIN USER pdb1_admin IDENTIFIED BY pdb123 ROLES=(CONNECT)
CREATE_FILE_DEST='/u01/app/oracle/oradata/cdb1/pdb1';
```

Which three are true about PDB1? (Choose three.)

options.text: Service PDB1 is created for remote logins to PDB1.
It is in mount state after creation.
It has no local users.
It has the same number of roles as CDB1.
It has the same common users defined as does CDB1.
It has only local roles.

explanation:
Option A is correct: creation of a PDB also creates its default service with the PDB name. Service existence does not mean clients can immediately use a closed PDB. The listener must know an active service and the PDB must be open in an appropriate mode.

Option B is correct. A newly created PDB is initially mounted; the statement shown does not contain a separate open operation. Local undo mode does not cause all newly created PDBs to open automatically.

Option E is correct. CDB-common users defined in the root are represented in the PDB. Their presence should not be confused with whether a particular common user has a usable login privilege in that PDB.

Option C is false because `ADMIN USER pdb1_admin` explicitly creates a local administrator. Option D is false because common and local role definitions have container-specific scope; there is no guarantee of equal total role counts between root and PDB. Option F is false because common roles coexist with local roles.

A practical post-creation sequence is:
```sql
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 OPEN;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 SAVE STATE;
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs WHERE name='PDB1';
```
Inspect the default service and, for managed applications, configure suitable user-defined services through the relevant management tool. The displayed trailing hyphen is a SQL*Plus line-continuation convention, not part of the SQL grammar to send unchanged through every client. This question assumes the statement has completed successfully, as stated; password-policy and file-placement checks therefore do not alter the answer.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 and CDB2 are two container databases.
2. PDB1 is a pluggable database in CDB1.
3. PDB1_C1_SRV is a service for PDB1.
4. CDB1_LINK is a database link in CDB2 referring to PDB1.
5. CDB2 is also an entry in tnsnames.ora pointing to the CDB2 database default service.

You execute these commands successfully:

```text
$ sqlplus sys/oracle_4U@cdb2 as sysdba

SQL> CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB1 FROM PDB1@CDB1_LINK -
     SERVICE_NAME_CONVERT=('PDB1_C1_SRV','PDB1_C2_SRV');
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: PDB1 will be created in CDB2 and automatically opened.
PDB1 will be created in CDB2 and left in MOUNT state.
PDB1_C1_SRV in CDB1 will be renamed PDB1_C2_SRV.
PDB1_C2_SRV will be created and started automatically.
PDB1_C2_SRV will be created but not started.

explanation:
Option B is correct: the destination PDB is created in mounted state. `CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE ... FROM ...` creates the clone; opening it is a subsequent administrative operation. A successful remote clone is not the same as an automatically opened application environment.

Option E is correct. `SERVICE_NAME_CONVERT` maps the source user-defined service name into a new destination service definition. The mapped service is not started by the creation statement while the new PDB remains mounted.

Option A incorrectly combines creation with automatic opening. Option C is incorrect because the source service in CDB1 is unchanged; the conversion applies to the service metadata of the clone in CDB2. Option D confuses defining the destination service with activating it. Do not infer that service creation has also opened a PDB or enabled client traffic.

For example, after checking clone compatibility and any plug-in violations, open the destination:
```sql
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 OPEN;
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs WHERE name='PDB1';
```
Then verify service activation using the appropriate service manager and listener registration. In Oracle Restart/RAC environments, manage application services with SRVCTL as appropriate.

The database link in the stem refers to the source PDB. Generic SQL remote cloning supports suitable root or PDB service endpoints subject to the documented privileges and source-container restrictions; do not impose the separate DBCA-specific workflow on this SQL example. In 19c, hot cloning can also be supported when the required local-undo/ARCHIVELOG conditions are met, so a blanket claim that every source must always be opened read-only would be misleading.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. COMMON_USER_PREFIX is set to an empty string.
3. PDB1 is a pluggable database in CDB1.
4. APP1_ROOT is an application container in CDB1.
5. APP1_PDB1 is an application PDB in APP1_ROOT.

You execute these commands:

```text
$ sqlplus sys/oracle@localhost:1521/cdb1 as sysdba

SQL> CREATE ROLE role1 CONTAINER=CURRENT;
```

What is true?

options.text: It will return an error because creation of a local role is not allowed in CDB$ROOT.
ROLE1 will be created only in CDB$ROOT and APP1_ROOT.
ROLE1 will be created in CDB$ROOT, PDB1, APP1_ROOT, and APP1_PDB1.
ROLE1 will be created only in CDB$ROOT.
It will return an error because common roles must start with C##.

explanation:
Option A is correct. The connection shown is to the CDB default service and therefore to `CDB$ROOT`. `CONTAINER=CURRENT` requests a local role, and Oracle does not permit creating a local role in the CDB root. The statement fails instead of creating the role in any collection of containers.

Option B and Option D assume local-role creation in the root succeeds, so both are incorrect. Option C describes the broad propagation expected of a CDB-common role, but the command explicitly asks for the current-container local scope rather than the all-container common scope.

Option E identifies the wrong reason for failure. Setting `COMMON_USER_PREFIX` to the empty string removes the default prefix requirement for common user/role names. It does not legalize a local role in the root, and it does not silently change `CONTAINER=CURRENT` into `CONTAINER=ALL`.

The practical diagnostic is to check container scope before changing security metadata:
```sql
SHOW CON_NAME
```
To create a local role for PDB1, connect to PDB1 and create it there. To create a CDB-common role, use the documented root/common-role workflow and the naming policy actually configured for that CDB. Application-common roles have yet another scope, rooted in the application root, and should not be inferred from this CDB-root command.

The key lesson is that naming and scope are independent controls. A name that satisfies the prefix policy can still be invalid for the requested container scope. Changing the prefix to an empty value is not a workaround for the root's local-role restriction.

text: Which statement correctly describes the SQL profiling performed by the SQL Tuning Advisor?

options.text: It is a set of recommendations by the optimizer to create new indexes.
It is a set of recommendations by the optimizer to restructure a SQL statement to avoid suboptimal execution plans.
It is auxiliary information collected by the optimizer for a SQL statement to help use better joins orders.
It is auxiliary information collected by the optimizer for a SQL statement to eliminate estimation error.
It is a set of recommendations by the optimizer to change the access methods used.

explanation:
Option D is the best definition. SQL profiling gathers auxiliary optimizer information for a particular SQL statement to correct estimation errors, especially cardinality and selectivity errors. Better estimates can let the optimizer compare candidate plans more accurately without rewriting the application's SQL text.

Option A describes an index recommendation, a separate category of SQL Tuning Advisor output. Accepting a SQL profile does not itself create that index. Option B describes restructuring SQL; that can be a tuning recommendation, but it is not the definition of a profile. Option E describes an access-method change as an instruction. A profile influences the optimizer through auxiliary information rather than simply ordering a particular access method.

Option C is related but too narrow. Improved estimates may cause a different join order, yet a profile is not defined as a join-order prescription. The optimizer can choose different plans as statistics, bindings, data or environment change; a profile is not the same as a SQL plan baseline that constrains accepted plans.

In practice, inspect the tuning task before accepting a recommendation:
```sql
SELECT DBMS_SQLTUNE.REPORT_TUNING_TASK('sales_tuning_task')
FROM dual;
```
Compare estimated and actual row counts and validate the proposed improvement with representative bind values and production-like data. A profile that helps one atypical bind value may not characterize the full workload. Review the separate index and statistics recommendations independently, and use the applicable management-pack licensing. The option's phrase eliminate estimation error expresses the intended purpose; it should not be read as a guarantee that every future optimizer estimate becomes mathematically exact.

sources.title: SQL profiles as auxiliary optimizer statistics

mnemonic.anchor: Better estimates can let the optimizer compare candidate plans more accurately without rewriting the application's SQL text.

text: Which two are true about OS groups and users for Oracle Grid Infrastructure and the Oracle Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)? (Choose two.)

options.text: By default, members of the OSASM group can access Automatic Storage Management and RDBMS instances.
The primary group for the Oracle Grid Infrastructure and Oracle Database owners must be the Oracle Inventory group.
The Oracle Grid Infrastructure installation must be owned by the grid user.
The Oracle Grid Infrastructure owner owns Oracle Restart and Oracle Automatic Storage Management binaries.
The Oracle Grid Infrastructure owner must have OSOPER, OSBACKUPDBA, and OSKMDBA as secondary groups.
The same OSDBA group must be used for Automatic Storage Management and the Oracle Database.

explanation:
Option B is correct in the documented Oracle installation ownership model. The Grid Infrastructure and database software owners use the Oracle central-inventory group as their primary group. This permits inventory maintenance while supplementary groups control administrative responsibilities.

Option D is correct. The Grid Infrastructure owner owns the Oracle Restart and ASM software binaries in the Grid home. The database owner owns the database home in a separated installation; these are software ownership relationships, not a claim that every process has identical database privileges.

Option A is incorrect. Membership in OSASM authorizes the ASM administrative context, `SYSASM`; it does not automatically authorize SYSDBA administration of an RDBMS instance. Option C confuses a conventional username with a requirement: `grid` is customary, but a properly configured alternative account name is permitted. Option E is incorrect because those optional job-role groups are not all mandatory supplementary groups for the GI owner. Option F is incorrect: the ASM OSDBA group and the database OSDBA group can be different for separation of duties.

A practical verification on Linux is:
```text
id grid
id oracle
```
Compare primary inventory membership and supplementary role groups with the installation plan rather than blindly copying another server's names. Database owners normally need the appropriate ASM access group to access ASM-managed storage, but that does not mean giving them the ASM administrator's group. Finally, changing operating-system group membership may require a new login session before the new group set is effective.

sources.title: Software-owner users and primary inventory group

mnemonic.anchor: in the documented Oracle installation ownership model.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database running in ARCHIVELOG mode.
2. Multiple uncommitted transactions are running in CDB1.
3. Redo log groups 1 and 2 are INACTIVE.
4. Redo log group 3 is the CURRENT group.

All members of redo log group 3 are lost before it is archived.

Examine these possible steps:

1. SHUTDOWN ABORT
2. STARTUP NOMOUNT
3. STARTUP MOUNT
4. ALTER DATABASE MOUNT
5. RESTORE DATABASE
6. RECOVER DATABASE NOREDO
7. RECOVER DATABASE UNTIL AVAILABLE REDO
8. RESTORE ARCHIVELOG ALL
9. ALTER DATABASE OPEN
10. ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS

Choose the minimum required steps in the correct order to recover the database.
explanation:
Option C is the valid sequence: abort the damaged instance, mount it, restore the database, recover using the available redo, and open with RESETLOGS. Losing every member of the current, unarchived redo group removes part of the redo needed for complete recovery. The presence of uncommitted transactions does not make that missing redo recoverable; recovery also needs redo for committed changes and subsequent rollback of unfinished transactions.

The abbreviated step 7 has been repaired to the documented RMAN syntax:
```text
RECOVER DATABASE UNTIL AVAILABLE REDO;
ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;
```
This assumes suitable backups and an available continuous redo chain up to a usable recovery point. Missing earlier archived logs or unsuitable backups can prevent the proposed recovery; the question does not establish unlimited recoverability.

Option A and Option B incorrectly use `NOREDO`. Restoring archived logs and then explicitly suppressing redo application does not implement recovery through those logs. `NOREDO` belongs to specific incremental/no-redo workflows, not this ordinary ARCHIVELOG loss scenario. Option D attempts to restore database files before mounting the control file, so its order is wrong. Option E also uses NOREDO and omits RESETLOGS despite the required incomplete recovery.

RESETLOGS starts a new database incarnation; it does not recreate transactions whose redo has been lost. Expect a recovery-point data-loss boundary and reconcile application transactions accordingly. Multiplexing current redo members across independent failure domains is the preventive control, while validated backups and archived logs provide the recovery path after every current member is gone.

All members of redo log group 3 are lost before it is archived.

2. STARTUP NOMOUNT

4. ALTER DATABASE MOUNT
5. RESTORE DATABASE
6. RECOVER DATABASE NOREDO
7. RECOVER DATABASE UNTIL AVAILABLE
8. RESTORE ARCHIVELOG ALL

text: Which three are true about an application container? (Choose three.)

options.text: It can contain a single application.
It can contain multiple applications.
It must have an application seed PDB.
It must have an application root PDB.
Two application containers can share an application seed PDB.
An application PDB can belong to multiple application containers.

explanation:
Option A and Option B are both correct. An application container can manage one application or several applications. An application is a named collection of common application objects and associated version-management operations; it is not synonymous with the entire application container.

Option D is correct. The application root is the defining parent PDB for an application container and holds application-common metadata and, depending on sharing type, common data. Member application PDBs synchronize installed application versions from that root.

Option C is incorrect because the application seed is optional. It is a provisioning template that can make new application-PDB creation easier; its absence does not prevent the root from defining a valid application container. Option E is incorrect because a seed belongs to its own application container rather than simultaneously being the seed for two independent roots. Option F is incorrect because an application PDB has one application-root parent; installing several applications in that parent does not create multiple container memberships.

To inspect the hierarchy, query from an appropriately privileged root session:
```sql
SELECT pdb_name, application_root, application_pdb, application_seed
FROM dba_pdbs;
```
For example, one application root may install both billing and inventory applications, with separate versions, and expose them to several tenant PDBs. A seed may preconfigure new tenants, but an existing tenant remains a single application PDB under that one root. Distinguish the number of applications, the number of PDBs, and the number of application containers when planning upgrades and synchronization.

sources.title: Application roots, PDBs and optional seeds

mnemonic.anchor: Option A and Option B are both correct.

text: Which two are true about the FLASHBACK DATABASE feature? (Choose two.)

options.text: FLASHBACK LOGS are archived after a log switch.
A database can be flashed back using SQL*PLUS.
Queries and DML have the same FLASHBACK LOG overhead when flashback is enabled for a database.
FLASHBACK DATABASE only uses FLASHBACK LOGS to get the database to the desired flashback time.
It always generates REDO and UNDO.
It requires that the target database be in ARCHIVELOG mode.

explanation:
Option B is correct: SQL*Plus can execute the SQL `FLASHBACK DATABASE` statement. RMAN provides another interface, but it is not the only way to invoke the feature. Option F is correct: the target must operate in ARCHIVELOG mode, with the applicable flashback logging, recovery-area and recoverability prerequisites satisfied.

Option A is incorrect because flashback logs are managed in the fast recovery area and are not archived redo logs. An online redo log switch does not archive a flashback log. Option C is incorrect because a read-only query and a block-changing DML workload do not impose identical flashback-log work.

Option D is incorrect: Flashback Database uses older block images from flashback logs and redo to reach the requested point consistently. Option E is also incorrect. Physical database rewind is not implemented as inverse SQL DML that always generates corresponding redo and undo. That description confuses database flashback with undo-based logical features such as Flashback Table.

There are therefore only two unequivocally true choices, and the original choose-three count has been corrected. A normal maintenance sequence includes mounting the database, validating the available flashback range, rewinding, and opening with RESETLOGS when committing the rewind:
```sql
FLASHBACK DATABASE TO RESTORE POINT before_change;
ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;
```
The restore point must be usable for that database and operation. Flashback Database depends on intact datafiles; it is not a substitute for restoring lost files. The retention target is also a goal rather than an unconditional promise that every timestamp remains recoverable under all storage-pressure conditions.
original_text: Which three are true about the FLASHBACK DATABASE feature? (Choose three.)

sources.title: Physical Flashback Database mechanisms and prerequisites

review_note: The original choose-three item has only B/F supported. E confuses physical database rewind with undo-based table operations; count corrected to two.

text: Which three are true about patchsets? (Choose three.)

options.text: They can be applied in a rolling fashion for Clusterware and the databases.
They can introduce new features.
They are installed via OPatch or OPatchAuto.
Installing a patchset is considered an 'upgrade'.
They are only released quarterly.
A base release is not needed to install patchsets.

explanation:
Option B, Option D and Option F describe historical database patch sets. This terminology must be separated from Oracle 19c Release Updates and interim patches; the current 19c maintenance model does not introduce a new traditional database patch-set release.

Option B is correct because historical patch sets could introduce features in addition to fixes. Option D is correct because moving an existing database to the patch-set release could require upgrading its dictionary/components, not merely replacing one binary. Option F is correct for the full-install patch-set distribution model used by later 11g Release 2 patch sets: it could install a new Oracle home without first installing the original base release.

Option A is incorrect as a combined unconditional statement about Clusterware and databases. Rolling support depends on the product and operation; a rolling Clusterware upgrade does not establish that a database patch-set upgrade is universally rolling. Option C confuses traditional database patch sets, installed through the product installer, with patches applied to an existing home using OPatch/OPatchAuto. Option E confuses patch sets with a quarterly patch-delivery schedule; historical patch sets were not exclusively quarterly releases.

For a real 19c environment, inspect the installed patch inventory rather than applying this historical terminology indiscriminately:
```text
opatch lsinventory
```
Read the exact patch readme for rolling eligibility, required tools and post-patch SQL processing. An RU, a one-off patch, a historical patch set and a major-release upgrade are different servicing operations, even when administrators casually refer to all of them as patching.

sources.title: 19c Release Updates versus historical patch sets
Patch sets, updates and servicing terminology

review_note: Historical full-install patch-set terminology is retained. Key corrected from ACF to BDF; current 19c RUs must not be confused with traditional patch sets.

text: Which two are true about backup set compression using RMAN default compression? (Choose two.)

options.text: Compressed backups can be written only to media.
Binary compression adds CPU overhead to backup operations.
Unused blocks below the high water mark are backed up.
Compressed backups cannot have a section size defined.
Compression can be done only for locally managed tablespaces.

explanation:
Option B is correct: binary compression trades additional CPU work for reduced backup output. Whether elapsed time improves depends on the relative costs of CPU, storage and network transfer. A smaller backup is not automatically a faster backup on a CPU-saturated server.

Option E is the intended answer only for the default unused-block compression mechanism. RMAN can omit blocks never used and, when the documented conditions hold, blocks below the high-water mark that no longer contain data. The locally managed tablespace restriction applies to unused-block compression, not to every possible use of binary compression. The question mixes these two meanings of compression and should be read with that distinction explicit.

Option A is incorrect because compressed backup sets can be written to disk or an SBT media manager. Option C is incorrect under the qualifying unused-block-compression conditions: unused blocks below the high-water mark can be omitted rather than always backed up. Option D is incorrect because compressed backup sets can use multisection backups; `SECTION SIZE` and binary compression solve different problems.

For example, explicitly request binary compression in a representative backup:
```text
BACKUP AS COMPRESSED BACKUPSET DATABASE;
```
Compare CPU utilization, bytes written and total elapsed time with an uncompressed backup under comparable workload. Then perform a restore test to measure decompression overhead and actual recovery throughput. Do not assume that the default omission of unused blocks is the same as explicitly requesting compressed backup sets, or extend a restriction on one mechanism to the other.

sources.title: Unused-block compression versus binary backup-set compression

review_note: BE retained for intended distinction: E applies to unused-block compression only, not a universal restriction on binary compression. Stem mixes the mechanisms.

mnemonic.anchor: binary compression trades additional CPU work for reduced backup output.

text: Which statement is true about memory advisors? (Choose one.)

options.text: If Automatic Shared Memory Management is enabled, both the SGA Advisor and PGA Advisor are always available.
If Automatic Memory Management is enabled, no memory advisors are available.
All memory advisors use data from Automatic Workload Repository.
If Manual Shared Memory Management is enabled, only the Shared Pool Advisor and Buffer Cache Advisor are available.
If Automatic Memory Management is enabled, the Shared Pool Advisor and Buffer Cache Advisor are available to set the maximum size for these individual System Global Area components.

explanation:
Option A is the supported intended statement for an ordinarily configured ASMM instance with automatic PGA management and the required statistics collection. SGA and PGA advice remains available for sizing their respective memory areas. The word always should be understood within those documented operating prerequisites; disabled statistics collection can undermine advisory output.

Option B is incorrect: Automatic Memory Management has a Memory Advisor that estimates the effect of changing the total memory target. Automatic control does not eliminate the need for sizing guidance.

Option C is too absolute. Memory-advisor data can appear in AWR reports, but that does not prove that every memory advisor requires AWR snapshots as its input. Oracle specifically describes background workload simulation for PGA advice, exposed through `V$PGA_TARGET_ADVICE`, with automatic PGA management and statistics-level prerequisites. In-memory simulation and AWR historical storage are different mechanisms.

Option D is incorrect because manual SGA management does not eliminate PGA advice when automatic PGA management is enabled. Option E is incorrect because ASMM/AMM component sizing and advisory estimates do not provide the claimed individual maximum-setting function; component parameters can establish minima in the applicable management mode rather than that proposed maximum policy.

Inspect advice directly:
```sql
SELECT pga_target_for_estimate, estd_pga_cache_hit_percentage,
       estd_overalloc_count
FROM v$pga_target_advice;
```
Use a representative workload and assess physical RAM before changing targets. The original choose-two count has been corrected to one; C's universal AWR claim is unsupported. This repaired item still assumes the normal statistics and automatic-PGA prerequisites for A, rather than treating always as overriding deliberately disabled advisor collection.
original_text: Which two are true about memory advisors? (Choose two.)

PGA advice workload simulation and prerequisites

text:
PDB1 and PDB2 are pluggable databases in CDB1.

Examine these commands:

```text
$ export ORACLE_SID=CDB1
$ sqlplus / as sysdba
Database opened.

SQL> SHOW PDBS

CON_ID CON_NAME  OPEN MODE  RESTRICTED
------ --------- ---------- ----------
     2 PDB$SEED  READ ONLY  NO
     3 PDB1      MOUNTED    
     4 PDB2      MOUNTED    

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 OPEN;
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 SAVE STATE;
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 CLOSE;
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb2 OPEN;
Pluggable database altered.
```

CDB1 is then restarted.

Which three are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: PDB2 will be MOUNTED.
PDB1 will be MOUNTED.
PDB$SEED will be opened READ ONLY.
PDB2 will be opened READ WRITE.
PDB1 will be opened READ WRITE.
PDB$SEED will be MOUNTED.

explanation:
Option E is correct: PDB1 was open read/write when `SAVE STATE` recorded its desired startup mode. The later CLOSE changes its current state, but does not discard that stored startup instruction. After a normal CDB restart it reopens read/write using the saved state.

Option A is correct: PDB2 was opened but its state was never saved. Merely being open immediately before shutdown does not instruct Oracle to reopen it after the next CDB startup, so it remains mounted. Option C is correct: the seed normally opens read-only as the provisioning template.

Option B is incorrect because it treats PDB1's final current state as if it had overwritten its saved state. Option D is incorrect because it assumes PDB2's last open state is automatically persisted. Option F is incorrect because it ignores the normal read-only seed state.

Verify the persistent configuration separately from the current open mode:
```sql
SELECT con_name, instance_name, state, restricted
FROM dba_pdb_saved_states;
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs;
```
If the intention is to stop PDB1 from reopening automatically, explicitly discard its saved state; closing it once is not the same operation. In RAC, saved states are instance-sensitive, so check the desired instance scope as well. The example is a normal CDB restart, not an upgrade or special recovery startup. Those special modes can change which PDBs open and should not be inferred from the ordinary startup behavior tested here.

sources.title: Saving and discarding PDB open state across CDB restart

mnemonic.anchor: PDB1 was open read/write when `SAVE STATE` recorded its desired startup mode.

text: Which four are true about Automatic Workload Repository (AWR) and Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM) in an Oracle multitenant environment? (Choose four.)

options.text: ADDM can run in a nonroot container.
AWR snapshots can be created in CDB$ROOT.
AWR reports can be generated while connected to any container.
All AWR data is stored in the CDB$ROOT SYSAUX tablespace.
AWR snapshots can be created in a PDB.
No AWR data is stored in the CDB$ROOT SYSAUX tablespace.

explanation:
Option A is correct for Oracle 19c: ADDM supports analysis in a PDB/nonroot container, subject to the appropriate diagnostic prerequisites and data collection. Older descriptions of ADDM as exclusively CDB-root analysis should not be carried forward as an unconditional 19c restriction.

Option B and Option E are correct: AWR snapshots can be created at CDB root and locally in a PDB. These are distinct repositories/scopes, and local PDB collection must be configured appropriately. PDB automatic snapshots are not simply guaranteed by the existence of root snapshots.

Option C is also correct as a statement of supported report-generation scope. Oracle's 19c multitenant administration documentation explicitly supports AWR reports in the root or any PDB. Normal prerequisites still apply: an appropriate user, available snapshots and the intended container's data. The ability to generate a report from a PDB does not grant visibility into every other PDB's local repository.

Option D is incorrect because PDB-local AWR data can reside in that PDB's SYSAUX rather than all AWR data being stored exclusively in root. Option F is the opposite false extreme: root also stores AWR data in its own SYSAUX.

Inspect local settings in the container being diagnosed:
```sql
SHOW PARAMETER awr_pdb_autoflush_enabled
SELECT snap_interval, retention FROM dba_hist_wr_control;
```
Collect a representative interval before running diagnostics and interpret root-wide resource pressure alongside local PDB activity. The original choose-three count has been repaired to four because C is an additional documented capability, not a false distractor. Diagnostic feature licensing and collection configuration remain prerequisites to actual use.
original_text: Which three are true about Automatic Workload Repository (AWR) and Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM) in an Oracle multitenant environment? (Choose three.)
