Oracle19c PDB ADDM and local AWR prerequisites

mnemonic.anchor: for Oracle 19c: ADDM supports analysis in a PDB/nonroot container, subject to the appropriate diagnostic prerequisites and data collection.

text: Which two are true about Optimizer Statistics? (Choose two.)

options.text: They can be gathered by the DBMS_STATS package.
They are gathered by the SQL Tuning Advisor.
They provide real-time data about schema objects.
They are ignored by Optimizer if they are stale.
By default, they are automatically gathered by a maintenance job.

explanation:
Option A is correct: `DBMS_STATS` is the supported package for gathering, exporting, importing, locking and managing optimizer object statistics. These statistics describe properties such as table row counts, column distributions and index characteristics used during cost-based optimization.

Option E is correct in the standard default configuration: an automatic maintenance task gathers missing or stale optimizer statistics during maintenance windows. Administrators can change or disable that policy, so default does not mean an unavoidable behavior in every configured database.

Option B is not the normal object-statistics collection mechanism described here. SQL Tuning Advisor can detect missing/stale statistics and recommend gathering them; its tuning analysis can also collect auxiliary information for SQL profiling. That is different from saying it is the regular provider of stored schema-object statistics instead of DBMS_STATS/the maintenance task.

Option C is incorrect as a general description: ordinary object statistics are a sampled or computed statistical picture, not a continuously exact live representation. Specific 19c real-time statistics features do not transform every optimizer statistic into real-time data. Option D is incorrect: stale statistics can still be used; stale status helps identify candidates for refresh rather than instructing the optimizer to ignore them completely.

For example, after a major controlled load:
```sql
EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS('SALES','ORDERS',CASCADE=>TRUE);
```
Choose appropriate sampling, histogram and partition preferences rather than gathering indiscriminately. Compare estimated versus actual rows before concluding that poor execution comes from stale statistics; bind selectivity, correlations and transformation choices can also matter even with recently gathered statistics.

sources.title: DBMS_STATS and automatic optimizer statistics collection

mnemonic.anchor: `DBMS_STATS` is the supported package for gathering, exporting, importing, locking and managing optimizer object statistics.

text: Which three resources are always shared among CDB$ROOT and pluggable databases (PDBs)? (Choose three.)

options.text: the data dictionary in CDB$ROOT
temporary tablespaces
the Process Monitor Process (PMON)
SYSAUX tablespaces
the log writer process (LGWR)
undo tablespaces

explanation:
Option A is correct for the common Oracle-supplied dictionary metadata housed in `CDB$ROOT`. PDBs use multitenant metadata-sharing mechanisms instead of each holding a fully independent copy of every Oracle dictionary definition. This does not mean all application-object dictionary information for every tenant is visible as one unrestricted shared dictionary.

Option C and Option E are correct because PMON and LGWR are instance background processes. PDBs share the CDB instance infrastructure rather than starting their own independent PMON and LGWR for every PDB. Sessions retain container identity even while using these common processes.

Option B is incorrect because PDBs can have their own temporary tablespaces; a single temporary tablespace is not always shared between every container. Option D is incorrect because each PDB has its own SYSAUX storage; root SYSAUX does not replace every PDB's auxiliary tablespace. Option F is incorrect because local undo mode gives PDBs their own undo arrangements. Shared undo mode exists, but the word always makes the universal claim false.

For example, identify container-specific tablespaces from root:
```sql
SELECT con_id, tablespace_name, contents
FROM cdb_tablespaces
ORDER BY con_id, tablespace_name;
```
A memory or background-process bottleneck can therefore affect several PDBs even when their datafiles, temporary space and undo are separately allocated. Conversely, a full local temporary tablespace need not mean every other PDB has exhausted its own temporary storage. Distinguish shared instance infrastructure, common dictionary definitions and container-local storage when diagnosing a multitenant system.

sources.title: Shared instance processes and dictionary metadata

mnemonic.anchor: for the common Oracle-supplied dictionary metadata housed in `CDB$ROOT`.

text: Which four are true about duplicating a database using Recovery Manager (RMAN)? (Choose four.)

options.text: Duplication can be done by having the auxiliary database instance pull backup sets from the target database instance.
A connection to an auxiliary instance is always required.
A subset of the target database can be duplicated.
A new DBID is always created for the duplicated database.
A connection to the recovery catalog instance is always required.
A backup of the target database is always required.
Duplication can be done by having the target database instance push copies to the auxiliary database instance.
A connection to the target database instance is always required.

explanation:
Option A is correct: active duplication using backup sets is pull-based. Auxiliary channels retrieve the required source files over the network. Option G is also correct: active duplication using image copies is push-based, with target channels sending copies to the auxiliary destination. These are alternative active-duplication methods, not contradictory descriptions of one mandatory transfer mechanism.

Option B is correct because DUPLICATE requires an auxiliary instance connection. The auxiliary instance is the destination being created, initially started in the documented state with the necessary parameter/password-file configuration. Option C is correct because supported duplication workflows can select a subset of tablespaces rather than requiring every source tablespace, subject to system/undo and object-dependency restrictions.

Option D is incorrect because of always. An ordinary independent duplicate receives a new DBID, but `DUPLICATE ... FOR STANDBY` retains the source DBID. Option E is incorrect because a recovery catalog is optional in supported duplication modes. Option F is incorrect because active duplication does not require a pre-existing source backup. Option H is incorrect because backup-based duplication can operate without a target connection when the required backup metadata and files are available through the chosen workflow.

A conceptual active duplicate begins with:
```text
CONNECT TARGET sys@source;
CONNECT AUXILIARY sys@destination;
```
The full command must specify appropriate file naming and storage isolation. Never use `NOFILENAMECHECK` casually on shared source/destination storage. The corrected key replaces D with G: a DBID exception invalidates an always claim, while both documented network-transfer directions are valid.

sources.title: Active push/pull duplication, auxiliary connections and standby DBID exception

mnemonic.anchor: active duplication using backup sets is pull-based.

text: Which two steps does Database Configuration Assistant (DBCA) take when cloning a remote pluggable database, starting with Oracle Database 19c? (Choose two.)

options.text: creating a database link from CDB$ROOT in the local database to the PDB in the remote system that is to be cloned
creating a database link from CDB$ROOT in the local database to CDB$ROOT in the remote system that is to be cloned
creating a new empty PDB in the local database from PDB$SEED
creating a database link from CDB$ROOT in the remote database to be cloned to CDB$ROOT in the local database
automatically dropping the database link to the remote database if it already exists
creating a database link from CDB$ROOT in the remote database to the PDB in the local database
opening the cloned PDB

explanation:
Option B and Option G are retained for the DBCA remote-clone workflow described here. DBCA uses source-CDB connection information to create the required link from the destination root toward the source root, performs the clone, and completes the workflow by opening the new PDB. This is the agreed two-choice interpretation of the DBCA-specific question.

Option A must be distinguished from generic SQL capability. A suitably privileged SQL remote-clone operation can use a database link whose service reaches the source PDB in supported configurations. That does not establish that DBCA performs both A and B as separate mandatory steps. The documented DBCA invocation uses the remote source CDB connection and PDB name as distinct inputs.

Option E is not accepted: DBCA should not be assumed to silently destroy a pre-existing database link. The practical lab evidence supplied for this bank reports DBT-19405 when the intended link already exists. That operational observation supports the exclusion, but it is not presented as an independently reproduced test or an official exam answer key.

Option C describes seed-based creation rather than copying the remote PDB. Option D and Option F reverse the connection direction: the destination needs to reach the source, not have the source clone into itself through a reverse link.

After cloning, inspect the actual result:
```sql
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs;
```
Also verify plug-in violations, service availability and application compatibility. Handle any existing link-name conflict deliberately before retrying. The accepted BG/count-two correction is preserved while separating DBCA behavior, general SQL link flexibility and the specific lab evidence concerning link collisions.

sources.title: DBCA/SQL remote cloning and source-container prerequisites

review_note: User-approved BG/select2 retained. Generic SQL can use source PDB/root endpoints; E exclusion is supported by supplied DBT-19405 lab evidence rather than an independently reproduced test.

mnemonic.anchor: Option B and Option G are retained for the DBCA remote-clone workflow described here.

text:
A schema owner truncated a table in error and must recover the data.

Which Oracle Flashback feature could be used to recover the data?

options.text: FLASHBACK TRANSACTION
FLASHBACK VERSION QUERY
FLASHBACK DATA ARCHIVE
FLASHBACK TABLE
FLASHBACK DATABASE

explanation:
Option E is the appropriate flashback feature among the choices. Flashback Database physically rewinds database blocks to a point before the TRUNCATE, provided the required flashback/redo information and intact files are available. It can cross this table DDL boundary because it does not reconstruct the table merely by applying row-level undo.

Option A is incorrect: Flashback Transaction works with supported transactional changes and cannot simply reverse TRUNCATE as ordinary DML. Option B is incorrect: a versions query is a query mechanism, not a restore operation, and undo-based row history cannot be relied upon across a truncation boundary. Option D is incorrect: Flashback Table cannot undo a TRUNCATE through its normal undo-based time-travel mechanism.

Option C is not a general remedy for the scenario. Flashback Data Archive must have been configured for the object and has documented DDL/history restrictions; the bare fact that a table was truncated does not establish a usable historical archive or make it the correct answer here.

A conceptual physical rewind is:
```sql
FLASHBACK DATABASE TO SCN <scn_before_truncate>;
```
Select a verified SCN or restore point and follow the required mounted-state/open procedure. Rewinding the production database affects other objects and transactions too. Where possible, use an isolated auxiliary/clone recovery workflow to reach the earlier state and extract only the lost table data, then restore the current production environment according to the recovery plan. The word could is important: no flashback feature guarantees recovery when its required history, logging or backups were never available.

mnemonic.anchor: Option E is the appropriate flashback feature among the choices.

text: Which three are true about using Database Upgrade Assistant (DBUA) to upgrade a database? (Choose three.)

options.text: The Pre-Upgrade Information Tool script is executed by DBUA.
DBUA must be launched from the target Oracle Home.
All pluggable databases are automatically upgraded as part of a container database upgrade.
A whole database backup must exist before upgrade
The database must be opened in read-only mode.
Multiple databases with the same ORACLE_HOME can be upgraded simultaneously.

explanation:
Option A is correct as the pre-upgrade-checking capability. DBUA invokes the release-appropriate prerequisite analysis and fixup workflow before dictionary upgrade. Older 19c workflows refer to the Pre-Upgrade Information Tool; updated documentation may describe AutoUpgrade preupgrade integration. The essential point is that DBUA performs prerequisite analysis rather than blindly starting upgrade scripts.

Option B is correct: launch DBUA from the target Oracle home so its scripts and utilities match the release being installed. Running an old home's assistant is not the supported way to select a new target release.

Option C is correct for the documented default CDB upgrade workflow: root, seed and plugged-in PDBs are included. Oracle permits staged PDB upgrade designs; the GUI documentation instructs administrators to unplug PDBs that should not be upgraded in that operation. Therefore this answer expresses the default workflow, not a claim that every possible upgrade method must upgrade every PDB simultaneously.

Option D is not a universal tool-enforced prerequisite, though a validated recoverable backup and rollback plan are essential operational preparation. Option E is incorrect because the source need not be opened read-only; DBUA manages the required shutdown/startup/upgrade modes. Option F is incorrect because one DBUA operation does not simultaneously upgrade multiple independent databases merely because they share an Oracle home.

After upgrading, inspect component status in every relevant container:
```sql
SELECT con_id, comp_id, version, status FROM cdb_registry;
```
Review logs and invalid objects, restore intended PDB services/open states, and run application validation. A successful assistant completion is evidence about the database upgrade, not a substitute for testing the workload that uses it.

sources.title: DBUA target home, prerequisite checks and default PDB selection

mnemonic.anchor: as the pre-upgrade-checking capability.

text:
You must migrate a non-CDB Oracle 11g Database to a CDB without first performing an upgrade to the non-CDB. User-defined objects are stored in several tablespaces in the non-CDB.

Which three methods can you use? (Choose three.)

options.text: the DBMS_PDB package
Data Pump full database export and import
Data Pump transportable tablespaces
replication using GoldenGate
cloning the non-CDB as a PDB
Data Pump full transportable database

explanation:
The defensible general pair is Data Pump logical export/import (B) and user transportable tablespaces (C). GoldenGate (D) is also a documented way to replicate a non-CDB into a precreated PDB without first upgrading that source. Thus B,C,D is the broad 11g interpretation. The source release needs more precision: full transportable export/import (F) is explicitly supported from 11.2.0.3 onward, making it an additional valid route for eligible 11g sources.

Option A is not valid directly against an 11g database: the DBMS_PDB adoption workflow requires a 12c-or-later non-CDB with the appropriate package and dictionary. Upgrading it first would violate the stated condition. Option E has the analogous physical-cloning release restriction and is not a way to turn an arbitrary 11g database into a PDB unchanged. Option D cannot be rejected simply because it is replication: Oracle explicitly documents replication followed by application cutover as a consolidation method.

Practical design starts by recording the exact source patch release, target character set, endian format, downtime budget, and unsupported data types. Create the destination PDB before a logical import or replication load. For a very large 11.2.0.4 source, compare full transportable import with GoldenGate initial load plus change capture. File transport moves user datafiles and imports metadata; replication can keep the target nearly current during the load. Neither approach means running DBMS_PDB on 11g. The choose-three formulation is provisional because F becomes valid once its source-release minimum is satisfied.
review_note: 11g is insufficiently precise. B,C,D work as general migration methods; F is additionally valid from 11.2.0.3 onward. DBMS_PDB is not available as the proposed direct11g route.

mnemonic.anchor: The defensible general pair is Data Pump logical export/import (B) and user transportable tablespaces (C).

text: Which three are true about backing up the control file? (Choose three.)

options.text: It gets backed up automatically by RMAN when the BACKUP SPFILE command is used
It can get backed up automatically as a binary copy
It can be backed up manually as a binary copy
It can be backed up manually as a trace file containing SQL statements for control file re-creation
It gets backed up automatically by RMAN as a trace file containing SQL statements for control file re-creation when a database backup occurs
It cannot be backed up manually as a binary copy

explanation:
A control-file backup preserves database structure and repository metadata needed to locate data files, online redo, and backups. Oracle supports binary control-file copies and a human-readable trace script that can recreate the control file.

Option analysis: B is true: RMAN CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP can create a binary copy. C is true: a DBA can explicitly make a binary copy with ALTER DATABASE BACKUP CONTROLFILE TO filename. D is true: TO TRACE writes recreation SQL into a trace file. A confuses a manual SPFILE backup with the configured autobackup triggers. E is false because automatic control-file backups are binary, not trace scripts. F is false because manual binary copies are supported.

Practical safeguard: configure control-file autobackup and retain a trace recreation script separately. Keep recovery metadata outside the database host so one disk or host failure does not remove both the database and its only control-file backup.

Read binary copy here as a binary control-file backup, not necessarily the RMAN image-copy output format. An autobackup is normally a backup piece containing a binary control file and, when used, the SPFILE. A trace is text, so it is not directly interchangeable with that backup piece.

```text
CONFIGURE CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP ON;
BACKUP CURRENT CONTROLFILE;
```

The qualification on A matters: BACKUP SPFILE can trigger a separate control-file autobackup when that feature is enabled. The statement is not unconditionally true in an unspecified configuration. A production plan should preserve the DBID, autobackup search location, and encryption credentials, and periodically test a control-file restore rather than merely confirming a backup job completed.
review_note: BCD is the intended supported-forms answer. A becomes true when CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP is ON; binary copy is used loosely for a binary backup piece.

sources.title: Backing up databases, control files and backup sets

keywords: can be backed up manually as a binary copy
can be backed up manually as a trace file
mnemonic.anchor: A control-file backup preserves database structure and repository metadata needed to locate data files, online redo, and backups.

text: Which two are true about PDB archive files? (Choose two.)

options.text: They contain all the data files only in compressed form for a PDB
They contain a PDB manifest file and all the data files in uncompressed form for a PDB
They contain all the data files only in uncompressed form for a PDB
They must be created using the DBMS_PDB package
They contain a PDB manifest file and all the data files in compressed form for a PDB
DBMS_PDB.CHECK_PLUG_COMPATIBILITY can be run against a PDB archive

explanation:
A PDB archive is a portable package for moving a pluggable database. It contains an XML manifest describing the PDB and the data files packaged in compressed form; the manifest alone is not the database contents.

Option analysis: E is correct because the archive includes both the manifest and compressed data files. F is correct because compatibility can be checked using the PDB archive as input. B describes an uncompressed package, while A and C omit the manifest. D is false: DBMS_PDB can create a manifest, but the package is not restricted to being created with that package.

Practical workflow: preserve the archive, check it against the target CDB, review compatibility violations, then create and open the PDB. A successful check is a useful preflight, not a substitute for validating the opened PDB and its application data. Keep the original archive until the new PDB has been backed up and accepted.

For example, the SQL unplug operation can create the archive directly:

```sql
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE sales CLOSE IMMEDIATE;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE sales UNPLUG INTO '/stage/sales.pdb';
```

This contrasts with unplugging to sales.xml, where the XML and datafiles must be transported separately. Although the DBMS_PDB reference describes an XML descriptor, the multitenant plug-in procedure explicitly permits a .pdb archive in the pdb_descr_file parameter of CHECK_PLUG_COMPATIBILITY. Run the check from the destination root, inspect PDB_PLUG_IN_VIOLATIONS, and ensure sufficient extraction space and access permissions. The archive may contain a wallet file as well as the manifest and datafiles; compressed packaging does not remove key-management requirements. Preserve the source archive until the plugged PDB has been opened, validated, and protected by a new backup.

sources.title: Plugging in unplugged PDBs and archives

mnemonic.anchor: A PDB archive is a portable package for moving a pluggable database.

text:
You want to install Oracle Grid Infrastructure for a Standalone Server using Oracle Universal Installer (OUI). There is no existing Oracle installation on the server.

Which two are prerequisites? (Choose two.)

options.text: a group called dba
the Oracle Inventory group oinstall
an operating system user to own this installation
an operating system account called grid
the installation of Oracle ASMLIB

explanation:
A Grid Infrastructure installation needs an operating-system owner and a central Oracle inventory group. It also uses OSASM/OSDBA group memberships for ASM and database administration, but group and account names are site conventions rather than fixed literal strings.

Option analysis: B is correct because an inventory group such as oinstall is needed when there is no existing Oracle inventory. C is correct because an OS user must own the installation. A is not universally required by the name dba; the OSDBA group can have another name. D is likewise not required to be literally named grid. E is not mandatory: ASM disk management can use supported platform alternatives.

Practical point: create the owner and inventory group according to local security policy, assign the required OSASM/OSDBA groups, and run the platform prerequisite checker. The question wording is incomplete because it omits the administration-group prerequisite while asking for only two answers; interpret the keyed pair as inventory group plus installation owner.

Separate functional roles from conventional Unix names. The inventory group controls access to the central installation inventory; the software owner owns the Grid home. Administrative groups confer SYSASM/SYSDBA-style OS authentication and can be combined or separated according to the platform's supported installation design.

Before starting OUI, inspect the owner's group memberships with the operating system's id command, validate inventory ownership, and run prerequisite checks. A username such as grid is a useful separation-of-duties convention, not a universally hard-coded required account. Similarly oinstall is the customary inventory-group name rather than a magic literal required by every installation. ASMLIB is one possible disk provisioning mechanism; supported device permissions or other platform mechanisms can satisfy storage access. Therefore B means the inventory-group role and C the installation-owner role. Do not use this question's abbreviated list as a complete platform prerequisite checklist.
review_note: B is valid as the inventory-group ROLE; the literal name oinstall is conventional, just as grid/dba are. Platform-specific administrative group requirements still apply.

mnemonic.anchor: A Grid Infrastructure installation needs an operating-system owner and a central Oracle inventory group.

text:
You execute this command successfully:

```text
SQL> ALTER DATABASE BACKUP CONTROLFILE TO TRACE;
```

What is the outcome?

options.text: It creates a file that contains SQL statements to re-create the control file
It creates a file that contains RMAN scripts to create a duplicate database
It creates a copy of the control file in the fast recovery area (FRA)
It creates a binary backup of the control file
It updates the alert log with the location and contents of the control file

explanation:
BACKUP CONTROLFILE TO TRACE writes a text trace containing SQL statements that can recreate the control file. It is useful recovery documentation when binary control-file copies are unavailable.

Option analysis: A is correct: the trace includes control-file recreation SQL and relevant file/log structure. B is incorrect because an RMAN duplicate script is unrelated. C and D describe binary copies, which use a filename rather than TO TRACE. E is incorrect because the command does not put the trace contents in the alert log as its result.

Practical use: locate the generated trace in the diagnostic destination, review it, and preserve it with recovery runbooks. It is a script template, not a ready binary control file; a DBA may need to adjust paths and log definitions before executing it. Keep it alongside RMAN autobackups, which provide a faster binary restore path.

To locate the session's diagnostic trace, an appropriately privileged session can inspect:

```sql
SELECT value FROM v$diag_info WHERE name='Default Trace File';
```

Review the generated CREATE CONTROLFILE alternatives, including the distinction between preserving redo history with NORESETLOGS and opening a new incarnation with RESETLOGS. The trace must be kept current after structural changes: a script predating a newly added datafile may require manual editing. TO TRACE is not a backup of user table data, the SPFILE, or archived logs, and executing the command does not perform a recovery. A binary control-file backup is usually more convenient to restore, while trace SQL is useful documentation and a fallback when valid binary metadata is unavailable. Treat the resulting text as recovery input requiring careful review, not an executable runbook for every failure.

sources.title: Backing up databases, control files and backup sets

mnemonic.anchor: BACKUP CONTROLFILE TO TRACE writes a text trace containing SQL statements that can recreate the control file.

text: Which three are true about upgrading an application in an application container? (Choose three.)

options.text: The upgrade can be performed when connected either to CDB$ROOT or to PDB$SEED
An application root clone gets created automatically
After an application upgrade, the application container’s PDBs remain synchronized with the existing application root
The upgrade must be performed when connected to CDB$ROOT
An application name and version number must be specified to upgrade the application
After an application upgrade, the application container’s PDBs are automatically synchronized with the application root clone

explanation:
B and E are unambiguous. An application upgrade automatically clones the application root and identifies the application plus its old/new versions. The PDBs continue using the preupgrade metadata through the read-only root clone while the original root receives the new version.

Option C is false if existing application root means the original root after its upgrade: unsynchronized PDBs are pointed at the old-version clone, not magically advanced to the new root version. Option F is the intended third choice only if synchronized means that their old-version metadata remains associated with the clone. Oracle's exact description is that the PDBs point to the clone; that should not be confused with an automatically issued application SYNC operation. A and D name incorrect execution containers: application DDL is managed in the application root, not CDB$ROOT or PDB$SEED.

```sql
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION salesapp
  BEGIN UPGRADE '1.0' TO '2.0';
-- Execute application DDL in the application root.
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION salesapp
  END UPGRADE TO '2.0';
```

After testing, connect to each selected application PDB and explicitly synchronize it. That PDB can then use the upgraded application root, while tenants not yet upgraded can continue on the clone. Thus B,E,F is a provisional interpretation of a poorly worded third statement. The important operational distinction is automatic root cloning/redirection versus administrator-controlled adoption of the upgraded application.
review_note: F is accepted only as automatic association with the old-version root clone. Oracle describes pointer redirection, not an automatic application SYNC. B and E are unambiguous; C contradicts the new-root/old-clone distinction.

sources.title: Multitenant architecture and application root clones

mnemonic.anchor: An application upgrade automatically clones the application root and identifies the application plus its old/new versions.

text: Which two are true about RMAN virtual private catalogs (VPCs)? (Choose two.)

options.text: RMAN uses Oracle Virtual Private Database (VPD) to implement VPCs
Each VPC is owned by the recovery catalog schema owner
VPC functionality is enabled by default
The RMAN catalog owner can grant access for an already registered database to a new virtual catalog owner
Only one target database can be registered in a VPC

explanation:
An RMAN Virtual Private Catalog (VPC) is a restricted view of the base recovery catalog. The base catalog owner controls which registered target databases each virtual-catalog owner may see; RMAN uses Oracle Virtual Private Database security policies to enforce that separation.

Option analysis: A is true because VPD provides the filtering mechanism. D is true because the catalog owner can grant a newly created virtual-catalog owner access to an already registered database. B is false: the VPC user owns the virtual catalog, while the base schema owns the complete catalog. C is false because VPC setup and grants are explicit. E is false because a VPC can be granted more than one database.

Practical example: delegate catalog visibility to a backup team for only its assigned targets while a central DBA retains global administration. This limits catalog metadata exposure; it does not replace target privileges or protection of backup media.

The restricted catalog owner's SQL account differs from the base catalog owner. The base owner grants catalog visibility and registration rights; this is not a grant of SYSBACKUP on every target database. A team can see backup metadata for two assigned DBIDs while another team sees a different subset of the same base repository.

For a practical validation, connect RMAN to the target and to the delegated catalog account, issue LIST BACKUP, and confirm that unauthorized targets are absent. Test the restricted account itself rather than checking only the base owner's all-database view. Existing backups are not physically copied to create a VPC: Oracle applies access policies to the shared repository metadata. Catalog visibility also does not grant decryption keys, access to disk backup paths, or media-manager credentials. Those independent controls must be provisioned for a real restore, and they explain why metadata isolation alone is not a complete backup-security architecture.

mnemonic.anchor: An RMAN Virtual Private Catalog (VPC) is a restricted view of the base recovery catalog.

text:
A container database called CDB1 is OMF-enabled.
PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT is not configured in CDB1.
PDB1 was unplugged from CDB1 earlier in the week.

Examine this command, which will be executed in CDB1:

```text
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb1 -
USING '/u01/app/oracle/oradata/pdb1.xml'
SOURCE_FILE_NAME_CONVERT = ('/u01/app/oracle/oradata/', '/u02/app/oracle/oradata/');
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: PDB1 data files already exist in the correct location.
DBMS_PDB.CHECK_PLUG_COMPATIBILITY must be run in CDB1 before executing the command.
PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT must be set before executing the command.
/u01/app/oracle/oradata/pdb1.xml does not contain the current locations of data files for PDB1.
PDB1 must be dropped from CDB1.

explanation:
The unplug manifest records the source file paths at unplug time. SOURCE_FILE_NAME_CONVERT maps those old paths to the data files' current location; enabling OMF does not rewrite stale paths stored in the XML.

Option analysis: D is true because the manifest still contains the paths that existed when the PDB was unplugged. E is true because the PDB was previously unplugged from this CDB and must be dropped from its source CDB before it can be plugged back under the same name. B is false: compatibility checking is recommended but not a mandatory prerequisite to issuing CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE. C is false because this command supplies path conversion and the CDB is OMF-enabled. A is false because the paths have changed, so files are not already at the intended destination.

Practical workflow: preserve the unplugged files, map the old manifest paths to their new location, plug in the PDB, inspect violations, and open it only after resolving compatibility issues.

SOURCE_FILE_NAME_CONVERT identifies the files to read; it is not the same as FILE_NAME_CONVERT for choosing names of newly copied destination files. OMF can generate destination filenames after the source files have been located. Thus specifying SOURCE_FILE_NAME_CONVERT does not require PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT as well.

The removable source-PDB registration is separate from its preserved datafiles. For an unplugged PDB that must be reused, DROP PLUGGABLE DATABASE ... KEEP DATAFILES removes the old registration without intentionally deleting the transport source. Review the XML and verify the files actually exist at the translated paths before issuing CREATE. D follows the intended purpose of the conversion clause, but the stem never explicitly states that the datafiles were moved: a DBA could supply an unnecessary or incorrect conversion mapping. Likewise E assumes the earlier unplugged PDB has not already been dropped. Those are normal intended assumptions, not facts logically proved by the displayed command alone.
review_note: DE assumes files were moved and the unplugged source registration still exists. The command alone does not prove either; source-file mapping is distinct from OMF destination naming.

sources.title: Plugging in unplugged PDBs and archives

mnemonic.anchor: The unplug manifest records the source file paths at unplug time.

text: Which two are true about backup encryption? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keystore-based encryption is the default mode for RMAN backup encryption
Vendor-specific media management software can be used for making encrypted RMAN backups to media
Image copies can be encrypted
Backup encryption can be enabled selectively for specific tablespaces
The BACKUP BACKUPSET command can encrypt and decrypt backup sets
The Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) keystore is backed up using RMAN

explanation:
A and D are the correct RMAN-native encryption choices. Transparent encryption uses the database keystore and is the default RMAN encryption mode; this does not mean encryption is enabled by default. Persistent CONFIGURE ENCRYPTION defaults OFF until explicitly enabled.

Option D is supported by per-tablespace encryption configuration. For example:

```text
CONFIGURE ENCRYPTION FOR TABLESPACE payroll ON;
```

Option B needs a scope distinction. Independent media-management or tape hardware can encrypt its own stored stream, but Oracle 19c documents Oracle Secure Backup as the supported SBT interface for RMAN's native encrypted backups directly to tape. B should not be used to assert that any vendor SBT library supports RMAN-native backup-set encryption. Option C is false for that native feature: encrypted backup sets are supported, not encryption of arbitrary image-copy output. Option E is not a general encrypt/decrypt conversion operation; BACKUP BACKUPSET preserves an existing backup set's encryption state rather than transforming it into plaintext. F is false because the keystore must be protected separately from an RMAN database backup.

Practical recovery requires both readable backup pieces and access to their keys. Back up keystores using the supported key-management procedure and retain historical keys needed by older backups. Test restoration on a separate host where the keystore configuration is explicitly understood. Losing the keystore or password can make an otherwise complete set of backup pieces unusable.
review_note: A is default encryption MODE, not default enablement. B is broadly possible for vendor-side media encryption but not the supported RMAN-native encrypted SBT interface; AD uses the RMAN-native interpretation.

mnemonic.anchor: A and D are the correct RMAN-native encryption choices.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. DEFAULT_SHARING is METADATA.
3. APP_ROOT is an application root contained in CDB1.
4. APP_PDB1 is an application PDB contained in APP_ROOT.
5. COMPANYAPP is an application contained in APP_ROOT.
6. EMP is a common table created in APP_ROOT and all its application PDBs, created when version 1.0 of COMPANYAPP was installed.

You execute these commands:

```text
$ sqlplus sys/oracle@localhost:1521/cdb1 as sysdba

SQL> ALTER SYSTEM SET DEFAULT_SHARING=DATA;
System altered.

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=app_root;
Session altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION companyapp BEGIN UPGRADE '1.0' TO '2.0';
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> ALTER TABLE emp ADD (sal NUMBER NOT NULL);
Table altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION companyapp END UPGRADE TO '2.0';
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=app_pdb1;
Session altered.

SQL> DESC emp;
 Name                                      Null?    Type
 ----------------------------------------- -------- ----------------------------
 ENO                                                NUMBER
 ENAME                                              VARCHAR2(20)

SQL> SELECT * FROM emp;

       ENO ENAME
---------- --------------------
       100 Alan
       200 Ben

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION companyapp SYNC;
```

What will be the outcome and why?

options.text: It will return an error because EMP is not empty in APP_PDB1
It will return an error because the SYNC operation is not allowed when constraints are added to common objects
SAL will be added to APP_PDB1.EMP, with NULLs in columns of existing rows
SAL will be added to APP_PDB1.EMP, with 0 in columns of existing rows
It will return an error because EMP.SAL is empty in APP_ROOT

explanation:
**Core concept: metadata links and application synchronization.** `DEFAULT_SHARING=METADATA` made `EMP` a metadata-linked common table: its definition is maintained in `APP_ROOT`, while each container has its own rows. Changing `DEFAULT_SHARING` to `DATA` changes the default for eligible objects created later; it does not convert this existing table or move its rows.

**Trace the commands.** The `ALTER TABLE` ran in `APP_ROOT` and returned `Table altered.` That proves the root copy had no rows at that moment. The two rows for Alan and Ben are displayed only after the session switches to `APP_PDB1`. During `SYNC`, Oracle applies the application upgrade DDL to that PDB so its metadata matches the application root.

**Why SYNC fails.** The replay tries to add `SAL NUMBER NOT NULL` without a `DEFAULT` to `APP_PDB1.EMP`, which already has two rows. Oracle cannot supply a non-NULL value for those existing rows, so it raises **ORA-01758: table must be empty to add mandatory (NOT NULL) column**. The synchronization fails at this DDL; it does not add `SAL` as NULL or fill it with zero.

**Option analysis.** A is correct: the failure occurs when `SYNC` replays the DDL in populated `APP_PDB1`. B is false because `SYNC` is allowed; the error comes from applying this DDL to a table with rows. C predicts a successful addition with NULLs, which is incompatible with `NOT NULL`. D invents a zero default that the statement never specifies. E is false because the successful `ALTER TABLE` proves the root table was empty.

**Practical upgrade.** Choose a business-valid default and include it in the upgrade DDL, or add the column nullable, populate valid values in each application PDB, and then enforce `NOT NULL`. For example, zero is suitable only if it has the intended business meaning:

```sql
ALTER TABLE emp ADD (sal NUMBER DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL);
```

**Takeaway:** application upgrades define shared metadata in the root, but SYNC replays changes against each PDB’s own data; validate DDL against populated PDBs before synchronizing.

For a staged upgrade without a universal default, perform the nullable-column addition in one application version, synchronize the PDBs, populate each tenant's values, and only then distribute a NOT NULL constraint in a subsequent application upgrade. The rows are tenant-local even though the definition is shared. Query PDB_APP_PLUG_IN_VIOLATIONS and the application's synchronization status after any failed replay, then resolve the underlying DDL/data problem before retrying. A change of DEFAULT_SHARING is neither a conversion of existing objects nor a data migration tool. A successful DDL in an empty application root must therefore be tested against representative populated application PDBs before rollout.

sources.title: Multitenant architecture and application root clones

mnemonic.anchor: Changing `DEFAULT_SHARING` to `DATA` changes the default for eligible objects created later; it does not convert this existing table or move its rows.

text: Which two are true about various Oracle security and auditing capabilities? (Choose two.)

options.text: Application-common Transparent Security Data Protection (TSDP) policies can be created only if all the PDBs in the application container are closed.
Application-common TSDP policies are always container specific.
Application-common OLS policies can be created only if all the PDBs in the application container are closed.
Fine-grained auditing (FGA) policies in an application root are automatically synchronized to all application PDBs contained in the application container when they are updated.
Unified auditing can be automatically synchronized to all application PDBs in an application container.

explanation:
Application security features do not all have identical propagation rules. B is correct: an application-root TSDP policy behaves as a policy local to that root, even when it operates on application common objects; it is not one policy automatically applied in every app PDB. E is also correct: application-common unified auditing policies can be created for the application container and synchronized to its PDBs. A is false because TSDP operations are not conditioned on closing every PDB; indeed TSDP statements inside application BEGIN/END install blocks fail, but that is a different restriction. C is false: OLS is not made available by closing PDBs; Oracle 19c disallows creating OLS policies in the application root. D is false because FGA policies do not automatically synchronize in this fashion. In practice, determine whether a policy is local or application-common and follow that feature's installation and synchronization rules rather than generalizing from another security feature.

For operational planning, distinguish policy definition, propagation, and enforcement. A unified audit policy captured as part of the application lifecycle can be replayed into application PDBs through synchronization; that does not mean every standalone local security change instantly propagates without the relevant application workflow. TSDP and FGA remain subject to their own container scope, while OLS has application-root restrictions.

When testing, inspect the policy from an application root and then from a synchronized application PDB, and perform the protected operation in the tenant itself. A policy row in the root alone does not prove tenant enforcement. Keep the user identities and application version constant during the test so that a missing grant or a stale application version is not mistaken for an auditing defect. The closed-PDB claims in A/C do not establish a supported configuration merely by taking every tenant offline.

mnemonic.anchor: Application security features do not all have identical propagation rules.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. There are several pluggable databases (PDBs) in CDB1.
3. Each PDB has several tables with referential integrity constraints.
4. FLASHBACK DATABASE is ON.
5. UNDO RETENTION GUARANTEE is enabled.

Multiple undesired multitable changes were made in all the PDBs.

Which method can be used to undo the changes using a single command?

options.text: restore and recover database
flashback transaction
flashback database
flashback table
flashback table and transaction

explanation:
C is correct. FLASHBACK DATABASE can rewind the CDB, including its PDB data, to a selected earlier point in a single database-level operation, assuming flashback logs cover the target. A restore and recover is a media-recovery path that requires restore/recovery steps and may require RESETLOGS; it is not the single-command flashback method. B, FLASHBACK TRANSACTION, repairs selected transactions rather than undoing multiple unwanted multitable changes across every PDB as one operation. D, FLASHBACK TABLE, targets selected tables and is not a whole-CDB rewind; it also has restrictions around dependencies and can require multiple statements. E combines table and transaction flashback but still does not perform a single CDB-wide rewind. The given UNDO RETENTION GUARANTEE supports undo availability for certain flashback operations, but it is not the feature that rewinds the entire database. For a real incident, identify the target time and validate flashback log coverage before issuing the operation.

The recovery unit is decisive. One whole-CDB FLASHBACK DATABASE operation rewinds root and tenant datafiles coherently, whereas logical table or transaction features operate on specified objects or transactions and require enough history and dependency handling. Guaranteed undo retention does not turn those logical operations into a single cross-PDB database rewind command.

In a lab, create a suitable restore point before the change, perform the changes in two PDBs, then examine the available flashback window before attempting a rewind. The database must be in the required mounted state for whole-database flashback, and recovery normally ends with an appropriate OPEN RESETLOGS after validation. Availability of flashback logging ON does not itself prove that every desired historical point is still retained. Choose the target SCN carefully: the physical rewind also reverses wanted changes committed after that point, not only the undesirable transactions mentioned in the stem.

mnemonic.anchor: A restore and recover is a media-recovery path that requires restore/recovery steps and may require RESETLOGS; it is not the single-command flashback method.

text:
Examine this extract from the show parameters command:

```text
SQL> show parameters

NAME                         TYPE        VALUE
---------------------------- ----------- ------------------------------
db_16k_cache_size            big integer 0
db_2k_cache_size             big integer 0
db_32k_cache_size            big integer 0
db_4k_cache_size             big integer 0
db_8k_cache_size             big integer 0
db_cache_size                big integer 0
java_pool_size               big integer 0
large_pool_size              big integer 0
memory_max_target            big integer 800M
memory_target                big integer 800M
pga_aggregate_limit          big integer 2G
pga_aggregate_target         big integer 0
sga_max_size                 big integer 800M
sga_min_size                 big integer 0
sga_target                   big integer 0
shared_pool_reserved_size    big integer 7130316
shared_pool_size             big integer 0
statistics_level             string      TYPICAL
workarea_size_policy         string      AUTO
```

How are System Global Area (SGA) and Program Global Area (PGA) memory managed by an instance using these parameter settings?

options.text: SGA and PGA memory are manually managed
SGA memory is manually managed and PGA memory is managed by using Automated SQL Execution Memory Management
SGA memory is managed by using Automatic Shared Memory Management (ASMM) and PGA memory is manually managed
SGA memory is managed by using Automatic Shared Memory Management (ASMM) and PGA memory is managed by using Automated SQL Execution Memory Management
SGA and PGA memory are managed by using Automatic Memory Management (AMM)

explanation:
E is correct because MEMORY_TARGET is nonzero, enabling Automatic Memory Management (AMM), which lets Oracle redistribute memory between the SGA and PGA within the configured memory target/max target. A is false: setting both SGA_TARGET and PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET to zero does not mean manual allocation when MEMORY_TARGET is 800M. B and C misstate the SGA/PGA management modes; AMM, rather than manually managed SGA or PGA, controls the overall allocation. D describes ASMM plus automatic PGA management, which typically uses SGA_TARGET and PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET without MEMORY_TARGET controlling both together. STATISTICS_LEVEL=TYPICAL and WORKAREA_SIZE_POLICY=AUTO support automatic work-area management but do not change the AMM conclusion. The 2G PGA_AGGREGATE_LIMIT is a cap, not the target amount allocated. Operationally, check operating-system memory and database memory advisories: the 800M target is a sizing envelope, not a guarantee that the host has enough physical RAM.

MEMORY_TARGET is the active control rather than SGA_TARGET. Values of zero for individual pools do not mean the instance runs without those pools; in automatic modes Oracle allocates and resizes the components within the active memory-management constraints. MEMORY_MAX_TARGET bounds a dynamic increase of MEMORY_TARGET, while PGA_AGGREGATE_LIMIT is a separate aggregate limit and is not the budget shared by SGA and PGA.

```sql
SELECT component, current_size, min_size, max_size
FROM v$memory_dynamic_components;
```

Inspect actual component sizes and resize operations rather than inferring allocations directly from the zero-valued initialization parameters. A larger PGA limit than MEMORY_TARGET is not evidence of manual PGA management. Platform prerequisites, such as appropriate shared-memory support, must already have been satisfied for this configuration to start successfully. AMM differs from ASMM because it can redistribute the overall managed budget between the SGA and the aggregate PGA target, not only between pools inside the SGA.

mnemonic.anchor: B and C misstate the SGA/PGA management modes; AMM, rather than manually managed SGA or PGA, controls the overall allocation.

text: Which are two of the steps taken by Database Configuration Assistant (DBCA) to clone a remote pluggable database (PDB) starting from Oracle 19c? (Choose two.)

options.text: backing up the cloned PDB
opening the cloned PDB
creating a database link from CDB$ROOT in the local database to CDB$ROOT in the remote system that is to be cloned
creating a database link from CDB$ROOT in the local database to the PDB in the remote system that is to be cloned
leaving the cloned PDB in mount state

explanation:
The correct choices are B and C. In the DBCA remote-clone workflow, the destination CDB root connects to the remote CDB root through a database link (C), and DBCA opens the cloned PDB when cloning completes (B). The Oracle 19c DBCA example supplies the remote CDB connection string and the remote PDB name separately, consistent with this root-level connection. D describes a valid endpoint for a database link in general SQL-based remote cloning, but it is not the DBCA step identified by this question. A is not a cloning step: a backup may be prudent after provisioning, but DBCA does not automatically back up the clone as part of this workflow. E is false because DBCA opens the completed PDB rather than leaving it mounted. In practice, check the PDB open mode and service after DBCA reports successful completion.

The documented DBCA example supplies the remote CDB service separately from the remote PDB name. A common account on the source CDB provides the database-link connection, and DBCA completes opening the resulting clone. This supports the root-to-root link represented by C and the final open represented by B.

Option D is technically valid for a SQL remote-clone database link: Oracle permits such a link to connect directly to the source PDB. That general SQL capability does not establish a second link-creation step in the DBCA workflow. The existing-link failure DBT-19405 reported in the practical test associated with the companion question is consistent with DBCA not silently deleting an already-conflicting link. A is not a stated automatic backup step, and E describes an intermediate SQL creation state rather than DBCA's normal completed result. After DBCA reports success, check the clone's open mode and then take its first usable backup.
review_note: BC preserves the reviewed DBCA-specific workflow. D is valid for general SQL cloning; the question must not imply direct-to-PDB links are universally invalid.

mnemonic.anchor: The Oracle 19c DBCA example supplies the remote CDB connection string and the remote PDB name separately, consistent with this root-level connection.

text: Which two are true about the Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor? (ADDM)? (Choose two.)

options.text: When ADDM reports multiple findings, summing all their impacts can yield to more than 100% of DB time.
It runs automatically after each AWR snapshot.
By default it analyzes a period of time corresponding to the last 4 hours of activity.
Results are written to the alert log.
By default it analyzes a period of time corresponding to the last 24 hours of activity.

explanation:
A and B are correct. ADDM analyzes AWR snapshots automatically, normally comparing the latest two snapshot intervals. Its finding impacts can overlap: multiple issues can affect the same DB time, so adding percentages can exceed 100%; the percentages are not exclusive slices of one pie chart. C and E are false because the default analysis interval is not a fixed last-four-hours or last-24-hours window; it is tied to the available AWR snapshot interval(s). D is false: ADDM results are retained in the Automatic Workload Repository and accessible through advisor/report interfaces, not written as its standard output to the alert log. For practical diagnosis, review the finding, recommendation, and estimated impact together, then correlate with the workload interval. Do not add overlapping impacts or treat an ADDM recommendation as proof that changing a parameter will improve every workload.

DB time is accumulated database foreground service time, not a mutually exclusive pie chart of root causes. The same slow SQL execution can contribute to a high-I/O finding and an undersized-cache finding, so adding their impacts double-counts some of the underlying work. Recommendation benefits can overlap as well.

```sql
SELECT task_name, status
FROM dba_advisor_tasks
WHERE advisor_name='ADDM';
```

Use two appropriate snapshot boundaries when requesting a focused report. A report for a quiet hour is not representative of the peak workload merely because it is the newest report. Automatic execution uses the last two relevant AWR snapshots rather than a fixed four-hour or 24-hour interval. Findings are stored in the advisor repository and can be reported through the documented ADDM interfaces. The alert log remains useful for errors and operational events, but it is not the ADDM result repository described in D.

mnemonic.anchor: ADDM analyzes AWR snapshots automatically, normally comparing the latest two snapshot intervals.

text: Which three are true about Data Pump in an Oracle multitenant environment? (Choose three.)

options.text: It can be used to clone a CDB.
It can be used to transport data from a PDB to a non-CDB.
It can be used to transport data between PDBs.
It can be used to create a new PDB.
It can be used to transport data from a non-CDB to a PDB.

explanation:
B, C, and E are true. Data Pump is a logical export/import tool, so it can move logical data from a PDB to a non-CDB, between PDBs, and from a non-CDB into a PDB, subject to version and object compatibility. A is false because Data Pump does not physically clone an entire CDB, including its control files and infrastructure; use supported database/PDB cloning or backup methods for that. D is false as stated: Data Pump import loads logical objects into a target database/PDB but does not itself create the PDB container. Administrators provision the PDB first, then import into it. In practice, plan schema/object remapping, character sets, tablespace mappings, directory objects, privileges, and downtime/consistency requirements. Data Pump is well suited to logical migration or selective data movement, whereas physical clones preserve database file-level structure and are a different operation.

Data Pump transfers logical database contents or transportable user tablespaces. It does not create the receiving CDB/PDB container or reproduce a CDB's physical root/seed topology. Prepare an empty destination PDB using CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE or DBCA, then connect expdp/impdp to the correct service for the required transfer.

For example, a schema export from one PDB can be imported into another PDB, or into an appropriately compatible non-CDB; a non-CDB schema export can likewise be imported into a PDB. Check the Data Pump source/target release rules, character sets, directory objects, and object privileges. A FULL export from within a PDB is full within that container's supported scope, not a physical clone of the whole CDB. Transportable mode adds self-containment and file-copy requirements, while conventional mode moves table rows through the dump/import process. Neither changes the receiving container creation prerequisite.

sources.title: Data Pump in CDBs and PDBs

mnemonic.anchor: Administrators provision the PDB first, then import into it.

text: Which three are true about Oracle Grid Infrastructure for a Standalone Server? (Choose three.)

options.text: It requires Oracle ASM Filter Driver (ASMFD) to manage Automatic Storage Management (ASM) disks.
It requires the operating system ORACLE_BASE environment variable to be predefined before installation.
It requires Oracle ASMLib to manage Automatic Storage Management (ASM) disks.
Automatic Storage Management (ASM) requires that O/S groups OSASM and OSDBA be assigned as secondary groups for its installation owner.
It creates one disk group during installation.
It includes both Oracle Restart and Oracle Automatic Storage Management (ASM) software.

explanation:
D, E, and F are the keyed answers. Oracle Grid Infrastructure for a standalone server includes Oracle Restart and Oracle ASM (F). Installation configures an initial ASM disk group (E) and requires the ASM installation owner to belong to the relevant OSASM and OSDBA groups (D). A is false: ASM Filter Driver is not a universal requirement for managing ASM disks. C is false for the same reason; ASMLib is an optional platform-specific disk-management choice, not mandatory. B is false: ORACLE_BASE need not be predefined as an operating-system environment variable for installation; the installer can configure or prompt for Oracle base locations. In practice, prepare OS groups and storage discovery according to the platform and chosen ASM disk mechanism. Check installer prerequisites and logs, then verify the resulting disk group and Oracle Restart configuration rather than assuming a particular driver was installed.

Oracle Restart is the single-server resource-management framework; it is not a multi-node RAC cluster. The ASM binaries and Restart components are delivered together in Grid Infrastructure. Disk-device access can be implemented by supported OS permissions, ASMLIB, or ASMFD where applicable, so neither optional mechanism is universal.

The standard configured standalone installation creates an initial ASM disk group for database storage. A software-only installation can instead defer configuration, so E must be read in the configured-installation sense. D also uses conventional group-placement terminology: the installation owner must have the required administrative group memberships, but a chosen administrative group may be its primary group rather than always an additional secondary group. B is not required because the installer can determine or request ORACLE_BASE. Inspect the owner's id output and confirm actual Restart/ASM resources after configuration, rather than treating conventional account names or a software-only inventory entry as proof of a running ASM installation.
review_note: DEF describes a configured standard install. Software-only mode can defer diskgroup creation; required group membership is not invariably secondary rather than primary.

mnemonic.anchor: Oracle Grid Infrastructure for a standalone server includes Oracle Restart and Oracle ASM (F).

text: Which two are true about Lockdown profiles in a container database (CDB) and its pluggable databases (PDBs)? (Choose two.)

options.text: A Lockdown profile created from a base Lockdown profile is always automatically modified if the profile on which it is based is modified.
A PDB Lockdown profile can be created in an application root.
A Lockdown profile created from a base Lockdown profile is never automatically modified if the profile on which it is based is modified.
A PDB Lockdown profile can be created in CDB$ROOT.
A PDB Lockdown profile can be created in a regular PDB.

explanation:
B and D are correct: a lockdown profile can be created in an application root or in CDB$ROOT, then applied at an allowed scope. A and C are both false because derived profiles may be static or dynamic. A profile created FROM a static base does not inherit later changes, while one created INCLUDING a dynamic base does inherit specified rule changes; the answer choices incorrectly claim one behavior is universal. E is false because the CREATE LOCKDOWN PROFILE statement must be issued from CDB$ROOT or an application root, not from a regular PDB. Do not confuse where a profile is defined with where it is enabled: profiles can be assigned at root, application-root, or PDB scope under supported precedence rules. In practice, choose static versus dynamic inheritance deliberately and test the effective restrictions in the target PDB before rollout.

Oracle distinguishes inheritance by BASE from copying by FROM. A BASE relationship can propagate later base-profile changes dynamically; a copied profile can be independent. Therefore always and never in A/C ignore the syntax used to create the derived profile.

```sql
CREATE LOCKDOWN PROFILE tenant_limits;
ALTER LOCKDOWN PROFILE tenant_limits
  DISABLE STATEMENT=('ALTER SYSTEM');
```

Run profile definition in the appropriate administrative root and assign it through the documented PDB_LOCKDOWN mechanism with suitable privileges. A lockdown profile constrains selected operations even for users who otherwise possess a broad privilege; it does not replace normal grants. When validating inheritance, modify a non-production base profile and inspect the effective restrictions from the consuming PDB. The fact that application roots can create profiles does not grant the same creation capability to every ordinary tenant PDB. Keep base and copied profiles distinct in names and change-management records so administrators know which tenants will inherit a change.

mnemonic.anchor: B and D are correct: a lockdown profile can be created in an application root or in CDB$ROOT, then applied at an allowed scope.

text: Which two are true about transporting databases across platforms using Recovery Manager (RMAN) image copies? (Choose two.)

options.text: By default, the transported database will use Oracle Managed Files (OMF)
Data files can be converted on the destination system.
Data files can be converted on the source system.
A new DBID is automatically created for the transported database.
Databases can be transported between systems with different endian formats.
The password file is automatically converted by RMAN.

explanation:
B and C are the unambiguous cross-platform CONVERT DATABASE choices: the conversion work can run on the source or be generated for execution on the destination. The whole database must move between platforms of the same endian format; therefore E is false. Do not generalize the different-endian support for user transportable tablespaces to an entire database, which includes undo and other special blocks.

Option A is false because transport does not enable OMF by default independently of destination configuration. F is false: password and network configuration files are outside the automatically converted database-file payload. D must not be assumed merely because a transport script uses NEW DATABASE to name a destination: a name change and a DBID change are distinct operations. The reviewed key is B,C, and the count is corrected to two rather than selecting unsupported E or an unproven automatically-new-DBID claim.

```sql
SELECT platform_name, endian_format
FROM v$transportable_platform;
```

Plan read-only source time, copied files, destination control-file/redo creation, and password-file handling explicitly. Even when byte order is the same, the CONVERT DATABASE procedure still handles platform-sensitive blocks and generates supporting scripts. A transport is not an RMAN DUPLICATE command: do not import DUPLICATE's automatically assigned identity semantics without checking the generated transport procedure. After opening the destination, inspect its DBID, DB_NAME and resetlogs history before catalog registration and backups.
original_text: Which three are true about transporting databases across platforms using Recovery Manager (RMAN) image copies? (Choose three.)
review_note: E is false for whole-database transport. B/C are explicit; automatic new DBID in D is not established by the supplied procedure. Count changed to two.

mnemonic.anchor: B and C are the unambiguous cross-platform CONVERT DATABASE choices: the conversion work can run on the source or be generated for execution on the destination.

text: Which two are true about a read-only Oracle home? (Choose two.)

options.text: Its configuration data and log files reside in subdirectories under the Oracle home.
It is enabled by performing an Oracle Database installation with database creation and then running the roohctl -enable script.
It requires the Rapid Home Provisioning service.
It contains an image that can be distributed across multiple servers.
It is enabled by performing a software-only Oracle Database installation and then running the roohctl -enable script.

explanation:
D and E are correct. A read-only Oracle home keeps the software image unmodified and relocates writable configuration and log data outside the home, so the same image can be distributed across servers. E is the supported enablement path: install database software in software-only mode, then use roohctl -enable. A is false because configuration and logs are separated from the read-only software home, not stored under its directories. B is false because a database-creation installation is not the stated software-only conversion workflow. C is false because a read-only home does not require Rapid Home Provisioning; RHP can help provision homes but is not a prerequisite. The operational benefit is simpler patch/image distribution and reduced per-home drift. Before enabling, review the documented restrictions and ensure the external Oracle base/configuration paths have appropriate ownership, permissions, and backup handling.

A read-only Oracle home separates reusable software binaries from host/database-specific writable configuration and diagnostic data. Its purpose is not to deny the database any writable files; those files are relocated to the appropriate Oracle base configuration and home directories.

```text
$ORACLE_HOME/bin/roohctl -enable
```

Enable the layout at the supported point after software-only installation and before creating/configuring databases in that home. This explains why B's create-database-first sequence is wrong. The resulting software image can be reused in deployment workflows without requiring every server to share one runtime configuration. C confuses a layout feature with Fleet/Rapid Home Provisioning: provisioning tools can use reusable homes, but they are not required simply to enable the read-only layout. In a lab, compare the Oracle home and Oracle base home/config paths before and after enabling the layout, and verify where Net configuration and diagnostic files actually reside rather than editing the original home path by habit.

mnemonic.anchor: E is the supported enablement path: install database software in software-only mode, then use roohctl -enable.

text:
Some archived log backups have been accidentally deleted from storage.

Which two commands should be used to update the status of backups in the recovery catalog to display only the missing backups? (Choose two.)

options.text: RESYNC CATALOG
REPORT OBSOLETE
LIST ARCHIVELOG ALL
CROSSCHECK BACKUP OF ARCHIVELOG ALL
LIST ARCHIVELOG
LIST EXPIRED

explanation:
CROSSCHECK compares RMAN repository records with actual backup pieces. Missing pieces are marked EXPIRED; LIST EXPIRED then reports them, so D and F are required. RESYNC CATALOG synchronizes catalog metadata, not file availability. REPORT OBSOLETE evaluates retention policy, a different issue. LIST ARCHIVELOG ALL lists archived logs, not only missing backups. In practice, crosscheck the device type, review expired entries, and investigate before DELETE EXPIRED removes their repository records. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.  Remember that repository status and physical file state are separate facts; repeat checks after media maintenance.

CROSSCHECK reconciles repository records with accessibility of the corresponding physical pieces. It does not delete the missing records, and it does not delete a still-existing backup merely because that backup is old. A missing piece becomes EXPIRED; OBSOLETE instead means that the retention policy no longer requires a backup.

```text
CROSSCHECK BACKUP OF ARCHIVELOG ALL;
LIST EXPIRED BACKUP OF ARCHIVELOG ALL;
```

Run the crosscheck using channels and credentials that can genuinely access the storage. A disconnected mount or unavailable media manager can otherwise make healthy pieces appear missing. LIST alone reports repository state and cannot discover a deletion that occurred outside RMAN. RESYNC CATALOG copies metadata from the target control file rather than probing every backup location. Delete expired metadata only after establishing that the apparent loss is permanent; an expired piece that becomes accessible again can be crosschecked back to AVAILABLE. This distinction prevents a transient storage outage from becoming an unnecessary repository cleanup.

sources.title: Maintaining RMAN backups and repository records

mnemonic.anchor: CROSSCHECK compares RMAN repository records with actual backup pieces.

text: Which three are true about post-upgrade activities when upgrading an Oracle database using Database Upgrade Assistant? (Choose three.)

options.text: The Oracle Application Express configuration should be updated after upgrading Oracle Database.
Time zone files must be upgraded manually using the DBMS_DST PL/SQL package.
Any Recovery Manager (RMAN) recovery catalog must be upgraded manually.
The new extended data type capability must be enabled by running the utlrp.sql script.
After a manual upgrade, TNSNAMES.ORA entries must be updated to reflect the new ORACLE_HOME.

explanation:
A and C are the clear post-upgrade administration topics, and E is the intended third choice only when read as migrating/reviewing Oracle Net configuration after a manual upgrade. The stem mixes DBUA and manual-upgrade contexts, so that third choice needs a qualification.

Option A concerns the installed APEX release and its configuration. Review the appropriate APEX upgrade/post-installation instructions rather than assuming a database dictionary upgrade configures every APEX component automatically. Option C is true: a separate recovery catalog schema is upgraded using its supported RMAN catalog-upgrade workflow, not by upgrading one target database with DBUA.

Option B is false as an unconditional statement. DBUA offers an Upgrade Time Zone Data option; manual DBMS_DST work is needed if that operation was not selected or requires a separate supported plan. D is false because utlrp.sql recompiles invalid objects; extended string types use MAX_STRING_SIZE and the documented conversion procedure.

Option E should not mean that every tnsnames connect descriptor contains ORACLE_HOME. It normally contains listener addresses and service names. Following manual upgrades, copy or migrate the required Net files and update configuration that actually references old paths, especially static listener entries. A shared TNS_ADMIN can make rewriting local descriptors unnecessary. Thus A,C,E is a provisional interpretation of the intended upgrade checklist, with E's path wording and the manual/DBUA context explicitly qualified.
review_note: B is not universally manual because DBUA can upgrade time-zone data. E is accepted only as Net configuration migration/review after manual upgrade; connect descriptors do not normally contain ORACLE_HOME.

sources.title: Upgrading using DBUA and time-zone options

mnemonic.anchor: The stem mixes DBUA and manual-upgrade contexts, so that third choice needs a qualification.

text: Which four are true about configuring CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP by using RMAN? (Choose four.)

options.text: The control file is backed up automatically each time the SPFILE is backed up manually.
The control file is backed up whenever an RMAN backup is successfully recorded in the catalog.
It requires the use of fast recovery area (FRA).
The control file is backed up whenever a new table is created.
The control file is backed up whenever a new tablespace is created.
The server parameter file (SPFILE) is automatically backed up each time the control file is backed up.

original_text: Which three are true about configuring CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP by using RMAN? (Choose three.)
review_note: The source Choose three omits A when CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP is enabled. F assumes the instance uses an SPFILE; a text-PFILE startup has no SPFILE to back up.

text: Which three are true about cloning databases into an existing CDB with RMAN? (Choose three.)

options.text: A user with SYSDBA or SYSBACKUP must be logged in with RMAN to the non-CDB being cloned when cloning a non-CDB.
The target and auxiliary instance passwords must be the same.
Two or more PDBs can be cloned with the same command.
A non-CDB can be cloned into a PDB.
Only one PDB can be cloned at a time.
A user with SYSDBA or SYSBACKUP must be logged in with RMAN to CDB$ROOT when cloning a PDB.

explanation:
B,E,F is the supported Oracle 19c existing-CDB duplication answer. The feature is active duplication of one source PDB into an already existing destination CDB. It must not be confused with duplicating a whole CDB that contains several PDBs, or with SQL adoption of a non-CDB.

Option B is true for the password-file authenticated active-duplication setup: the relevant SYS/SYSBACKUP credentials in source and auxiliary password files must match. E is explicit in the restrictions: only one PDB can be duplicated at a time into an existing CDB. F identifies the source connection scope: connect to the source CDB root as an appropriately privileged common user, not merely to a local tenant account.

Options A and D are false for this RMAN 19c feature because duplicating a non-CDB as a PDB in an existing CDB is not supported. C is false because the existing-CDB operation does not duplicate two or more PDBs in one command. A different DUPLICATE workflow for a whole CDB does not make C true for the stated destination type.

Prepare network connectivity, auxiliary root access, compatible source/destination settings and file naming before issuing DUPLICATE. On completion, inspect the destination PDB's open mode and its independent identity, and take a backup. The distinction is destination scope: a new whole-CDB duplicate and a PDB duplicate into an existing CDB have different syntax and restrictions. Privilege requirements and a matching password file alone do not bypass the one-PDB limitation.

original_options.text: A user with SYSDBA or SYSBKUP must be logged in with RMAN to the non-CDB being cloned when cloning a non-CDB.
The target and auxiliary instance passwords must be the same.
