A non-CDB can be cloned into a PDB.
Only one PDB can be cloned at a time.
A user with SYSDBA or SYSBKUP must be logged in with RMAN to CDB$ROOT when cloning a PDB.

mnemonic.anchor: B,E,F is the supported Oracle 19c existing-CDB duplication answer.

text: Which two are true about creating pluggable databases (PDBs) in Oracle 19c and later releases? (Choose two.)

options.text: A snapshot copy PDB can be a full copy of a source PDB.
A PDB snapshot can be a sparse copy of a source PDB.
A snapshot copy PDB does not depend on an existing storage snapshot of the source PDB.
A PDB snapshot depends on an existing storage snapshot of the source PDB.
A PDB snapshot can be a full copy of a source PDB.

explanation:
A PDB snapshot may be sparse when storage supports it or full otherwise, making B and E the keyed choices. A snapshot-copy PDB clone is a separate storage-aware operation and depends on storage snapshot capability, so C is not generally true. D confuses that dependency with whether every PDB snapshot must use a pre-existing storage snapshot. The terminology is easy to conflate; A is not the intended keyed statement. Sparse copies save space but depend on snapshot/source storage, whereas full copies use more space and are independent. Check the 19c cloning documentation for the storage platform in use. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

Do not equate a named PDB snapshot with a snapshot-copy PDB. A PDB snapshot is a point-in-time archive used by the PDB snapshot feature; on supported sparse-file storage the first snapshot can be full and later snapshots sparse. A snapshot-copy PDB is a space-efficient clone dependent on its supporting storage snapshot or sparse-copy arrangement.

```sql
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE sales SNAPSHOT sales_before_change;
```

For planning, identify whether the requested object is an archive snapshot, an independently materialized full PDB, or a storage-dependent snapshot-copy clone. Their lifecycle and space requirements differ. The mere presence of the word snapshot does not guarantee that the PDB is an independent physical copy or that its underlying parent can be removed. Use the documented snapshot views and storage support checks to inspect the actual arrangement before deleting parent files. The full-versus-sparse distinction supports B and E without treating snapshot-copy PDBs and named PDB snapshots as interchangeable terms.

mnemonic.anchor: A PDB snapshot may be sparse when storage supports it or full otherwise, making B and E the keyed choices.

text:
SQL Performance Analyzer (SPA) has reported several regressed SQL statements for one of your databases.

Which action could help in the performance management of these regressed SQL statements?

options.text: Create SQL plan directives for each of the regressed statements.
Use the SQL Tuning Advisor for each of the regressed statements.
Use the SQL Access Advisor for each of the regressed statements.
Create an adaptive execution plan for each of the regressed statements.

explanation:
SQL Tuning Advisor is the targeted tool for individual regressed statements SPA identifies (B). It can recommend statistics changes, SQL profiles, or other statement-level actions. SQL Access Advisor (C) focuses on workload access structures such as indexes and materialized views. SQL plan directives (A) are optimizer metadata, not a routine manual fix for each regression. Adaptive plans (D) are optimizer behavior, not something created as a tuning step per statement. SPA detects and compares performance but does not repair it. Inspect plans and recommendations, test changes with representative binds and workload, and verify before production. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

SPA identifies which individual statements changed their execution performance under the tested system change. SQL Tuning Advisor then investigates candidate causes and can recommend actions such as improved statistics, SQL profiles, access-path changes, or SQL restructuring. Its recommendations still require validation against the application's workload and change policy.

For example, capture the regressed statement's old and new plan, compare its elapsed time and execution statistics in the SPA report, and run the tuning task for that specific SQL. A SQL profile is not equivalent to creating a SQL plan directive by hand, so A is not the automatic next action. SQL Access Advisor primarily evaluates physical access structures across a workload; C is not the most direct diagnostic answer. D is not a general manual command that repairs every regression merely by creating an adaptive plan. After applying a justified change, repeat the comparison and confirm both the regressed statement and the broader workload benefit.

mnemonic.anchor: SQL Tuning Advisor is the targeted tool for individual regressed statements SPA identifies (B).

text: Which two restrictions apply when the RMAN BACKUP AS COPY command is used to create a backup? (Choose two.)

options.text: Backups can be written only if checksums are stored for each block.
Binary compression cannot be applied to the backup.
Backups can be written only to disk.
Backups can be written only to media.
Backups can be taken only if a fast recovery area is configured.
Backups can be taken only for data files.

explanation:
BACKUP AS COPY creates an image copy, not an RMAN backup set. Image copies are written to disk (C), not directly to SBT tape (D); RMAN backup-set compression does not apply (B). Checksums are not a prerequisite (A), and an FRA is optional (E). F is too narrow because supported files besides datafiles can be copied. Image copies can be switched into place quickly but consume disk space. For tape, use a backup set with an SBT channel. Balance restore speed against storage capacity. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

An image copy is a database-file copy that can be cataloged and, for supported file types, switched into service. Binary compressed backup sets use RMAN's backup-piece representation, so their format is different from an image copy; that is why B is a format restriction rather than a general claim that file-system compression is impossible.

```text
BACKUP AS COPY DATAFILE 5 FORMAT '/backup/users05.dbf';
```

The DISK device type is the supported destination for image-copy output. Tape/SBT output is a backup set, so C is true and D false. RMAN can copy eligible control files and archived logs as well as datafiles, making F too restrictive. An FRA is optional because FORMAT can identify another suitable disk destination. The checksum statement A confuses backup validation behavior with a prerequisite requiring preexisting stored block checksums. Decide between image-copy and backup-set strategies according to recovery procedures, capacity, incremental-merge use and media requirements, then validate the intended restore path.

sources.title: Backing up databases, control files and backup sets

mnemonic.anchor: BACKUP AS COPY creates an image copy, not an RMAN backup set.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. APP1_ROOT is an application container contained in CDB1.
3. APP1_ROOT$SEED is the application seed contained in APP1_ROOT and synchronized with APP1_ROOT.
4. APP1_PDB1 and APP1_PDB2 are application PDBs contained in APP1_ROOT.
5. APP1_USER_APP is an application installed in APP1_ROOT at version 1.0.
6. USER1 is a common user in APP1_ROOT and all its application PDBs, created when version 1.0 of APP1_USER_APP was installed.

You execute these commands:

```text
$ sqlplus sys/oracle@localhost:1521/cdb1 as sysdba

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=app1_root;
Session altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION app1_user_app BEGIN UPGRADE '1.0' TO '2.0';
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> GRANT CREATE SESSION TO USER1;
Grant succeeded.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION app1_user_app END UPGRADE TO '2.0';
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=app1_pdb1;
Session altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION app1_user_app SYNC;
Pluggable database altered.
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: USER1 can connect to APP1_ROOT and APP1_PDB1.
USER1 can connect only to APP1_ROOT.
USER1 can connect to APP1_ROOT, APP1_ROOT$SEED, and APP1_PDB1.
USER1 can connect only to APP1_PDB1.
USER1 can connect to CDB1.
USER1 is defined in APP1_PDB2.

explanation:
USER1 is an application common user in APP1_ROOT and its application PDBs. The grant was made during application upgrade; APP1_PDB1 was synchronized afterward and receives the upgraded definition, while APP1_PDB2 remains unsynchronized. Thus A and F are true. B and D omit applicable containers. C incorrectly treats the seed as the requested connection target. E confuses application-common with CDB-wide common user: it does not grant access to CDB1 root. Track application versions and synchronize each PDB after an application upgrade; out-of-sync PDBs do not receive new grants. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

The version1 common-user definition and the version2 privilege change are different pieces of application state. Existing application PDB2 already knows the application-common USER1 from the installed first version; it does not automatically receive the later CREATE SESSION grant just because its root was upgraded. Application seed state likewise remains at its last synchronization until explicitly synchronized.

In a lab, connect to each container and inspect both the user definition and its effective CREATE SESSION privilege. Existence in DBA_USERS does not prove login authorization. The displayed successful SYNC in APP1_PDB1 replays the version2 grant there, while the root already has it from the upgrade session. Nothing in this application-local grant creates a CDB-root common user or grants access to CDB1, so E does not follow. The two results are A for the updated root/PDB1 access and F for the already-installed user definition in PDB2.

sources.title: Multitenant architecture and application root clones

text:
A container database, CDB1, contains a pluggable database PDB1. Another container database is called CDB2. You want to relocate PDB1 from CDB1 to CDB2 with near-zero down time.

Which three are required? (Choose three.)

options.text: CDB2 must be in archivelog mode.
CDB1 and CDB2 must both be in local UNDO mode.
CDB2 must be in shared UNDO mode only.
CDB1 must be in shared UNDO mode only.
CDB1 must be in archivelog mode.
CDB1 and CDB2 must be in shared UNDO mode.

explanation:
Online PDB relocation uses redo to synchronize the destination while the source remains available. Both CDBs must be in ARCHIVELOG mode (A,E), and both must use local undo for this workflow (B). Shared-undo-only choices C, D, F are wrong. The source must archive redo too; it is not just a destination requirement. Verify modes, compatible releases, connectivity, and storage before starting. Near-zero downtime still includes a final cutover and depends on successful synchronization; it does not promise literally zero interruption. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

ABE is the intended fully online relocation configuration, but the word required is broader than the current SQL prerequisites. The source must use local undo for the online block/redo/undo copy. The database link and receiving root need the documented privileges, compatible options, file access and destination space as well.

Oracle's current SQL relocation description explicitly allows a target CDB not in ARCHIVELOG mode, with a read-only target phase during the operation. It specifically lists source local undo, rather than stating every destination must already be in local undo. DBCA's documented remote-relocation prerequisites are stronger in their archive-mode wording. Therefore do not extrapolate B's both-CDB statement or A's target-archive statement into an unconditional rule for every SQL relocation path.

During cutover, Oracle drains/redirects sessions, completes recovery and opens the destination; the source closes. Verify forwarding and service state and plan application behavior during the brief cutover. Near-zero downtime is not a promise that all sessions and uncommitted transactions survive unchanged. ABE is retained provisionally to describe the intended archivelog/local-undo online design; the question should state its DBCA/SQL workflow and target-phase assumptions explicitly before those settings can be called universally required.
review_note: ABE is the intended fully online design, not a universal SQL requirement. Current SQL docs require source local undo and permit a NOARCHIVELOG target with read-only operation phase.

sources.title: PDB relocation prerequisites and target read-only phase

mnemonic.anchor: Online PDB relocation uses redo to synchronize the destination while the source remains available.

text:
Examine this command:

```text
$ rhpctl move database -sourcehome Oracle_home_path -destinationhome Oracle_home_path
```

For which two purposes can you use this command? (Choose two.)

options.text: to switch an existing Oracle Database home to a newer release of Oracle software on the same server
to switch to a read-only Oracle home
to switch back to the previous Oracle home as part of a rollback operation
to switch the Oracle Database home when using a centralized Rapid Home Provisioning server
to switch to a patched Oracle Database home

explanation:
RHP move database switches a database to another prepared Oracle home. It can move to a patched home (E) and switch back to the previous home for rollback (C). It does not itself perform a major release upgrade (A); the destination home must already be installed. B is a separate read-only-home configuration. D confuses centralized RHP provisioning with this move operation. Stage and validate the destination home, check compatibility and services, perform the switch, and retain the old home through the rollback window. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

The operation switches the database's associated executable home; it does not use the word move to mean copying every datafile into the software directory. A patched home can be prepared out of place, then the instance resources and patch SQL steps are handled according to the supported workflow. Moving back to a suitable prior home is a rollback operation, subject to patch compatibility and any required SQL rollback.

Do not use this patching command as a substitute for a major-release database upgrade. The dictionary-upgrade phase and target-release prerequisites require the appropriate upgrade operation. Similarly the command is not the roohctl operation that enables a read-only home. The displayed sourcehome/destinationhome form represents the independent-home automaton; managed Fleet Patching and Provisioning examples instead use working-copy syntax such as patchedwc. Inspect rhpctl help and patch inventory for the installed RU before executing a maintenance plan, and distinguish a centralized service requirement from an available server-managed workflow.
review_note: CE is the intended patch/rollback purpose. The displayed independent-home syntax differs from managed-working-copy syntax in the current FPP reference; check installed-version help.

sources.title: Fleet Patching and Provisioning database operations

mnemonic.anchor: RHP move database switches a database to another prepared Oracle home.

text: Which three are true about recovering tables using RMAN? (Choose three.)

options.text: RMAN can recover tables owned by the SYS user.
RMAN can recover tables in the SYSAUX tablespace.
RMAN can recover tables owned by the SYSTEM user.
RMAN can recover a table after a DDL operation has altered the table structure.
RMAN can recover tables in the SYSTEM tablespace.
RMAN can recover tables in a standby database.
RMAN always uses an auxiliary instance.

explanation:
RMAN table recovery uses an auxiliary instance to restore to a point in time and import the recovered table (G). It supports SYSTEM-owned tables (C) and recovery across later DDL changes (D). It does not support SYS-owned tables (A), tables located in SYSTEM or SYSAUX (E,B), or standby tables (F). Ownership and tablespace placement differ: SYSTEM-owned is not the same as stored in SYSTEM. Verify both, ensure backups and archived redo cover the target, and reserve auxiliary space. Resolve name conflicts and check dependent objects after import. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

The owner and the tablespace restrictions are independent. A table owned by SYSTEM can be recoverable if it resides in an eligible user tablespace; that does not authorize recovery of a table physically stored in SYSTEM or SYSAUX. SYS-owned objects and tables from a standby database are outside the listed table-recovery support.

RMAN restores the needed database state into an auxiliary environment, recovers it to the requested historical point, then uses Data Pump to export the recovered table and optionally import it into the target. This is why it can recover the table as it existed before a later DDL change, rather than requiring current undo to undo the structure change in place. Plan AUXILIARY DESTINATION and Data Pump dump space, verify that required backups and archived redo cover the target time, and consider renaming/remapping the import to inspect recovered rows before replacing anything used by the application. A successful restore of files alone is only one stage of table recovery.

sources.title: RMAN table and partition recovery restrictions

mnemonic.anchor: RMAN table recovery uses an auxiliary instance to restore to a point in time and import the recovered table (G).

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is an Oracle container database from an older release.
2. PDB1, PDB2, PDB3, and PDB4 are pluggable databases in CDB1.

A priority list UpgrdList has these entries:
1, pdb2
2, pdb1, pdb3

You execute this command:

```text
$ /u01/app/oracle/product/18.1.0/db_1/rdbms/admin/dbupgrade -L UpgrdList
```

In which order will the upgrade occur?

options.text: CDB$ROOT, PDB1, PDB2, PDB3, and PDB4
CDB$ROOT, PDB2, PDB1, and PDB3
CDB$ROOT, PDB$SEED, PDB2, PDB1, PDB3, and PDB4
CDB$ROOT, PDB$SEED, PDB1, PDB3, PDB2, and PDB4
CDB$ROOT, PDB$SEED, PDB2, PDB1, and PDB3

explanation:
Option C is the correct answer. In a Multitenant container database upgrade using dbupgrade (catctl.pl), execution strictly follows these rules:

1. CDB$ROOT and PDB$SEED first: CDB$ROOT must always be upgraded first because all PDBs rely on the core root data dictionary and common components. Immediately following CDB$ROOT, PDB$SEED is upgraded so that the system template seed database matches the new release.

2. Priority List (-L UpgrdList): The priority list determines the order in which user PDBs are processed. PDB2 is specified with priority 1 (1, pdb2), so it is upgraded first among user PDBs. Next, PDB1 and PDB3 share priority 2 (2, pdb1, pdb3), so they are processed concurrently/in parallel using available worker processes.

3. Unlisted PDBs (PDB4): The -L option defines a priority schedule, not an inclusion or exclusion filter. Any PDB in the CDB that is not explicitly defined in UpgrdList is automatically assigned the lowest priority and upgraded last (unless explicitly excluded using the -C parameter). Therefore, PDB4 is upgraded after PDB1, PDB2, and PDB3.

Distractor analysis:
- A omits PDB$SEED and disregards the priority list ordering.
- B omits PDB$SEED and incorrectly drops PDB4.
- D reverses the priorities (processes priority 2 before priority 1).
- E is a common trap; it omits PDB4 under the false assumption that -L acts as an exclusion list.

The priority file controls relative order; it is not the same as an inclusion-only container list. Root and seed form the mandatory initial infrastructure, then lower-numbered priorities are processed first. PDB2 has priority1, PDB1/PDB3 share priority2, and an unlisted eligible PDB is processed according to the utility's default trailing priority.

For a lab, use the tool's documented dry-run or priority-reporting facilities before a production upgrade, and read the generated per-container logs. A comma-separated line sharing a priority groups containers at that priority; it should not be mistaken for a guarantee that two PDBs start and finish in one exact serial order when parallel workers are enabled. C is the conceptual ordering available among these choices. Check all PDB open states and upgrade eligibility separately: a priority list does not fix a mounted/incompatible tenant or automatically substitute for the utility's container inclusion/exclusion options.
review_note: C gives priority groups. PDB1/PDB3 can be processed in the same priority group, so their exact serial completion order is not guaranteed.

mnemonic.anchor: In a Multitenant container database upgrade using dbupgrade (catctl.pl), execution strictly follows these rules: 1.

text: Which three are true about changing the LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED property to false in a CDB? (Choose three.)

options.text: After the change, only a common user with the required privilege can create an undo tablespace in CDB&ROOT.
Any new PDB and existing PDBs are automatically configured to use the default undo tablespace in CDB$ROOT.
After the change, only one undo tablespace can exist in CDB$ROOT.
After the change, any user with the required privilege can create an undo tablespace in the PDBs.
Undo tablespaces existing in PDBs must be dropped before the change.
After the change, each existing PDB has to be reopened for the new undo mode to take effect.

explanation:
A,B,F are true in the intended shared-undo interpretation, so the count is corrected to three. Switching the CDB to shared undo makes root-hosted undo service the PDBs; the new mode applies to a container when it is first opened after the change. A container does not continue permanently using its former local undo merely because the old undo tablespace files still exist.

Option A follows root privilege scope: an ordinary local PDB user cannot create an undo tablespace in CDB$ROOT; an appropriately privileged common user can. B describes the shared-undo outcome for existing and subsequently created PDBs. F describes the first-open transition for an existing PDB. In RAC, shared undo still means a root undo tablespace per active instance, not one physical undo tablespace for the entire cluster.

Option C is false: only one active undo tablespace per instance does not mean only one undo tablespace may exist in root. D is false because tenant-local undo management is not available in shared undo mode. E is false: old local undo tablespaces need not be preemptively dropped to permit the mode change.

Inspect DATABASE_PROPERTIES from the root, perform the documented restricted upgrade/startup transition, restart as required, and verify each reopened PDB. Plan the mode change as a database-wide maintenance operation and account for its consequences for cloning, relocation, PDB flashback and point-in-time recovery.
original_text: Which two are true about changing the LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED property to false in a CDB? (Choose two.)
review_note: B also describes the shared-undo outcome; original select-two is inconsistent. Shared undo uses root undo per instance, and the new mode takes effect on each container first open.

mnemonic.anchor: A,B,F are true in the intended shared-undo interpretation, so the count is corrected to three.

text:
While backing up to an SBT channel, you determine that the read phase of your compressed Recovery Manager (RMAN) incremental level 0 backup is a bottleneck. FORCE LOGGING is enabled for the database.

Which two could improve read performance? (Choose two.)

options.text: Increase the size of tape I/O buffers.
Disable FORCE LOGGING for the database.
Increase the size of the database buffer cache.
Enable asynchronous disk I/O.
Increase the level of RMAN multiplexing.

explanation:
The bottleneck is disk reading during compressed level 0 streaming to tape. Asynchronous disk I/O (D) and increased RMAN multiplexing (E) can improve concurrent read throughput. Larger tape buffers (A) target tape-side buffering, not the stated bottleneck. A larger database buffer cache (C) generally does not speed RMAN direct reads. Disabling FORCE LOGGING (B) risks protection and does not solve disk reads. Measure storage, CPU, channel count, and tape rates; excessive multiplexing can hurt restore time. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

RMAN's disk read phase is different from the output phase and the CPU copy/compress phase. Tape-buffer enlargement addresses output streaming, while buffer-cache resizing generally does not accelerate RMAN's direct file-read path. FORCE LOGGING affects redo for eligible database operations, not the reading of existing blocks for a backup.

Asynchronous disk I/O can allow requests to overlap, while appropriate multiplexing interleaves reads from multiple input files and may keep storage busy. More is not always better: excessive multiplexing can reduce per-file buffer sizes or create seek contention, and compressed backups can become CPU-bound even after source I/O improves. Compare channel statistics and operating-system throughput before and after one change, and verify enough CPU for compression and a destination that can sustain the resulting stream. A read bottleneck should be supported by measured channel read behavior rather than inferred solely from the total backup duration.

sources.title: Diagnosing RMAN read, write and copy bottlenecks

mnemonic.anchor: The bottleneck is disk reading during compressed level 0 streaming to tape.

text: Which two are true about SQL Performance Analyzer (SPA)? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is integrated with the SQL Access Advisor.
It predicts the impact of system changes on SQL workload response time.
It provides before and after execution statistics for each SQL statement in the analysis task
It offers fine-grained analysis of all the SQL statements in the analysis task as a group.
SQL statements that were originally run concurrently are run concurrently by SPA.

explanation:
SPA predicts SQL workload impact from system changes (B) and compares before/after statistics for statements in its task (C). It is not integrated with SQL Access Advisor as A says. Its analysis is fine-grained by statement, not just group-level (D). It does not necessarily preserve original concurrency (E). Use it to test upgrades, parameter changes, or optimizer statistics changes against a captured workload. SPA estimates under test conditions, not guaranteed production performance. Follow up regressions with tuning tools and realistic validation. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

SPA normally tests statements individually under controlled conditions, comparing a baseline trial with another trial after a proposed change. It is not a full concurrent workload replay engine. Database Replay is the separate tool for evaluating workload concurrency and interactions, so E is false and D's group-only wording misses SPA's per-statement diagnosis.

For example, capture SQL and its execution context in a SQL tuning set, create a pre-change execution trial, apply the proposed optimizer or system change in the test environment, then create a post-change trial. Compare the chosen metric and inspect the SQL responsible for the largest regressions or improvements. The collection must represent the application's workload and bind conditions; a clean result for an incomplete sample cannot guarantee all production SQL is unaffected. Integration with SQL Tuning Advisor helps investigate specific regressed statements, whereas SQL Access Advisor has a different physical-design focus. Preserve both trials so a later tuning action can be evaluated against the same baseline.

mnemonic.anchor: SPA predicts SQL workload impact from system changes (B) and compares before/after statistics for statements in its task (C).

text:
A user complains about poor database performance. You want to verify if the user's session has waited for certain types of I/O activity.

Which view displays all waits waited on by a session at least once?

options.text: V$SESSION_EVENT
V$SESSTAT
V$SESSION_WAIT
V$SESSION_WAIT_CLASS
V$SESSION

explanation:
V$SESSION_EVENT accumulates wait statistics by session and event, including events waited on earlier (A). Filter by SID and inspect counts. V$SESSION_WAIT shows a current or latest wait, not full history (C). V$SESSTAT contains session statistic counters (B), V$SESSION_WAIT_CLASS aggregates by class (D), and V$SESSION shows current state (E). Compare counter deltas over a time interval and correlate SID/serial number; long-lived session totals may include irrelevant old waits. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.  Use event names to distinguish physical read waits from other I/O, and avoid drawing conclusions from a single sample.

V$SESSION_EVENT accumulates wait-event statistics for a session, such as total waits and time waited for an event since the session began. It answers whether the session has experienced an event over its lifetime, rather than merely which wait is current at the instant of the query.

```sql
SELECT event, total_waits, time_waited
FROM v$session_event
WHERE sid=:session_id
ORDER BY time_waited DESC;
```

Use V$SESSION or the current/last-wait interfaces for an immediate observation. V$SESSTAT contains session statistics rather than the same per-event history. V$SESSION_WAIT_CLASS aggregates at the broader wait-class level rather than listing all individual events. A large cumulative total does not prove that the event is the current complaint: take two measurements over the relevant interval, confirm the SID/SERIAL# identity, and correlate with the SQL and service involved. Session reuse and long connection lifetimes make absolute lifetime totals especially easy to misinterpret.

mnemonic.anchor: V$SESSION_EVENT accumulates wait statistics by session and event, including events waited on earlier (A).

text: Which two are true about gathering optimizer statistics? (Choose two.)

options.text: Executing DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS while connected to CDB$ROOT gathers object statistics in all open PDBs except PDB$SEED.
Executing DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS while connected to a PDB opened in read/write mode gathers object statistics for that PDB.
Executing DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS while connected to CDB$ROOT gathers object statistics only in CDB$ROOT.
System statistics can be gathered only while connected to CDB$ROOT.
Executing DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS while connected to CDB$ROOT gathers object statistics in all open pluggable databases (PDBs)

explanation:
DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS follows current-container scope. In an open read/write PDB it gathers that PDB's object statistics (B); from CDB$ROOT it gathers root objects only (C), not all PDBs (A,E). System statistics are not restricted to CDB$ROOT (D). Connect to each PDB needing local statistics or use the appropriate cross-container procedure and privileges. Confirm container context and inspect timestamps afterward; locked or pending statistics can affect interpretation. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.  In multitenant maintenance, schedule collections so each container receives appropriate statistics without unintended plan churn.

The word database in a container-aware package must be interpreted in the current container's scope. A privileged call from CDB$ROOT is not an implicit catcon-style loop across tenants. The documented ROOT_TRIGGER_PDB preference pertains to an application root's metadata-linked objects; the CDB root does not trigger tenant collection through that preference.

```sql
SHOW CON_NAME
EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS(options=>'GATHER STALE');
```

Run this only in the intended maintenance container and inspect its statistics history afterward. To service several PDBs, connect to each appropriate tenant or use the documented automatic maintenance/container orchestration mechanism. System statistics and application-root behavior have separate multitenant rules, so D's only-root generalization is not a substitute for checking package operation scope. Recollecting everything indiscriminately can consume resources and invalidate plans; prefer a justified sampling, stale-object and publication policy rather than treating a root connection as a safe shortcut for an entire CDB.

mnemonic.anchor: DBMS_STATS.GATHER_DATABASE_STATS follows current-container scope.

text:
Examine this output:

```text
SQL> select pluggable_database, shares, parallel_server_limit
  2  from dba_cdb_rsrc_plan_directives where plan = 'MY_PLAN'
  3  order by pluggable_database;

PLUGGABLE_DATABASE            SHARES  PARALLEL_SERVER_LIMIT
------------------------- ---------- ----------------------
ORA$AUTOTASK                     100                       
ORA$DEFAULT_PDB_DIRECTIVE          1                      0
PDB1                               2                    100
PDB2                               2                     25
PDB3                               1                       

SQL> select name, value from v$parameter
  2  where name = 'resource_manager_plan';

NAME                  VALUE
--------------------- ------------------------------
resource_manager_plan MY_PLAN
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Any PDB not specified in the plan will be unable to execute statements in parallel.
PDB3 can use all available parallel execution processes at times.
PDB1 is always limited to 40% of the available system resources regardless of demand.
Any PDB not specified in the plan will be able to use a maximum of 16.5% of the available system resources.
PDB3 is guaranteed to receive at least 20% of the available system resources if there is enough demand.
PDB2 is guaranteed at least 25% of the available parallel execution processes if there is enough demand.

explanation:
PDB3 has no explicit PARALLEL_SERVER_LIMIT and can use all available parallel processes at times (B). ORA$DEFAULT_PDB_DIRECTIVE sets the limit to zero, preventing parallel execution in PDBs without their own directive (A). Shares do not impose a fixed 40% cap (C) or guarantee the percentages in D/E. PDB2's 25% limit is a ceiling, not a guaranteed minimum (F). Resource Manager shares divide resources under contention; distinguish them from hard limits and guaranteed allocations. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

Parallel-server limits are ceilings, while shares express relative entitlements under contention and available demand. A ceiling of zero on ORA$DEFAULT_PDB_DIRECTIVE prohibits parallel statement servers for unnamed PDBs covered by that directive. A blank PDB3 parallel limit does not impose PDB2's25% ceiling on PDB3; idle capacity can therefore be available to it.

PDB1's two shares out of the displayed2+2+1 user-PDB shares are not a perpetual40% ceiling, so C is false. An unnamed PDB's share entitlement is neither a universal16.5% nor independent of how many active tenants fall under the default directive. E's20% calculation depends on the actual competing PDBs and active directives; the display alone does not establish a universal minimum across every possible workload. F incorrectly turns PDB2's maximum25% parallel-server limit into a guaranteed allocation. In practice, test both a contention period and an idle-capacity period and inspect resource-manager metrics: low observed usage can reflect lack of demand, not necessarily throttling.

mnemonic.anchor: PDB3 has no explicit PARALLEL_SERVER_LIMIT and can use all available parallel processes at times (B).

text: Which two are true about the execution of operating system scripts starting from Oracle Database 19c? (Choose two.)

options.text: orainstRoot.sh can be executed automatically by the Database installer by using sudo or root credentials.
root.sh can be executed automatically by the Database Installer only if it is provided with root credentials.
The sudo password can be specified in a response file.
root.sh can be executed automatically by the Database installer only by using sudo credentials.
The sudo password must be specified in a response file.
The root password cannot be specified in a response file.

explanation:
Installer automation can run orainstRoot.sh using root or sudo credentials (A). The root password cannot be stored in a response file (F). B and D wrongly restrict root.sh automation to only one credential type. C and E incorrectly say the sudo password can or must be placed in the response file. Use documented privilege delegation and keep passwords out of files and logs. Verify sudo rights and platform-specific 19c installer options. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

Oracle 19c adds installer-driven execution of privileged root scripts using an explicitly configured root or sudo authentication method. The authentication method and the target privileged script are separate concepts: neither script is restricted exclusively to one of the two supported methods merely because it performs root work.

For unattended installation, use the supported installer options and prompt-based secret handling rather than embedding a root password in a plain response file. A response-file choice of authentication method is not the same as a response-file field containing the root password. This explains why A and F are the intended pair and why the sudo-only/root-only restrictions in B/D are false. C/E should not be read as instructions to store sudo credentials in installation templates. Test the permitted sudo command scope with the platform/security administrators before installation so that privilege delegation succeeds for the required scripts without granting arbitrary unrestricted administration.

mnemonic.anchor: Installer automation can run orainstRoot.sh using root or sudo credentials (A).

text:
Automatic Shared Memory Management is disabled for one of your database instances. Some SQL statements perform poorly due to excessive hard parse activity, thereby degrading performance.

What would be your next step?

options.text: Run the SQL Access Advisor.
Run the Memory Advisor for the shared pool.
Run the SQL Tuning Advisor.
Run the Memory Advisor for the Program Global Area.
Run the Memory Advisor for the System Global Area.

explanation:
Hard parses can indicate shared-pool pressure because Oracle repeatedly locates or creates cursor structures. With ASMM disabled, the Shared Pool Advisor estimates the effect of changing shared-pool size on parse time (B). SQL Access Advisor (A) recommends access structures; SQL Tuning Advisor (C) tunes statements. PGA Advisor (D) covers private work areas, while SGA Advisor (E) evaluates total SGA sizing. Check parse rates, cursor sharing, invalidations, and advisory data before adding memory; literal-heavy SQL or poor cursor reuse may be the real cause. Operationally, document the baseline and expected outcome before changing anything. Confirm the relevant container, release, privileges, and storage or device configuration; test on a representative nonproduction system where possible. Afterward, verify status and retain logs so the DBA can explain the result and recover safely if assumptions were wrong.

The symptom points to the shared pool, where parsed SQL and PL/SQL structures reside. A PGA advisor targets work areas such as sorts and hash joins, not the cache of reusable parsed statements. An SGA-wide advisor is more directly relevant to an automatically redistributed SGA budget; the question explicitly disables ASMM and asks for the next focused sizing investigation.

```sql
SELECT shared_pool_size_for_estimate, estd_lc_time_saved
FROM v$shared_pool_advice;
```

A memory recommendation is evidence to evaluate, not proof that every hard parse is caused by an undersized pool. Check literals instead of bind variables, invalidation, version counts and parse behavior as well. SQL Tuning Advisor diagnoses individual SQL execution opportunities; SQL Access Advisor evaluates physical structures, and neither is the first sizing answer for an observed shared-pool reuse problem. Compare parse CPU and library-cache behavior before and after a justified memory or application change, keeping the workload comparable so that apparent benefit is not merely a quiet measurement interval.

mnemonic.anchor: Hard parses can indicate shared-pool pressure because Oracle repeatedly locates or creates cursor structures.

text: Which two are true about flashback features in Oracle Database 19c and later releases? (Choose two.)

options.text: Flashback logs are automatically purged when DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET is set lower than the time they have already been retained.
Flashback logs are monitored and proactively deleted when beyond the retention period defined in DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET only after there is space pressure.
Flashback logs are monitored and proactively deleted when beyond the retention period defined in DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET before there is space pressure.
Flashback logs are monitored for being older than the retention period defined in DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET and can be deleted by an administrator written event trigger.
Flashback logs are automatically purged whenever the value of DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET is changed.

explanation:
Flashback Database uses flashback logs in the fast recovery area (FRA) to rewind data files, while DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET expresses a desired history window rather than guaranteeing an exact duration. A is true: when the target is lowered, logs older than the new target become eligible for removal. C is true because Oracle can monitor and proactively remove eligible logs before the FRA is full. B incorrectly delays cleanup until space pressure; D invents a user event trigger; E overstates the effect, since changing the target does not purge every log immediately. A guaranteed restore point is an important exception: Oracle retains flashback logs needed to honor it, even if doing so consumes FRA space. In operations, monitor FRA usage and the actual flashback window, and do not treat the target as a contractual recovery guarantee.

This is specifically the improved 19c FRA-management behavior, rather than the older model in which expired flashback history primarily disappeared under space pressure. Option B's word only is therefore decisive: it excludes the proactive deletion that makes C correct. Option E overstates A; increasing the target is not a request to purge all existing history, and reducing it makes only history beyond the new target eligible.

```sql
ALTER SYSTEM SET DB_FLASHBACK_RETENTION_TARGET=720;
SELECT oldest_flashback_time, retention_target
FROM v$flashback_database_log;
```

The example changes the desired window to twelve hours. Review the oldest available time and FRA usage afterward rather than assuming the target is a recovery guarantee. Guaranteed restore points impose separate preservation requirements and can prevent otherwise reclaimable flashback logs from being removed. D is not the supported management interface: Oracle creates and manages these files; do not delete them using a home-written trigger or filesystem cleanup job.

sources.title: Automatic deletion of expired flashback logs

mnemonic.anchor: A is true: when the target is lowered, logs older than the new target become eligible for removal.

text:
Examine these queries and their output:

```text
SQL> select log_mode from v$database;

LOG_MODE
------------
ARCHIVELOG

SQL> select property_name, property_value
  2  from database_properties where property_name like '%UNDO%';

PROPERTY_NAME                  PROPERTY_VALUE
------------------------------ ------------------------------
LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED             FALSE

SQL> select p.name, f.file#, t.name
  2  from v$containers p, v$datafile f, v$tablespace t
  3  where p.con_id = f.con_id
  4    and p.con_id = t.con_id
  5    and t.ts# = f.ts#
  6  order by 1, 2;

NAME                           FILE# NAME
------------------------------ ----- ------------------------------
CDB$ROOT                           1 SYSTEM
PDB1                              24 SYSTEM
PDB2                              16 SYSTEM
```

After a system crash, an instance restart and an attempted opening of the PDBs result in:

```text
SQL> startup
ORACLE instance started.
Database mounted.
Database opened.

SQL> alter pluggable database all open;
*
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-01157: cannot identify/lock data file 24 - see DBWR trace file
ORA-01110: data file 24: '/u01/oradata/V122CDB1/516000726D464D04E054000C29704164/datafile/o1_mf_system_dmj30kld_.dbf'
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Data file 24 can be recovered while PDB2 is opened.
Data file 24 must be recovered while the CDB is opened.
Data file 24 can be recovered while CDB$ROOT and PDB$SEED are opened.
Data file 24 cannot be recovered while the CDB is opened.
Data file 24 must be recovered while PDB2 is closed.

explanation:
Options A and C are correct. This is recovery of a PDB SYSTEM data file, not loss of CDB$ROOT's SYSTEM tablespace. The root can remain open and unaffected PDBs such as PDB2 can remain available while the damaged PDB is closed for restore and recovery. Sharing undo does not turn every tenant's SYSTEM-file failure into a requirement to close all tenants.

Option B says recovery must take place with the CDB open. Open-root recovery is possible, but the word must excludes the alternative of performing recovery with the CDB mounted. Option D incorrectly says open-root recovery is impossible. Option E incorrectly makes PDB2's closure a prerequisite; nothing about the described failure requires disrupting that unaffected tenant.

```text
RMAN> RESTORE DATAFILE 24;
RMAN> RECOVER DATAFILE 24;
```

Execute the appropriate RMAN restore/recovery while the affected PDB is closed and the CDB/root is in a supported recovery state, then open PDB1 after recovery succeeds. First confirm that file24 really belongs to PDB1 and that the backup and redo cover its recovery requirements. An OPEN failure identifies the inaccessible file; it does not by itself establish corruption of other PDBs. In a practical exercise, query V$DATAFILE with CON_ID from root, record PDB open modes, perform recovery, and verify that PDB2 stayed available throughout. This is an important operational advantage of container-level recovery, although root/control-file failures have broader scope.

mnemonic.anchor: This is recovery of a PDB SYSTEM data file, not loss of CDB$ROOT's SYSTEM tablespace.

text: Which two are true about RMAN duplexed backup sets? (Choose two.)

options.text: A duplexed backup set uses the same number of SBT channels as a non-duplexed backup set for the same number of files.
A non-duplexed backup set written to disk can be duplexed to disk by backing up the backup set that is already on disk.
A non-duplexed backup set written to SBT can be duplexed to tape by backing up the backup set that is already on tape.
A non-duplexed backup set written to disk can be duplexed to tape by backing up the backup set that is already on disk.
A non-duplexed backup set written to SBT can be duplexed to disk by backing up the backup set that is already on tape.
A duplexed backup set always uses twice as many SBT channels as a non-duplexed backup set for the same number of files.

explanation:
A duplexed backup set has multiple identical copies of each backup piece, normally created during the backup operation; it is not a general tape-copy feature. B is true: RMAN can back up an existing disk backup set to another disk destination. D is true: RMAN can read an existing disk backup set and write a copy to SBT. C and E are false because RMAN does not support copying an SBT backup set to tape or disk through this operation. A and F make incorrect universal claims about required SBT channel counts; channels depend on the configured job and device allocation, not a simple fixed one-versus-two rule. For resilience, duplex to distinct destinations or media where possible, and remember that two copies on the same failure domain do not protect against loss of that domain.

Distinguish creating several copies during an original BACKUP from backing up an existing backup set. BACKUP BACKUPSET reads existing disk pieces and can create additional copies on disk or write them to SBT. RMAN does not support reading an SBT backup set as input to BACKUP BACKUPSET for a tape-to-tape or tape-to-disk copy, which eliminates C and E.

```text
BACKUP DEVICE TYPE SBT BACKUPSET ALL;
```

Here the input is accessible disk backup sets; the output uses the media manager. Option F's automatic doubling of channel count is false: copies and channel parallelism are separate controls. A is less precise than the intended B/D pair. Duplexing can use the same configured number of channels as a nonduplexed backup, but the channel count is not an invariant guaranteed by the word duplexed: it remains a configuration choice, and tape duplexing also requires sufficient output devices. Thus A can describe a valid setup, rather than an unconditional requirement. If A is intended merely to say that extra channels are unnecessary, the question has a third defensible statement and should not be treated as an unambiguous select-two item.
review_note: B/D are the intended backup-existing-set capabilities. A can also describe valid duplexing with unchanged channel parallelism; its universal wording makes the select-two interpretation uncertain.

sources.title: Backing up databases, control files and backup sets

mnemonic.anchor: A duplexed backup set has multiple identical copies of each backup piece, normally created during the backup operation; it is not a general tape-copy feature.

text: Which three are true about RMAN persistent configuration settings, administration, and their effects? (Choose three.)

options.text: A target database's persistent RMAN configuration settings are always stored in the target's control file
Backup older than the recovery window retention policy are always deleted automatically if the backup location has insufficient space.
Backups written to the fast recovery area (FRA) that are obsolete based on the redundancy retention policy can be deleted automatically to free space.
The RMAN SHOW ALL command displays only settings with nondefault values.
A target database's persistent RMAN configuration settings are always synchronized automatically with the RMAN catalog.
The V$RMAN_CONFIGURATION view displays only settings with values that have been modified.
A DBA must specify either a redundancy retention policy or a recovery window retention policy.

explanation:
A, C, and F are correct. A: RMAN CONFIGURE settings for a target are stored in its control file; a recovery catalog can also hold repository metadata, but it does not replace the target control file as the persistent configuration store. C: when the FRA needs space, Oracle may automatically remove eligible obsolete files, subject to retention and file dependencies. F: V$RMAN_CONFIGURATION reports configured values that differ from defaults. B is too strong: a recovery window does not mean every old backup is automatically deleted just because some location is short on space. D misstates SHOW ALL, which reports configuration settings, including defaults. E wrongly says catalog synchronization happens automatically in all cases. G is false because RMAN has a default redundancy policy even if the DBA has not explicitly configured a recovery window. Operationally, run CROSSCHECK and DELETE OBSOLETE deliberately and monitor FRA pressure.

Persistent settings in the target control file let RMAN operate without a recovery catalog; a catalog adds a separate repository and longer-lived history but does not replace that target copy. SHOW ALL includes defaults, whereas V$RMAN_CONFIGURATION reports the persistent settings explicitly configured in the control file, explaining D versus F.

```text
SHOW ALL;
REPORT OBSOLETE;
```

Obsolete means unnecessary under the configured retention policy; expired means absent when crosschecked. Neither means every old backup in every arbitrary directory is automatically deleted. Automatic space reclamation applies to eligible FRA files when space is needed. Backups in other disk locations normally require explicit maintenance such as DELETE OBSOLETE. C should be read in that FRA eligibility/space-management sense, not as immediate deletion at the moment a newer backup changes redundancy. Catalog resynchronization also requires the relevant connections and operations, so E's always is too broad. Finally, there is a default redundancy policy; choosing a custom recovery window is useful planning, not a prerequisite to using RMAN.

mnemonic.anchor: C: when the FRA needs space, Oracle may automatically remove eligible obsolete files, subject to retention and file dependencies.

text: For which two requirements can you use the USER_TABLESPACES clause with the CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE command? (Choose two.)

options.text: to specify a default tablespace in a PDB cloned from another PDB in the same CDB.
to exclude all tablespaces except SYSTEM, SYSAUX, and TEMP when plugging in a PDB
to include specific user tablespaces only when relocating a PDB
to specify the list of user tablespaces to include when moving a non-CDB to a PDB
to exclude a temp tablespace when plugging in a PDB
to specify the list of tablespaces to include when creating a PDB from the CDB seed

explanation:
B and D are the valid uses. USER_TABLESPACES lets an administrator control which user tablespaces are included or excluded when plugging in a compatible database or PDB, while required SYSTEM, SYSAUX, and temporary structures are treated separately. B describes excluding user tablespaces so that only core tablespaces remain. D describes specifying user tablespaces to include during non-CDB-to-PDB conversion. A is wrong because choosing a default tablespace is unrelated to this clause. C overstates applicability to relocating an existing PDB. E misunderstands the clause as a TEMP selector; TEMP is not one of the user tablespaces being filtered this way. F is wrong because a PDB created from PDB$SEED is cloned from the seed rather than assembled by selecting user tablespaces. In migration planning, verify source metadata and preserve tablespaces needed by application schemas.

The SQL clause is USER_TABLESPACES, plural. It filters user tablespaces during supported plug/clone conversions; it does not specify the default tablespace for the new administrator, does not select the seed's system files for ordinary seed creation, and is not restricted exclusively to relocation. TEMP is not a selectable permanent user tablespace in the sense asserted by E.

```sql
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE salespdb USING '/stage/noncdb.xml'
  COPY USER_TABLESPACES=('SALES_DATA','SALES_INDEX');
```

This illustrates the purpose, not a complete production migration script: compatibility, file destinations and the non-CDB conversion procedure must also be satisfied. B's NONE-style use excludes the source's user tablespaces while preserving the required dictionary/system infrastructure. Its wording listing only SYSTEM, SYSAUX and TEMP must not be interpreted as a promise that local undo cannot exist; a local-undo PDB requires its undo infrastructure too. Review the file manifest and application dependencies before filtering a tablespace: omitting a user tablespace can leave an application's expected objects unavailable. The intended B/D answer therefore concerns user-data inclusion, with a qualification for B's abbreviated mandatory-tablespace list.
review_note: B is intended to describe excluding user tablespaces; the mandatory SYSTEM/SYSAUX/TEMP list is abbreviated and must not exclude local undo infrastructure.

sources.title: Plugging in unplugged PDBs and archives

original_text: For which two requirements can you use the USER_TABLESPACE clause with the CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE command? (Choose two.)

mnemonic.anchor: B describes excluding user tablespaces so that only core tablespaces remain.

text: Which three are true about Optimizer Statistics Advisor? (Choose three.)

options.text: It can be run only manually.
It is part of the DBMS_ADVISOR package.
It can recommend changes to improve the statistics gathering process.
It always analyzes all schemas in the database.
It runs automatically every night by default.
It is part of the DBMS_STATS package.

explanation:
C, E, and F are correct. Optimizer Statistics Advisor is implemented through DBMS_STATS, and its task evaluates statistics collection practices against Oracle recommendations. It can report actions that improve gathering quality or efficiency, so C is true; recommendations should be reviewed before changing production collection policy. The advisor runs automatically as part of the automated maintenance framework by default, making E true, although administrators can also manage tasks manually. It is not part of DBMS_ADVISOR (B), and it is not manual-only (A). D is false because its analysis scope depends on the task and configured filters; it does not necessarily inspect every schema. A useful DBA workflow is to review advisor findings alongside workload evidence, then adjust preferences or jobs and observe plan stability rather than blindly applying every recommendation.

Optimizer Statistics Advisor evaluates the quality of statistics-management practices, such as missing/stale statistics and collection preferences; it is not limited to investigating an individual SQL execution plan. It uses DBMS_STATS APIs, which makes F true and B's DBMS_ADVISOR claim incorrect for the advertised interface.

The predefined AUTO_STATS_ADVISOR_TASK runs automatically in the maintenance-window framework, normally once daily. E's every-night language is the conventional scheduled-window description, not a guarantee that a database with disabled or rescheduled maintenance still runs at a particular wall-clock time. A is therefore false. D's always/all-schemas claim also overstates the advisor's scope and execution: tasks have configuration, execution and object-selection rules.

```sql
SELECT DBMS_STATS.REPORT_ADVISOR_TASK('AUTO_STATS_ADVISOR_TASK')
FROM dual;
```

Read the findings and the proposed implementation script before applying changes. An advisor recommendation to adjust a global preference can affect many future collection jobs, so assess both a representative workload and the existing statistics-publication policy. This is how C's process improvement differs from simply gathering everything again.

mnemonic.anchor: Optimizer Statistics Advisor is implemented through DBMS_STATS, and its task evaluates statistics collection practices against Oracle recommendations.

text:
You issued this command:

```text
RMAN> BACKUP RECOVERY FILES;
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: All Oracle recovery files not in the current FRA that have not been backed up already, are backed up.
All non-Oracle files in the current FRA that have not been backed up already, are backed up.
All Oracle recovery files in the current FRA that have not been backed up already, are backed up.
All Oracle recovery files in the current fast recovery area (FRA) are backed up.
These backups can be written to disk or SBT.

explanation:
A and C are correct. BACKUP RECOVERY FILES selects Oracle recovery-related files that have not already been backed up, including eligible files outside the current FRA (A) and files in the current FRA (C). It is not a command to back up every file indiscriminately: already-backed-up files are excluded according to RMAN selection rules, so D is too broad. B is wrong because arbitrary non-Oracle files are not Oracle recovery files. E is not a safe general conclusion from the command syntax; available destinations depend on RMAN device configuration and the command rules, so do not infer that every target type is permitted. In practice, inspect the FRA configuration, device type, and RMAN output, and remember this command does not substitute for a deliberate retention and off-site strategy. Oracle 19c BACKUP reference also states RECOVERY FILES backups can go to SBT or disk (disk requires TO DESTINATION), so option E appears true too; the supplied key may be incomplete.

The important scope is Oracle recovery files, whether located inside or outside the current FRA. RECOVERY FILES considers the supported recovery-file types, not arbitrary files merely placed in an FRA directory. Backup optimization is automatically applied to this operation, so D's all-files interpretation ignores the already-backed-up filtering unless FORCE is added.

The unchanged command in the stem is significant. Although the RECOVERY FILES feature can write to disk, the documented disk form requires TO DESTINATION; without that clause the default output is SBT. Thus E is not selected for this exact bare command, while it would describe the broader feature when appropriately amended.

```text
BACKUP RECOVERY FILES TO DESTINATION '/backup/recovery_copy';
```

That example illustrates the separate disk-destination form, rather than silently adding a clause to the question's command. Verify available channels/media-manager configuration for the bare SBT form, then inspect LIST BACKUP and the command log to see which files optimization skipped. Copying recovery files is different from backing up ordinary non-Oracle content that happens to share the storage volume.
review_note: Retained A/C for the exact bare command. E is true as a broader feature capability only when the disk TO DESTINATION form is supplied; interpretation of its wording changes the count.

keywords: Oracle recovery files in the current FRA
mnemonic.anchor: It is not a command to back up every file indiscriminately: already-backed-up files are excluded according to RMAN selection rules, so D is too broad.

text: Which two are true about the Oracle database methodology? (Choose two.)

options.text: The Oracle Database time model should be used to find the database and instance areas most in need of tuning.
Tuning activities should stop once the user is satisfied with performance.
Tuning activities should stop once agreed service levels for performance have been met.
The database instance memory should always be tuned before tuning any file systems.
SQL statements should always be tuned before tuning any file systems.
The alert log should be used to find the database and instance areas most in need of tuning.

explanation:
A and C are correct. Oracle's performance method uses the time model, especially DB time and its breakdown, to find where sessions spend time and identify the dominant database or instance bottleneck. A is therefore the evidence-based starting point. C gives the stopping criterion: stop tuning when agreed service-level objectives are met, so effort remains tied to measurable business needs. B is weaker because subjective user satisfaction is not a clear engineering target. D and E prescribe a fixed tuning order regardless of evidence; memory, SQL, and storage should be investigated according to the measured bottleneck. F is also inadequate as a primary method: the alert log is essential for errors and events but does not quantify workload time distribution. In practice, compare representative time-model intervals, identify the top contributor to DB time, make one targeted change, and measure again.

Time-model statistics identify where database time is consumed; service objectives tell the DBA whether that consumption matters to the users and workload being investigated. These two views establish a useful starting point without presupposing that storage, SQL syntax, physical design or a particular memory component must always be the first culprit.

```sql
SELECT stat_name, value FROM v$sys_time_model
WHERE stat_name IN ('DB time','DB CPU');
```

Take interval deltas and compare them with response-time or throughput objectives for the affected service. Cumulative startup totals can conceal a recent regression. The rejected alternatives impose a rigid order, or treat an alert log as a complete performance diagnosis; an alert log is valuable for exceptional events but does not normally quantify all application response time. Once the dominant category is known, investigate its contributing SQL, waits or concurrency with appropriate evidence. Validate a change against the original user objective and a comparable load, rather than declaring success merely because a single wait event decreased.

mnemonic.anchor: A is therefore the evidence-based starting point.

text:
While backing up to the Oracle Fast Recovery Area (FRA), you determined the backup is taking too long and suspect a performance bottleneck.

Which three are true about diagnosing and tuning these problems? (Choose three.)

options.text: If an RMAN BACKUP VALIDATE command takes roughly the same time as an actual backup, then both read and write I/O are likely bottlenecks.
Setting DBWR_IO_SLAVES to a non zero value can improve backup performance when using synchronous I/O.
If an RMAN BACKUP VALIDATE command takes noticeably less than an actual backup, then write I/O is a likely bottleneck.
If an RMAN BACKUP VALIDATE command takes roughly the same time as an actual backup, then read I/O is a likely bottleneck.
Data files with a high value in V$BACKUP_SYNC_IO.DISCRETE_BYTES_PER_SECOND are a potential performance bottleneck when synchronous I/O is used.
Setting DBWR_IO_SLAVES to a non zero value can improve backup performance when using asynchronous I/O/
Data files with a high value in V$BACKUP_ASYNC_IO.SHORT_WAITS are a potential performance bottleneck when asynchronous I/O is used.

explanation:
B, C, and D are correct. BACKUP VALIDATE reads and checks source files without writing a normal backup set, so comparing its duration with a real backup helps separate source-read cost from destination-write cost. If validate is much faster than backup, destination writing is a likely bottleneck (C). If times are similar, source reads dominate (D); A's claim that both sides must be bottlenecks does not follow. B is correct for synchronous I/O: setting DBWR_IO_SLAVES above zero can let Oracle use I/O slave processes to simulate asynchronous I/O for backup operations. F describes asynchronous I/O, where this setting is not the same remedy. E reverses the interpretation of a high throughput rate, and G's SHORT_WAITS count alone is not direct proof of a bottleneck. Use RMAN I/O views and operating-system measurements to confirm before changing parameters.

The read, copy/CPU and write phases form a pipeline. BACKUP VALIDATE performs the read/validation work without writing the normal backup output; comparing it with the actual backup helps identify whether the destination/write phase is adding most of the elapsed time. It is an isolation technique, not proof that every difference is exclusively physical storage: compression, encryption and concurrency must remain comparable.

```text
BACKUP VALIDATE DATABASE;
```

Inspect synchronous/asynchronous I/O statistics and channel waits alongside elapsed time. Nonzero DBWR_IO_SLAVES can provide I/O slaves for synchronous platforms; it is not a way to improve native asynchronous I/O by making it synchronous. A high observed throughput alone does not establish a bottleneck without a capacity or demand baseline. Similarly, a count of short waits is not as persuasive as the time lost and the ratio of long waits to I/O requests. Change channel parallelism and buffering only after identifying the constrained phase, then check that the apparent improvement has not simply moved the bottleneck to CPU or the backup destination.

sources.title: Diagnosing RMAN read, write and copy bottlenecks

mnemonic.anchor: If validate is much faster than backup, destination writing is a likely bottleneck (C).

text:
You are managing this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. PDB1 and PDB2 are two pluggable databases in CDB1.
3. USER1.EMP is a table in PDB1 and USER2.DEPT is a table in PDB2.

CDB1 user SYS executes these commands after connecting successfully to PDB2:

```text
SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=pdb1;
Session altered.

SQL> INSERT INTO user1.emp VALUES(100, 'Alan', 1);
1 row created.

SQL> INSERT INTO user1.emp VALUES(101, 'Ben', 1);
1 row created.

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=pdb2;
Session altered.

SQL> INSERT INTO user2.dept VALUES(1, 'IT');
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The inserts on USER1.EMP remain uncommitted when the session connected to PDB2.
The inserts on USER1.EMP were committed when the session inserted a row into USER2.DEPT.
The insert on USER2.DEPT fails because of the active transaction in the parent container.
The insert on USER2.DEPT is a recursive autonomous transaction by the child session and is committed.
The inserts on USER1.EMP were rolled back when the session connected to PDB2.
The insert on USER2.DEPT is uncommitted.
The inserts on USER1.EMP were committed when the session connected to PDB2.

mnemonic.anchor: ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER changes the current container for the session; it does not commit or roll back the existing transaction.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is an Oracle Database 12c Release 2 database containing pluggable databases PDB$SEED, PDB1, and PDB2.
2. PDB$SEED is open READ ONLY
3. PDB1 is open READ WRITE
4. PDB2 is MOUNTED.
5. ORACLE_HOME is /u01/app/oracle/product/18.1.0/dbhome_1.

You execute these commands before upgrading the database to the current release:

```text
$ . oraenv
ORACLE_SID = [cdb1] ? cdb1
The Oracle base remains unchanged with value /u01/app/oracle

$ $ORACLE_HOME/jdk/bin/java -jar preupgrade.jar TERMINAL TEXT
```

For which databases will fixup scripts be created?

options.text: CDB1, PDB$SEED, PDB1, and PDB2
PDB$SEED, PDB1, and PDB2 only
CDB1 and PDB$SEED only
CDB1, PDB1, and PDB2 only
CDB1, PDB$SEED, and PDB1 only

explanation:
E is correct: fixup scripts are produced for CDB1 (the root), PDB$SEED, and PDB1, which are open in the stated configuration. PDB2 is mounted, so the preupgrade analysis does not inspect it as an open PDB and does not generate its fixup script. A includes PDB2 incorrectly; B omits the root; C omits open PDB1; D omits the seed. The question tests scope as well as the tool: preupgrade.jar must be run against the database and containers in appropriate states for useful checks. Before an upgrade, open every PDB that should be evaluated, review terminal output and generated logs, and run required fixups with the correct target Oracle home. A generated fixup script is an action artifact, not proof that every upgrade prerequisite is already satisfied.

The intended result is E: the legacy preupgrade tool can process the open containers, here CDB$ROOT, PDB$SEED and PDB1, but cannot complete the same checks for a mounted, unopened PDB2. Being listed in the control file is not equivalent to having its dictionary open and available to the tool.

```sql
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs;
```

Before the real preupgrade run, follow the target-release guide to open all intended PDBs in the required modes, confirm component health, and execute the generated fixups in the correct containers. A result covering only three containers is not evidence that the fourth PDB is ready for upgrade. The stated source release and ORACLE_HOME/tool path need care: upgrade tools may be supplied by a newer target home, and the path alone does not change the source database's release. Treat this as the described legacy preupgrade.jar scenario rather than a universal prediction for every later AutoUpgrade version or invocation. The open-state reasoning is the intended answer; a production command must match the documented source-to-target upgrade path and tool version.
review_note: E is the intended legacy preupgrade.jar open-container result; the source-release/tool-home details must be validated for an actual upgrade and do not specify every later tool behavior.

mnemonic.anchor: fixup scripts are produced for CDB1 (the root), PDB$SEED, and PDB1, which are open in the stated configuration.

text: Which two are true about Oracle Flashback features? (Choose two.)

options.text: FLASHBACK QUERY can retrieve REDO records from ONLINE and ARCHIVED REDO LOG files.
FLASHBACK VERSION QUERY can retrieve REDO records from ONLINE and ARCHIVED REDO LOG files.
FLASHBACK TABLE can undrop a column.
FLASHBACK DROP can undrop an index when undropping a table.
After a database is restored from flashback logs using the FLASHBACK DATABASE command, it is sometimes rolled forward using redo logs.

explanation:
D and E are correct. FLASHBACK DROP uses the recycle bin to restore a dropped table and can restore its dependent indexes along with it, so D is true. FLASHBACK DATABASE uses flashback logs to rewind data blocks to the chosen SCN or time, then applies redo as needed to reach a consistent target, making E true. A and B confuse logical flashback queries with redo-log mining: Flashback Query and Version Query reconstruct row versions using undo, not by returning redo records. C is not a general way to undrop a column; column handling and table structure have separate limitations. For recovery planning, distinguish row-level historical queries, recycle-bin recovery, and whole-database rewind. Each relies on different prerequisites: undo retention, recycle-bin retention, or flashback logging and FRA capacity.

Flashback Drop restores a retained recycle-bin object and eligible dependent objects such as indexes; it does not need to reconstruct every historical row from undo. By contrast, Flashback Query and Version Query use historical undo to present past row states. Their results are not a stream of redo records, so A/B describe a different mechanism.

```sql
FLASHBACK TABLE orders TO BEFORE DROP;
```

This requires an eligible table still available in the recycle bin, appropriate privileges, and handling any name collision. It is not a way to reverse every DDL operation, including an arbitrary DROP COLUMN. Flashback Database rewinds data-file blocks using flashback logs and may apply redo to arrive at a consistent target SCN, explaining E. Check that the desired target is reachable before assuming the configured retention target guarantees success. A practical comparison is to recover an accidentally dropped table from the recycle bin versus rewind the entire database after a deployment: the former has object scope, while the latter affects committed changes throughout its recovery scope and requires a much broader operational decision.

sources.title: Flashback query, archive and transaction technology

mnemonic.anchor: FLASHBACK DROP uses the recycle bin to restore a dropped table and can restore its dependent indexes along with it, so D is true.

text: Which three are true about an application seed pluggable database (PDB)? (Choose three.)

options.text: It is automatically synchronized with its application root PDB when an application is upgraded.
It cannot be added to an application container after the application container has already been created.
A new application PDB created by cloning an application seed PDB can have an old version of the application installed after cloning completes.
It is automatically synchronized with its application root PDB when an application is installed.
It cannot be dropped from its application container.
