A new application PDB created by cloning an application seed PDB can have an up-to-date version of the application installed after cloning completes.
It is not required in an application container.

explanation:
C, F, and G are correct. An application seed is optional, so G is true; an application container can exist without one. Cloning from the seed creates a copy of the seed's current application contents, which may be behind the application root if changes were made after the seed's last synchronization. Therefore a new application PDB can initially have an older application version (C), or it can be brought up to date after cloning by synchronizing or upgrading it (F). A and D wrongly assume the seed follows root changes automatically. B and E wrongly treat the seed as mandatory or undeletable. The practical lesson is to manage the seed lifecycle explicitly: synchronize it after application maintenance when fast, current clones are desired, but account for time and storage needed to upgrade a newly cloned PDB when the seed is stale.

An application seed is a reusable template, not an automatically updated mirror of its application root. Application maintenance in root and synchronization in member containers are separate steps. This explains why A and D are false and why a stale seed can produce a new application PDB initially containing an older version.

```sql
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION sales_app SYNC;
```

Run synchronization in the intended application seed or application PDB, using the appropriate application/version procedure. If the seed is current, a clone starts with that current application state; if not, synchronize or upgrade the clone as required before admitting traffic. B is false because the optional seed can be added after application-container creation, and E is false because it can be dropped using the documented lifecycle operations. G means an administrator can provision application PDBs without maintaining an application seed at all. In a lab, record the root and seed application versions, upgrade only root, create a clone from the unsynchronized seed, and compare versions before and after explicit synchronization.

sources.title: Multitenant architecture and application root clones

mnemonic.anchor: An application seed is optional, so G is true; an application container can exist without one.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. PDB1 and PDB2 are pluggable databases in CDB1.
3. PDB1 and PDB2 are OPEN in READ WRITE mode.

You execute these commands successfully:

```text
$ export ORACLE_SID=CDB1
$ sqlplus / as sysdba

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = PDB1;
Session altered.

SQL> SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Uncommitted transactions in PDB1 have been rolled back.
PDB1 is closed.
Uncommitted transactions in CDB1 and PDB1 have been rolled back.
CDB1 is shut down.
CDB1 is in MOUNT state

explanation:
A and B are correct. SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE issued while the session's current container is PDB1 shuts down that PDB, not the entire CDB. Immediate shutdown prevents new work, disconnects sessions, and rolls back uncommitted transactions in the target PDB. Therefore A and B are true. C is wrong because the command does not roll back transactions in CDB$ROOT. D and E are wrong because the CDB instance remains running and open; only PDB1 is closed. This differs from issuing SHUTDOWN while connected to the root, which affects the whole instance. In scripts, verify CON_NAME before shutdown commands and use explicit container-level administration to avoid disrupting unrelated PDBs. Afterward, check PDB status and reopen it when appropriate. Confirm the intended container in the session before running this command.

SQL*Plus SHUTDOWN is container-sensitive. In the supplied sequence, ALTER SESSION has moved the privileged session into PDB1, so IMMEDIATE closes that PDB and rolls back its unfinished work. It does not stop the CDB instance or move root from OPEN to MOUNT, and transactions in PDB2/root are not part of PDB1's shutdown.

```sql
SHOW CON_NAME
-- After reconnecting to the root:
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs;
```

Expect PDB1 to be MOUNTED while unaffected PDB2 remains READ WRITE. That mounted PDB state must not be confused with the whole CDB's MOUNT state. Before using this command in a maintenance script, check the active container and ensure application connection pools handle disconnection/reconnect appropriately. To resume service, open PDB1 from a suitable administrative connection and validate the service. The IMMEDIATE keyword avoids waiting for users to finish their transactions; a normal or transactional close has different waiting semantics. The question explicitly says the commands succeed, so there is no need to invent a privilege or shutdown-failure branch.

mnemonic.anchor: SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE issued while the session's current container is PDB1 shuts down that PDB, not the entire CDB.

text: Which three are true about Automatic Workload Repository (AWR), Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM), and the Manageability Monitor (MMON) background process? (Choose three.)

options.text: ADDM can recommend shrinking the buffer cache.
ADDM can recommend extending the buffer cache.
By default, MMON creates an AWR snapshot every 30 minutes.
ADDM performs its analysis only when a DBA requests it.
By default, AWR snapshots are automatically purged after eight days.
AWR snapshots must be deleted when no longer required by ADDM.

explanation:
A, B, and E are correct. ADDM analyzes AWR data and can recommend either reducing or increasing the buffer cache when its analysis indicates a different size could improve performance; it does not always recommend growth. MMON creates AWR snapshots at a one-hour default interval, so C's 30-minute value is incorrect. ADDM analysis is normally performed automatically after snapshots, so D's only-when-requested statement is false. The default AWR retention is eight days, making E correct. F is false: snapshots are retained according to configured retention and are not required to be manually deleted for ADDM. In real systems, check licensing and retention requirements before changing AWR settings, and treat ADDM findings as evidence to evaluate against workload patterns and service objectives.

AWR retains workload history; ADDM analyzes an interval of that history; MMON participates in automatic snapshot and manageability activity. Conflating these jobs leads to the false alternatives. Snapshot frequency and retention are separately configurable, and a retention setting is not the same thing as the period examined by a particular ADDM task.

```sql
SELECT snap_interval, retention FROM dba_hist_wr_control;
```

The default interval is one hour and default retention eight days. Baseline preservation and configured changes can alter what is retained, so E is a default-setting statement rather than a promise that every database purges every snapshot at exactly the eight-day instant. ADDM can identify an oversized cache wasting memory or an undersized cache causing avoidable I/O, explaining both A and B. A recommendation still needs workload validation; shrinking the cache solely because a quiet interval suggests little benefit can harm a later peak. Keep before/after snapshots that cover comparable business periods and measure the user-visible objective along with the suggested memory change.

mnemonic.anchor: MMON creates AWR snapshots at a one-hour default interval, so C's 30-minute value is incorrect.

text: Which two are true about requirements for various FLASHBACK operations? (Choose two.)

options.text: FLASHBACK transaction query requires undo to retrieve all versions of a row that existed between two points in time.
FLASHBACK drop requires that the RECYCLEBIN parameter be set to ON.
FLASHBACK version query requires that the RECYCLEBIN parameter be set to ON.
FLASHBACK DATA ARCHIVE requires undo to store all versions of all rows of a table being tracked.
FLASHBACK drop requires undo to retrieve all versions of a row that existed between two points in time.
FLASHBACK version query requires undo to retrieve all versions of a row that existed between two points in time.

explanation:
The defensible intended pair is B and F, with an important timing qualification for B. RECYCLEBIN must be enabled when an eligible table is dropped for its normal retention in the recycle bin. It does not have to remain ON at the later FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP invocation: switching it OFF does not purge or otherwise invalidate objects already retained. B should therefore describe drop-time eligibility, not an unconditional recovery-time setting.

Option F correctly identifies ordinary undo-based Flashback Version Query, which reconstructs row versions between two times while the necessary undo remains available. Option C is false: that row-history query does not use the recycle bin. Option E wrongly assigns the same undo mechanism to Flashback Drop, which restores retained segments and metadata.

Option A confuses two interfaces. Flashback Transaction Query identifies transaction changes and related information, whereas retrieving all row versions over an interval is Version Query's purpose. Option D is false as written: Flashback Data Archive stores long-lived row history in archive tables. Undo can participate in capturing recent changes, but it does not store the archive's entire retained history.

```sql
SELECT versions_startscn, versions_endscn, salary
FROM employees VERSIONS BETWEEN SCN :start_scn AND :end_scn
WHERE employee_id=100;
```

This example illustrates F, not Transaction Query or Flashback Drop. The original select-three count cannot be justified by pretending D says the opposite of its actual wording; the count has been corrected to two and the timing assumption is explicit.
original_text: Which three are true about requirements for various FLASHBACK operations? (Choose three.)
review_note: Original third answer D is false: FDA archives history in archive tables. B is valid for eligible-object drop-time recycle-bin retention, not a requirement that RECYCLEBIN remain ON at recovery time.

sources.title: Flashback query, archive and transaction technology

mnemonic.anchor: The defensible intended pair is B and F, with an important timing qualification for B.

text:
Examine the command for creating pluggable database PDB2 in container database CDB2.

```text
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb2
ADMIN USER pdb2_adm
IDENTIFIED BY "123pdb"
ROLES=(CONNECT);
```

Select three options, any one of which is required for it to execute successfully. (Choose three.)

options.text: Add the FILE_NAME_CONVERT clause to the statement and set the PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT parameter.
Add only the CREATE_FILE_DEST clause to the statement.
Set only the PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT parameter.
Set the PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT parameter and enable OMF.
Enable only OMF.
Add the FILE_NAME_CONVERT clause to the statement and enable Oracle Managed Files (OMF)

explanation:
B, C and E are the intended independent file-placement mechanisms. CREATE_FILE_DEST supplies a destination for Oracle-managed PDB files; PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT supplies a source/destination conversion when no higher-precedence mechanism determines names; an appropriate OMF configuration also allows automatic naming.

A/D/F must not be described as invariably illegal simply because they combine mechanisms. For example, an explicit FILE_NAME_CONVERT can take precedence over the initialization parameter, and a configured conversion may be irrelevant when OMF determines placement. Their defect in this intended question is that they add redundant mechanisms instead of identifying the minimal alternatives, not that every combination must fail. The wording 'any one ... required' is imprecise: these are alternatives, and a supported explicit FILE_NAME_CONVERT by itself is another route not offered alone.

```sql
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb2
  ADMIN USER pdb2_adm IDENTIFIED BY "123pdb"
  ROLES=(CONNECT)
  CREATE_FILE_DEST='/u02/oradata';
```

The password is quoted because it starts with a digit. In a real script use a suitable private credential, ensure the destination exists with proper permissions, and check free space. File naming is only one prerequisite; administrator privileges, password syntax and seed availability still matter. The preserved key represents the intended minimal-strategy reading, with these assumptions rather than an absolute claim that all other configurations fail.
original_text:
Examine the command for creating pluggable database PDB2 in container database CDB2.

```text
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb2
ADMIN USER pdb2_adm
IDENTIFIED BY 123pdb
ROLES=(CONNECT);
```

Select three options, any one of which is required for it to execute successfully. (Choose three.)
review_note: B/C/E are intended minimal alternatives; A/D/F are redundant or precedence-dependent rather than universally invalid. Quoted the digit-leading example password so the stem is executable.

mnemonic.anchor: B, C and E are the intended independent file-placement mechanisms.

text: Which two are true about Recovery Manager (RMAN) diagnostic message output? (Choose two.)

options.text: Media Management messages for SBT devices are always written to sbtio.log.
RMAN error stacks should be read from the bottom up as that is the order in which errors are generated.
RMAN error stacks should be read from the top down as that is the order in which errors are generated.
The RMAN LOG command line clause causes output issued during RMAN command compilation to be written to a log file and to standard output.
The RMAN LOG command line clause causes output issued during RMAN command compilation to be written to a log file only.
Media Management messages for SBT devices are written to an Oracle trace file.

explanation:
B and E are correct. RMAN error stacks should be read from the bottom upward: the lowest-level message is usually the original failure, while higher-level RMAN errors describe its propagation. Thus C reverses the useful diagnostic order. The LOG command-line clause directs RMAN output to a log file only, so E is true and D is false because it claims the output is also sent to standard output. A and F make unjustified claims that media-management messages always appear in one fixed Oracle log or trace file; vendor media-management software may record its own diagnostics, and output depends on integration and configuration. For an SBT failure, inspect the full RMAN stack, channel allocation and trace output, and the media manager's own logs. Starting from the originating error helps identify whether the issue is Oracle, the library, credentials, or tape infrastructure.

For an SBT failure, the high-level RMAN error may merely report that a channel operation failed. Read down to the originating Oracle or media-manager message, then trace the propagation upward. B describes that bottom-up diagnostic approach; it is not a claim that every repeated line is a separate root cause.

```text
rman target / LOG=backup.log
```

LOG redirects the RMAN output to the file rather than simultaneously retaining ordinary standard output. If the goal is file plus terminal display within an RMAN session, SPOOL LOG is the distinct supported mechanism; shell-level redirection/tee has its own semantics. This distinction separates E from D.

Oracle trace files can diagnose Oracle-process, channel and library-loading problems, while the media manager controls its own diagnostic destinations, often sbtio.log or a vendor-specific alternative. Thus A's always is too strong and F should not be taken as the universal location of the vendor's messages. Preserve the full error stack, execution timestamp, channel identity and vendor return code when correlating logs; retaining only the final RMAN error usually removes the evidence needed to identify the failing component.

sources.title: RMAN diagnostic output and error stacks

mnemonic.anchor: Thus C reverses the useful diagnostic order.

text: Which three are true about managing memory components in an Oracle database instance? (Choose three.)

options.text: With Automatic Shared Memory Management, the database instance can increase the Large Pool size by reducing the Shared Pool size.
With Automatic Memory Management, the database instance can increase the System Global Area size by reducing the Program Global Area size.
Automatically tuned and resized System Global Area components will always revert to their initial sizes after an instance restart.
Automatic Memory Management must be used together with locking the System Global Area into physical memory.
With Automatic Shared Memory Management, the database instance can increase the Program Global Area size by reducing the System Global Area size.
On Line Transaction Processing systems often use less Program Global Area than Decision Support Systems.

explanation:
A, B, and F are correct. With Automatic Shared Memory Management, Oracle can resize SGA components dynamically; it may enlarge the large pool by reducing the shared pool when workload demand justifies it, so A is true. Automatic Memory Management manages both SGA and PGA through MEMORY_TARGET, allowing memory to shift between them, so B is true. C is false because dynamically chosen component sizes are not guaranteed to revert to initial sizes after each restart; startup sizing depends on configuration and saved state. D confuses AMM with separately configured memory locking. E describes PGA growth by shrinking SGA, which is not ASMM's purpose. F is generally true: OLTP sessions often need modest work areas, while DSS sorts and hash joins can consume substantial PGA. Monitor workarea spills and memory advisories before adjusting targets.

ASMM distributes SGA_TARGET among eligible shared-memory components; it does not itself transfer the SGA budget to PGA. AMM with MEMORY_TARGET coordinates both SGA and PGA targets within its supported platform constraints. That boundary makes A/B true and E false without requiring a claim that an individual session's PGA can always be reclaimed immediately.

```sql
SELECT component, current_size, min_size, max_size
FROM v$memory_dynamic_components;
```

Use the corresponding SGA dynamic-component view when investigating ASMM. Component minimums, maximums and granule sizes constrain redistribution. Oracle can retain internally determined startup sizing in an SPFILE, so C's always-reset assertion is false. LOCK_SGA is not a required companion to AMM, which has platform-specific incompatibilities and prerequisites; D is false. F describes a usual workload tendency, not a sizing formula: DSS often needs larger sort/hash work areas, but an OLTP workload with large reporting queries can also demand substantial PGA. Measure workarea spills, concurrency and peak demand before adopting a memory split based only on the application's label.

keywords: increase the System Global Area size by reducing the Program Global Area size
mnemonic.anchor: Automatic Memory Management manages both SGA and PGA through MEMORY_TARGET, allowing memory to shift between them, so B is true.

text:
A database is configured in ARCHIVELOG mode. Full RMAN backups are taken daily and no backup to trace has been taken of the control file. A media failure has occurred.

In which three scenarios is complete recovery possible? (Choose three.)

options.text: when any archived log from, before, or after the most recent backup is corrupt.
after losing all copies of the control file
after losing an archived log from after the most recent backup
after losing an archived log from before the most recent backup
after losing the SYSTEM tablespace

explanation:
B, D and E describe scenarios in which complete recovery is possible, subject to the normal backup, metadata and redo requirements. The original select-two count incorrectly excluded B merely because no control-file trace backup exists. A trace script is convenient metadata, not the only route: a binary control-file backup/autobackup may exist, or the control file can be recreated manually with correct database/file/log metadata. Oracle's advanced recovery guidance explicitly includes complete recovery after control-file loss when the necessary online redo and metadata are available.

Option E is the standard restore-and-recover path for lost SYSTEM data files. Option D is possible when the missing old archived log precedes the redo required by the selected usable backup. An online/fuzzy backup may need redo beginning at its recovery checkpoint, which can precede backup completion; 'before the backup' must not be simplified to 'any log whose timestamp precedes the backup end'.

Options A and C cannot guarantee recovery when the corrupt/missing archived log is required and no other usable copy, incremental path or retained online redo supplies the changes. Conversely, an irrelevant missing log need not prevent recovery; the exact redo coverage determines the outcome.

```text
RESTORE DATABASE;
RECOVER DATABASE;
```

These commands illustrate the data-file stage, not a complete all-control-files-lost procedure. Establish the correct control-file strategy and incarnation first. Complete recovery means reaching the required current consistent endpoint; OPEN RESETLOGS requirements depend on the recovery/control-file path and do not by themselves prove that committed data was lost.
original_text: A database is configured in ARCHIVELOG mode. Full RMAN backups are taken daily and no backup to trace has been taken of the control file. A media failure has occurred. In which two scenarios is complete recovery possible? (Choose two.)
review_note: Corrected count to three possible scenarios. B is possible without a trace backup via binary backup or correct manual recreation; D depends on the missing log being outside the selected backup recovery range; required redo must be available.

keywords: losing all copies of the control file
losing an archived log from before the most recent backup
mnemonic.anchor: B, D and E describe scenarios in which complete recovery is possible, subject to the normal backup, metadata and redo requirements.

text: Which three are true about Database Point-in-Time Recovery? (Choose three.)

options.text: The database must have FLASHBACK DATABASE ON to perform Database Point-in-Time Recovery.
The database must be in MOUNT state when performing Database Point-in-Time Recovery.
Database Point-in-Time Recovery is performed by the Managed Recovery Process (MRP)
The Database must be in ARCHIVELOG mode.
The target point for the recovery must be specified as a stime or System Change Number (SCN).
The database must be open RESETLOGS after Database Point-in-Time Recovery.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Database point-in-time recovery (DBPITR) restores a database backup and applies redo only up to a chosen target.

text: Which three are true about the SQL Tuning Advisor? (Choose three.)

options.text: It checks each query being analyzed for stale statistics.
It checks each query being analyzed for missing statistics.
It only recommends syntactic changes to SQL statements.
It can recommend semantic changes to SQL statements.
It considers all SQL statements being analyzed by the advisor task as a group.
It builds SQL profiles for each poorly performing SQL statement to prevent regressions.

explanation:
The correct choices are A, B and D. SQL Tuning Advisor runs the Automatic Tuning Optimizer on individual statements. It investigates optimizer estimates, statistics, access paths, SQL structure and the potential benefit of a SQL profile. Its output is advice, not a guarantee that every statement receives a profile or retains one execution plan forever.

Option A is correct because stale object statistics can make cardinality and cost estimates inaccurate. Option B is correct for missing statistics: the advisor can recommend gathering the relevant statistics when their absence affects optimization.

Option D is correct. Structural analysis can identify syntactic, semantic and design problems and recommend changes such as appropriate SQL rewrites. These recommendations still require checking application semantics; the advisor does not authorize changing the intended business result.

Option C is false because analysis is not limited to syntax. Option E describes workload-level analysis rather than this advisor's statement-specific treatment. A tuning set may supply many statements, but they are not optimized as one combined SQL statement. Option F is false: profiles are recommended for suitable statements and require acceptance or configured automatic implementation. A SQL profile improves estimates; it is not an unconditional plan-regression prevention mechanism.

Practically, obtain a tuning report for a high-load SQL_ID, check the evidence behind its statistics and profile findings, and compare representative execution statistics before accepting changes. Distinguish a profile from a SQL plan baseline: correcting optimizer estimates and constraining accepted execution plans are different mechanisms.

sources.title: SQL Tuning Advisor analysis and recommendations

mnemonic.anchor: The correct choices are A, B and D.

text: Which two are true about duplicating pluggable databases (PDBs) with RMAN? (Choose two.)

options.text: Two or more PDBs can be duplicated with the same RMAN DUPLICATE command.
All tablespaces belonging to a PDB must be duplicated when duplicating the PDB.
The auxiliary instance is automatically created with ENABLE_PLUGGABLE_DATABASE = TRUE.
A user with SYSDBA or SYSBKUP must use RMAN logged in to a PDB in order to duplicate it.
CDB$ROOT and PDB$SEED are automatically duplicated if a PDB is duplicated.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN PDB duplication creates PDB copies inside a valid destination CDB. The destination therefore needs its CDB-level foundation as well as the PDB data and metadata being copied.

Option analysis: A is correct: a single DUPLICATE operation can specify multiple PDBs. B is false because RMAN supports duplication of selected PDB tablespaces in supported workflows; the claim that every tablespace must always be duplicated is too broad. C is false: when creating a new auxiliary CDB, ENABLE_PLUGGABLE_DATABASE must be specified in its initialization setup; RMAN does not simply set it automatically. D is false: the connection is made to the CDB root with SYSDBA or SYSBACKUP privileges, not by logging into the source PDB. E is correct: RMAN also duplicates CDB$ROOT and PDB$SEED to form a functional CDB.

Practical point: plan for root and seed creation even when the requested payload is only a subset of PDBs.

The destination is the missing qualifier. For a NEW CDB, the documented form can list multiple PDBs and duplicates the root and seed. Into an EXISTING CDB, 19c supports only one complete PDB per active-duplication operation; that workflow reuses the existing root and seed. Thus A and E describe the new-CDB workflow, not an invariant of every possible DUPLICATE PDB operation. Prepare the auxiliary initialization file yourself and verify that RMAN connects to the appropriate roots. Never apply the existing-CDB restrictions to the new-CDB syntax indiscriminately.

sources.title: RMAN duplication: new-CDB and existing-CDB workflows

review_note: A/E apply to duplicating selected PDBs into a new CDB. Existing-CDB duplication has different cardinality and root/seed behavior; the stem omits the destination workflow.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: RMAN PDB duplication creates PDB copies inside a valid destination CDB.

text: Which three are true about Rapid Home Provisioning (RHP), which has been available since Oracle 18c? (Choose three.)

options.text: It is an Oracle Database service.
It can be used to deploy Oracle Database homes.
It cannot be used to provision applications.
It can be used to deploy Grid Infrastructure homes, including Oracle Restart.
It cannot be used to provision middleware.
It is an Oracle Grid Infrastructure service.

explanation:
Core idea: Rapid Home Provisioning (RHP) centrally provisions and manages Oracle software images. It is delivered as a Grid Infrastructure service and covers more than Database homes alone.

Option analysis: A is false: RHP is not an Oracle Database service. B is correct: it can deploy Database homes. C is false because RHP also supports provisioning applications. D is correct: it can deploy Grid Infrastructure homes, including Oracle Restart. E is false because supported targets include middleware as well. F is correct: RHP runs as a Grid Infrastructure service.

Practical example: an administrator can maintain a standardized software image and deploy consistent Database or GI homes to servers, reducing manual installation differences. RHP handles the software-home lifecycle; it does not remove the need to check version compatibility, storage, network, and patch requirements.

Takeaway: associate RHP with centralized provisioning of Oracle homes and supported applications under Grid Infrastructure.

In 19c the service is documented as Fleet Patching and Provisioning, the successor name for Rapid Home Provisioning. Keep image, working copy and target home separate: an image is the maintained source, a working copy is a provisioned deployment, and an Oracle home contains the installed binaries. A practical deployment should record both the image version and the homes instantiated from it, then validate the patch inventory at the target. Provisioning a consistent binary image does not automatically create all application schemas or prove database upgrade compatibility.

sources.title: Fleet Patching and Provisioning of database, GI, applications and middleware

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Rapid Home Provisioning (RHP) centrally provisions and manages Oracle software images.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. COMMON_USER_PREFIX is C##.
3. PDB1 is a pluggable database contained in CDB1.
4. APP1_ROOT is an application container contained in CDB1.
5. APP1_PDB1 is an application PDB contained in APP1_ROOT.

You execute these commands successfully:

```text
$ sqlplus sys/oracle_4U@localhost:1521/cdb1 as sysdba
SQL> CREATE USER c##user1 IDENTIFIED BY oracle_4U CONTAINER=ALL;
User created.

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=pdb1;
Session altered.

SQL> CREATE USER p1_user1 IDENTIFIED BY oracle_4U;
User created.

SQL> ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=app1_root;
Session altered.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION app1_cdb1_app BEGIN INSTALL '1.0';
Pluggable database altered.

SQL> CREATE USER app1_user1 IDENTIFIED BY oracle_4U;
User created.

SQL> ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE APPLICATION app1_cdb1_app END INSTALL '1.0';
Pluggable database altered.
```

Which three are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: APP1_USER1 can be created in PDB1.
APP1_USER1 can be created in CDB1.
APP1_USER1 can have different privileges in each Application PDB contained in APP1_ROOT.
C##_APP_USER1 can be created in CDB1.
P1_USER1 can be created in CDB1.
C##_USER1 will have the same privileges and roles granted in all PDBs in CDB1.

explanation:
A, C and D are true with the supplied names and COMMON_USER_PREFIX=C##. The previous two-answer count misses D: C##_APP_USER1 begins with C##; the underscore after that prefix is permitted and does not invalidate the common-user name.

Option A is true. APP1_USER1 is application common within APP1_ROOT's application container. PDB1 is a separate regular PDB, so an unrelated local account can use that same unprefixed name there. Those accounts are different identities in different scopes.

Option C is true. Common identity does not force identical local grants. An application common user can receive local privileges in one application PDB without receiving those local grants in every sibling PDB.

Option D is true: while connected to CDB$ROOT, a new CDB common account named C##_APP_USER1 satisfies the configured prefix. It is different from C##USER1, so the shown earlier creation does not itself cause a collision.

Options B and E are false when CDB1 means its CDB root, because these unprefixed names cannot be created there as CDB common users under this setting. Option F is false: common grants and local grants have different scopes, so privileges need not be uniform in every PDB.

For diagnosis, first check the current container and account scope:
```sql
SHOW CON_NAME
SELECT username, common FROM dba_users;
```
Then inspect the relevant common/local privilege grants. A name collision is evaluated in its actual container hierarchy, not by assuming one global namespace for every local account.

text: Which two are facets of performance planning that should always be considered or implemented for an Oracle Database environment? (Choose two.)

options.text: defining primary keys for all tables to speed up all queries
using check constraints to speed up updates
defining foreign keys for all tables to speed up joins
the physical data model
the configuration of storage arrays

explanation:
Core idea: Performance planning includes logical design and the physical path by which the database stores and reads data. Poor data organization or a storage subsystem that cannot meet workload latency and throughput can dominate response time.

Option analysis: D is correct: the physical data model affects access patterns, table organization, partitioning, and the amount of work queries perform. E is correct: storage-array design and configuration affect I/O capacity and latency. A is false because a primary key enforces uniqueness and may create an index, but does not speed every query. B is false because check constraints enforce valid values; they are not a general update accelerator. C is false because foreign keys express relationships and do not automatically speed joins; index design depends on workload.

Practical example: measure whether a workload is storage-bound and review schema layout before adding indexes or changing memory settings.

Takeaway: plan physical design and storage together; constraints are integrity features, not universal tuning switches.

A useful planning exercise estimates rows read, rows modified, peak concurrent sessions and expected I/O response times for the proposed physical design. A normalized logical model alone does not decide partition placement, index organization or storage redundancy. Conversely, a fast array cannot compensate indefinitely for SQL that reads unnecessary rows. Constraints should be added for correctness where required; index and physical-layout choices should then be tested against the workload. This is why the two planning facets are real design inputs rather than universal claims about constraint-based acceleration.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Performance planning includes logical design and the physical path by which the database stores and reads data.

text: Which three actions are performed by the Oracle Preinstallation RPM, oracle-database-server-xxxx-preinstall, for Oracle Grid Infrastructure, where xxxx is the Oracle version and release? (Choose three.)

options.text: performing checks to ensure minimum configuration requirements for Oracle Grid Infrastructure are met
creating the oracle OS user
creating the OSDBA (dba) group
creating the oraInventory (oinstall) group
creating the grid OS user
configuring the OS for Oracle Automatic Storage Management shared storage access

explanation:
Core idea: The Oracle Linux preinstallation RPM prepares common operating-system prerequisites for Oracle software. It creates the oracle account and standard groups and configures selected OS settings; it does not install or fully validate Grid Infrastructure.

Option analysis: B is correct: this preinstallation package creates the oracle OS account. C and D are correct: it creates the dba OSDBA group and oinstall inventory group. A is not one of the keyed actions: package configuration does not prove that every GI minimum requirement has been met. E is false for this package workflow because the RPM does not create a separate grid account. F is false: the RPM does not configure all shared ASM storage access as a substitute for the storage and cluster setup.

Practical point: after using the RPM, check the exact GI installation guide for the target release, including kernel settings, packages, storage permissions, and network configuration.

Takeaway: the RPM is baseline preparation, not a replacement for prerequisite checks.

After package installation, inspect the resulting account and group membership and run the release-specific prerequisite checks. A package can set kernel parameters and resource limits while still leaving cluster interconnects, shared storage, device ownership and GI-owner separation unresolved. A site that uses a separate grid owner must create and configure it deliberately. Do not confuse satisfying package dependencies with proving every cluster prerequisite. This also explains why the preinstallation RPM is optional assistance: equivalent supported OS configuration can be performed manually.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: The Oracle Linux preinstallation RPM prepares common operating-system prerequisites for Oracle software.

text: Which three actions are performed by Database Upgrade Assistant (DBUA)? (Choose three.)

options.text: It recompiles all stored PL/SQL code by using utlrp.sql.
It empties the RECYCLE BIN.
It performs prerequisite checks to verify if the Oracle database is ready for upgrade.
It sets all user tablespaces to 'read-only' before starting the upgrade.
It removes the AUDSYS schema and the AUDIT_ADMIN and AUDIT_VIEWER roles
It increases tablespace size, if required, to meet upgrade requirements.

explanation:
Core idea: DBUA automates a guided database upgrade, including prerequisite checks and some cleanup or space preparation. It does not eliminate every manual post-upgrade task.

Option analysis: B is correct: DBUA empties the recycle bin as part of upgrade preparation. C is correct: it runs prerequisite checks and reports conditions that should be addressed before upgrading. F is correct: when required, DBUA can increase tablespace size to meet upgrade space needs. A is not one of the keyed actions; recompilation is handled as a post-upgrade recompilation step rather than meaning that DBUA recompiles all stored PL/SQL with utlrp.sql as a universal action. D is false: DBUA does not switch all user tablespaces to read-only. E is false: removing AUDSYS and audit roles is not a general DBUA upgrade action.

Practical point: review the prerequisite report and verify available space before the maintenance window; plan separately for post-upgrade checks and recompilation.

After DBUA completes, inspect its logs, invalid-object counts and component status. Option A's word ALL is important: the documented recompilation scripts identify/recompile invalid objects; running a recompilation phase does not imply forcibly recompiling every valid stored PL/SQL unit. DBUA has configurable post-upgrade operations, so do not misread this answer as saying DBUA never invokes recompilation. Verify the selected options and run the required post-upgrade driver when appropriate. Space checks and fixups belong before upgrade execution rather than being postponed until an upgrade fails halfway.
review_note: A overstates recompilation as all stored PL/SQL. DBUA can run recompilation; B/C/F remain the intended actions, with post-upgrade options distinguished.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: DBUA automates a guided database upgrade, including prerequisite checks and some cleanup or space preparation.

text: Which two are true about RMAN backups when using a media manager to write backups to tape when there are only two tape drives? (Choose two.)

options.text: SBT tape compression can be used even if no RMAN compression is configured.
Any backup set written to the SBT device in this configuration can contain a maximum of two backup pieces.
Any backup written to the SBT device in this configuration can contain a maximum of two backup sets.
SBT tape compression and RMAN backup compression should be used in parallel.
The SBT device should be configured to use PARALLELISM 2 to allow both tape drive to be used simultaneously.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN binary compression and tape-device compression are separate mechanisms. RMAN can compress backup data before sending it to SBT, while a tape drive or media manager may compress the incoming stream independently.

Option analysis: A is correct: tape hardware compression can be used without RMAN compression. B and C are false: having two tape drives does not impose a fixed two-piece or two-set limit on every backup; pieces, sets, and channels are different RMAN concepts. D is false as a universal recommendation because stacking compression can spend CPU for little extra reduction. E is correct for this setup: SBT parallelism of two lets RMAN use two channels, subject to the media manager and channel configuration.

Practical example: test a representative backup with two channels and compare throughput, CPU, and tape utilization before enabling software compression.

Takeaway: match channel parallelism to available drives and evaluate hardware and RMAN compression separately.

For a capacity test, compare backup elapsed time, media-manager channel allocation and drive busy time. Two channels can stream to two drives, but actual concurrent access also depends on the media manager and device reservation policies. One channel may write many pieces sequentially; channel count is not a limit on the total number of pieces produced. If the data is already compressed by RMAN, repeating compression at the tape layer generally has little remaining redundancy to remove. Measure both CPU cost and media throughput instead of assuming stacked compression is best.

sources.title: RMAN backup scope, archival backups and output

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: RMAN binary compression and tape-device compression are separate mechanisms.

text:
You plan to install Oracle Grid Infrastructure for a Standalone Server and Oracle Database for the first time on a server.

Examine this command and its outcome:

```text
# id oracle
uid=54321(oracle) gid=54321(oinstall) groups=54321(oinstall),54322(dba)
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: oracle will be an owner of the Oracle Inventory.
oracle must be the owner of every Oracle Database installation.
oracle can own an Oracle Database installation but not an Oracle Grid Infrastructure installation.
oracle will be granted the SYSASM privilege when installing the Oracle Database software.
The user account, oracle, and group, oinstall, can be used for all Oracle software installations.

explanation:
Core idea: Oracle software ownership is an OS installation choice. The oinstall group is associated with the central inventory, while administrative groups map OS membership to database privileges; root-only scripts remain a separate installation responsibility.

Option analysis: A is correct: oracle belongs to the oinstall primary group and can own or update the Oracle Inventory when the installer assigns that owner. E is correct: one oracle account can be used for Database and standalone Grid Infrastructure installations if the site chooses a single-owner design. B is false because Oracle permits different installation owners. C is false because oracle may own GI for a standalone server. D is false: SYSASM is associated with OSASM configuration and is not granted simply because the Database software is installed.

Practical point: select a single-owner or separate-owner model deliberately, map groups to the intended privileges, and execute root scripts through the supported root mechanism.

Takeaway: OS account ownership, inventory ownership, and SYSASM are related but distinct decisions.

Before installation, record the primary inventory group separately from supplementary OSDBA, OSOPER and OSASM group selections. The name oracle is conventional, not a reserved requirement that forces every home to share one owner. For a single-owner standalone setup, the installer can use the displayed account and inventory group across both products. If separation of duties is selected, create the separate owners and groups consistently and document which account may administer ASM. A successful id command proves membership, not that root scripts or every directory permission have already been configured.

sources.title: Oracle Database installation and image-based installation

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Oracle software ownership is an OS installation choice.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database running in ARCHIVELOG mode.
2. Controlfiles of CDB1 are multiplexed in:

   '/u01/app/oracle/oradata/CDB1/controlfile/controlfile01.ctl' and
   '/u02/app/oracle/fast_recover_area/cdb1/CDB1/controlfile02.ctl'.
3. The only backup of CDB1 was taken when CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP was OFF.
4. SNAPSHOT CONTROLFILE NAME is:

   '/u01/app/oracle/product/12.2.0.1/db_1/dbs/snapcf_cdb1.f'.

While CDB1 is open, '/u02/app/oracle/fast_recover_area/cdb1/CDB1/controlfile02.ctl' is accidentally deleted.

To recover from this critical failure, you execute these commands:

```text
$ rman target sys/oracle_4U@localhost:1521/cdb1
RMAN> SHUTDOWN ABORT
Oracle instance shut down

RMAN> STARTUP NOMOUNT
RMAN> RESTORE CONTROLFILE FROM '/u01/app/oracle/oradata/CDB1/controlfile/controlfile01.ctl';
```

What will be the outcome?

options.text: It will create '$ORACLE_HOME/dbs/cdb1/CDB1/controlfile02.ctl'
It will create '/u01/app/oracle/oradata/CDB1/controlfile/controlfile02.ctl'.
It will re-create '/u02/app/oracle/fast_recover_area/cdb1/CDB1/controlfile02.ctl'
It will create '/u01/app/oracle/product/12.2.0.1/db_1/dbs/snapcf_cdb1control02.ctl'.
It will fail because there is no autobackup of the controlfiles.

explanation:
Core idea: Multiplexed control files are copies of the same control-file contents at locations listed by CONTROL_FILES. If one copy is lost but another survives, the surviving file can be used directly as the restore source.

Option analysis: C is correct: RMAN reads the supplied surviving control-file copy and recreates the configured copies, including the missing FRA location. A and D give invented or malformed destination paths. B points into the first control-file directory, not to the configured missing FRA location. E is false: a control-file autobackup is unnecessary when a valid surviving multiplexed copy is explicitly supplied.

Practical example: after the restore, verify that every configured control-file path exists before mounting. Then perform any required database recovery and confirm the control files and data files are consistent.

Takeaway: the CONTROL_FILES initialization setting defines restore destinations; an available multiplexed copy can avoid autobackup discovery.

The source filename is explicit, so RMAN does not need to search for an autobackup by DBID. The configured CONTROL_FILES destinations, rather than the snapshot-controlfile setting, determine where the restored multiplexed copies belong. Once a usable current copy has been restored to the configured paths, mount the database and verify consistency. Recovering a genuinely old backup control file is a different case that may require media recovery and RESETLOGS; do not automatically impose that case on a surviving current multiplexed control file. Verify device accessibility as well as path spelling.

sources.title: Complete recovery of CDBs, PDBs and application containers

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Multiplexed control files are copies of the same control-file contents at locations listed by CONTROL_FILES.

text:
Examine these actions:

1. Create a new database for a recovery catalog.
2. Create a tablespace with sufficient space in the catalog database for the recovery catalog.
3. Configure ARCHIVELOG mode for the catalog database.
4. Create a user to own the recovery catalog schema with quota on the tablespace that will contain the catalog.
5. Grant the RECOVERY_CATALOG_OWNER role to the recovery catalog schema owner.
6. Grant the SYSBACKUP privilege to the recovery catalog schema owner.

Which are the minimum actions that must be performed before executing the CREATE CATALOG command?
explanation:
D, actions 2, 4 and 5, is the minimum combination offered. A recovery catalog is an RMAN repository schema in a database, not an auxiliary recovery instance. Its owner requires a storage tablespace, quota and the RECOVERY_CATALOG_OWNER role. The existing database can be reused, so creating a brand-new database in action 1 is unnecessary.

Action 3, ARCHIVELOG mode, is strongly advisable for protecting the catalog but is not a prerequisite for executing CREATE CATALOG. Action 6 confuses two connections: SYSBACKUP authorizes backup/recovery operations on a target database; it is not required merely to own the catalog schema.

Option A therefore adds an unnecessary administrative privilege. Option B adds a new database, ARCHIVELOG and SYSBACKUP. Option C unnecessarily requires a new database. Option E also includes new-database and ARCHIVELOG actions and omits the explicit tablespace preparation in the listed minimal workflow.

The intended sequence is to prepare the schema as a database administrator, then connect RMAN as that schema owner:
```sql
CREATE USER rco IDENTIFIED BY "Example_password"
  DEFAULT TABLESPACE tools QUOTA UNLIMITED ON tools;
GRANT recovery_catalog_owner TO rco;
```
Run the release's required dbmsrmansys.sql setup as documented before CREATE CATALOG. That additional modern requirement is absent from the supplied action list; D is the minimum among the offered actions, not an exhaustive installation checklist. Protect the catalog with an independent recovery strategy rather than treating its repository as the only record of its own backups.

sources.title: Creating and managing the recovery catalog

mnemonic.anchor: D, actions 2, 4 and 5, is the minimum combination offered.

text: Which two are true about creating pluggable databases (PDBs) using snapshots in Oracle 19c and later releases? (Choose two.)

options.text: A PDB snapshot is always a full copy of the source PDB.
A PDB snapshot is always a sparse copy of the source PDB.
A snapshot copy PDB depends on a storage snapshot which can only be stored on specific file systems.
A PDB snapshot depends on a storage snapshot which can be stored on any file system.
A PDB snapshot depends on a storage snapshot which can only be stored on specific file systems.
A snapshot copy PDB depends on a storage snapshot which can be stored on any file system.
A snapshot copy PDB can be created from a stand-alone clone PDB.

explanation:
Core idea: A PDB snapshot and a snapshot-copy PDB are related but distinct. A PDB snapshot captures a point-in-time state; a snapshot-copy PDB is a clone whose files depend on supported storage snapshot or sparse-file capabilities.

Option analysis: C is correct: snapshot-copy creation depends on supported storage, so it is not guaranteed on every filesystem. G is correct: a snapshot-copy PDB may be created from a standalone clone PDB. A and B are false because a PDB snapshot is not always full or always sparse; storage configuration determines the implementation. D and F overstate support by saying any filesystem works. E confuses the storage restriction for snapshot-copy clones with the characteristics of a PDB snapshot itself.

Practical example: before using snapshot copies for many test PDBs, confirm that the storage platform supports the required snapshot mechanism and understand the clone's dependency on the source storage.

Takeaway: do not treat a database snapshot as an independent full copy or assume snapshot-copy support on arbitrary storage.

Distinguish the snapshot carousel's archive files from SNAPSHOT COPY clones. The carousel can use a full first snapshot followed by sparse snapshots when the filesystem supports sparse files; without that capability its implementation differs. SNAPSHOT COPY also has storage-specific mechanisms and a CLONEDB fallback with source read-only restrictions. Check the actual storage integration rather than assuming a native filesystem snapshot in every case. A sparse clone depends on backing storage and is not an independently portable full backup. Materialize a full PDB before removing a dependency it still needs.
review_note: C is intended as a storage-support restriction, but SNAPSHOT COPY has multiple implementations including CLONEDB. Native storage snapshots are not the only mechanism.

keywords: snapshot copy PDB depends on a storage snapshot which can only be stored on specific file systems
mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: A PDB snapshot and a snapshot-copy PDB are related but distinct.

text: Which two are true about Oracle Database Configuration Assistant (DBCA) templates? (Choose two.)

options.text: The General Purpose of Transaction Processing templates are most suitable when concurrency and recoverability are key criteria.
Oracle DBCA templates can store only logical structure and not database files.
New templates can only be created by modifying an existing user-created template.
The Data Warehouse template is most suitable when transaction response time is the key criterion.
Oracle DBCA templates can be used to create new databases and duplicate existing databases.

explanation:
Core idea: DBCA templates capture choices for creating databases. Some templates are structural; others include a seed database image and can make database creation or duplication faster.

Option analysis: A is correct: General Purpose / Transaction Processing templates are aimed at transactional workloads where concurrency, response time, and recoverability matter. E is correct: templates can create databases and, depending on template type, duplicate existing database configurations. B is false because templates may include physical data files as well as logical structure. C is false: a user-defined template can be created from an existing database or by modifying a template. D is false because a Data Warehouse template targets analytical workloads, not transaction response time as its defining priority.

Practical example: choose the template matching the workload, then review its memory, process, and storage settings against actual requirements.

Takeaway: know whether a template contains only structure or a seed image, and avoid treating its defaults as final tuning.

Before using a template for repeated deployments, determine whether it is a non-seed template containing structure only or a seed template with an associated database image. Review character set, block size, memory choices and file destinations rather than accepting a workload label as a universal tuning prescription. A transactional template emphasizes many concurrent short transactions, while a warehouse template assumes analytical access patterns. Both are starting configurations that still require capacity planning. Creating a template from an existing database does not mean copying that database's future changes into every deployment.

sources.title: DBCA templates and silent-mode command reference

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: DBCA templates capture choices for creating databases.

text:
Your SALES_ROOT application container has two application PDBs.
The SALES_APP application has a common table, FIN.REVENUE, in the two PDBs.

Examine this query and its output:

```text
SQL> SELECT containers_default, container_map, container_map_object, table_name
  2  FROM dba_tables WHERE owner='FIN';

CONTAINERS_DEFAULT CONTAINER_MAP CONTAINER_MAP_OBJECT TABLE_NAME
------------------ ------------- -------------------- ----------
NO                 YES           NO                   REVENUE
NO                 NO            YES                  MAPTABLE
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The CONTAINERS clause cannot be used in queries on the REVENUE table.
The REVENUE table must be a list-partitioned table.
The MAPTABLE tables defines a logical partition key on a commonly used column for the REVENUE table.
The MAPTABLE table is a metadata-linked table.
A container map exists for the REVENUE table, but is not enabled.
The REVENUE table partitions are not pruned across the PDBs automatically.

explanation:
C and F are the defensible choices for ordinary queries issued in the application root. A container map is a partitioned map object that associates key values with application PDBs. The application data table, REVENUE, need not be physically partitioned in the same way as the map.

Option C describes the logical partitioning role of MAPTABLE. Its partition names identify application PDBs and the mapping enables routing/pruning based on relevant predicates. Option F follows from CONTAINERS_DEFAULT=NO only in the default-query sense: an unqualified REVENUE reference is not automatically expanded to a CONTAINERS() query. An explicit CONTAINERS(REVENUE) query may still use map pruning because CONTAINER_MAP=YES.

Option A is false: the explicit CONTAINERS clause remains available. Option B is false: the application data table is not required to be list-partitioned; the map object carries the routing partitioning. Option D confuses the two objects. REVENUE is the metadata-linked application table; CONTAINER_MAP_OBJECT=YES does not prove that MAPTABLE is itself metadata-linked. Option E is false because CONTAINER_MAP=YES denotes enabled map use for REVENUE.

Inspect both flags and the database property:
```sql
SELECT property_name, property_value FROM database_properties
WHERE property_name='CONTAINER_MAP';
```
Then compare an explicit CONTAINERS() query with an ordinary table reference. Map-based pruning and automatic query expansion are separate controls.
