text:
Your container database, CDB1, has an application container, HR_ROOT, with an application PDB, HR_PDB1. You have the required privilege to clone HR_PDB1 to container database CDB2, which does not contain HR_ROOT.

Which two are always true? (Choose two.)

options.text: CDB1 and CDB2 must be in shared undo mode.
A common user must exist in CDB2 with the CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE privilege.
All transactions in HR_PDB1 of CDB1 must commit before the cloning process starts.
Cloning HR_ROOT automatically clones HR_PDB1.
The HR_PDB1 clone created in CDB2 will be in mount state when cloning ends.

explanation:
Core idea: Remote PDB cloning uses a database link to copy a PDB from a source CDB into a destination CDB. The destination must authorize PDB creation; a clone is not the same as cloning its entire application container.

Option analysis: B is correct: a common destination user must have CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE. E is correct: after creation, the new PDB is left mounted and must be opened as a separate administrative step. A is not an always-required condition based solely on the described remote clone. C is false: the operation handles transactional consistency; there is no blanket requirement for a manual commit of every source transaction before cloning. D is false: cloning HR_PDB1 does not automatically clone HR_ROOT or the other PDBs in that application container.

Practical example: grant the destination privilege, establish the database link and clone, then open the PDB and verify its state and application-container association.

Takeaway: remote clone prerequisites are destination-side privileges and connectivity; a PDB clone remains a PDB-level operation.

The mounted result belongs to CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE completion, not to a DBCA workflow that subsequently opens the clone. Likewise, shared undo is not the universal requirement for hot cloning; local undo and ARCHIVELOG enable important online clone cases. Application identity and version compatibility must be checked if the destination is to remain an application PDB. The stem does not show creation or synchronization of an equivalent target application root, so successful preservation of the application-container relationship cannot be assumed merely from CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE privilege.

sources.title: Application objects, container maps and application administration

review_note: B/E describe destination privilege and initial clone state; target application-root compatibility is omitted. The destination type and relationship must be validated separately.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Remote PDB cloning uses a database link to copy a PDB from a source CDB into a destination CDB.

text: Which three are true about backup, restore, and recovery operations done without using Recovery Manager (RMAN)? (Choose three.)

options.text: Backing up a database in NOARCHIVELOG mode using O/S utilities requires that the database instance be started and the database be in the MOUNT state.
Backing up a database in ARCHIVELOG mode using O/S utilities requires that the database instance be started and the database be in MOUNT state.
An Oracle database can be restored from backup files copied using O/S utilities.
Oracle data file backups, copied using an O/S utility, can be added to the RMAN catalog as IMAGE COPIES.
Backing up a database in NOARCHIVELOG mode using O/S utilities requires that the database instance be shut down.
Oracle archive log backups, copied using an O/S utility, can be added to the RMAN catalog as a backup set.
Backing up a database in ARCHIVELOG mode using O/S utilities requires that the database instance be started and the database be in OPEN state.

explanation:
Core idea: A user-managed backup copies database files with operating-system tools. Its consistency requirements depend on ARCHIVELOG mode; RMAN can catalog certain copied files later, but an OS copy is not an RMAN backup set.

Option analysis: C is correct: a database can be restored from files copied by OS utilities if the copies are consistent and required redo is available. D is correct: copied data-file image copies can be registered with RMAN using CATALOG DATAFILECOPY. E is correct: in NOARCHIVELOG mode, take a whole-database OS backup after a clean shutdown. A is false because merely mounting the instance is not the required consistent state. B and G are false because ARCHIVELOG mode permits user-managed online backups when the procedure and redo handling are correct. F is false: copied archive logs are not converted into RMAN backup sets by cataloging.

Practical takeaway: distinguish user-managed consistency from RMAN metadata; plan how archived redo will be preserved for recovery.

For a user-managed online backup in ARCHIVELOG mode, use the documented BEGIN BACKUP/END BACKUP sequence and preserve the required archived logs; copying open data files arbitrarily is not a valid substitute. With NOARCHIVELOG, take a consistent offline backup after clean shutdown. A mounted, closed database following clean shutdown can also have consistent files; therefore E's requirement that the instance itself remain shut down is stricter than the underlying file-consistency requirement. C/D are clear, and CDE is retained as the intended conventional cold-backup workflow with this state distinction made explicit.

sources.title: Complete recovery of CDBs, PDBs and application containers

review_note: E describes conventional cold OS backup, but cleanly closed files can also be copied after STARTUP MOUNT. Closed/consistent is the essential requirement, not necessarily a nonexistent instance.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: A user-managed backup copies database files with operating-system tools.

text: Which two are true about common objects? (Choose two.)

options.text: They can be created only in CDB$ROOT.
They can be only metadata-linked in an application container.
They can exist in user-defined schemas only in application containers.
They can exist in CDB$ROOT and an application root.
They can be extended data-linked in CDB$ROOT.
They can be created only in an application root.

explanation:
C and D are correct under Oracle's distinction between Oracle-supplied common objects and application common objects. The word common describes metadata/object sharing across a container hierarchy; it does not mean every common object must be created in one particular root.

Option D is true: Oracle-supplied common objects exist in CDB$ROOT, while application common objects are defined in an application root. Their scope is different: CDB common objects belong to the CDB hierarchy; application common objects belong to the relevant application container.

Option C is true for user-created common schema objects. Applications introduce common objects in user-defined schemas in application containers. Ordinary user-created schema objects in the CDB root do not become arbitrary user-defined CDB common objects in the same way as Oracle-maintained dictionary objects.

Option A is false because it excludes application roots. Option B is false because supported application sharing includes metadata links, data links and extended data links. Option E incorrectly assigns extended data linking to CDB$ROOT rather than the application-container sharing model. Option F is false as a statement about all common objects: it would exclude the Oracle-supplied common objects explicitly recognized in D.

For a practical investigation, inspect SHARING in DBA_OBJECTS in the relevant root and compare the data visible from its application PDBs. A metadata link shares definitions while each application PDB owns its data; a data link exposes common root data. Do not infer row-sharing behavior merely from a common name, common owner or common user's privileges.

sources.title: Application objects, container maps and application administration

mnemonic.anchor: C and D are correct under Oracle's distinction between Oracle-supplied common objects and application common objects.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. CDB1 is a container database.
2. PDB1 and PDB2 are pluggable databases in CDB1.

You execute these commands successfully:

```text
$ export ORACLE_SID=cdb1
$ sqlplus / as sysdba

SQL> SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE
Oracle instance shut down.

SQL> STARTUP MOUNT
Database mounted.
```

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: PDB1 and PDB2 are in MOUNT state.
Redo logs are opened.
PDB1 and PDB2 are in READ ONLY state.
CDB$ROOT is in MOUNT state.
PDB$SEED is in READ ONLY state.

explanation:
A and D follow from STARTUP MOUNT. Oracle starts the instance and mounts the CDB, opening its control files but not opening the database data files and online redo logs for normal operation. The CDB root is mounted, and the PDBs are not opened merely because their normal saved/default state may be read-only or read/write when the CDB is open.

Option A is correct: PDB1 and PDB2 are in MOUNTED state. Option D is correct: CDB$ROOT is mounted, exactly as the successful command reports.

Option B is false in the database-startup state distinction: mounting reads control-file metadata; opening the database is the next step that opens data files and online redo logs. Option C is false because neither regular PDB was opened read-only. Option E confuses the normal open state of the seed with its state while the entire CDB remains mounted. PDB$SEED is not accessible as an open read-only database in this shown state.

Inspect container state explicitly rather than guessing:
```sql
SELECT con_id, name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs ORDER BY con_id;
```
After a later ALTER DATABASE OPEN, the seed normally becomes read-only, and saved-state rules may open other PDBs. Those later transitions are absent from the command sequence. A normal seed behavior after OPEN cannot be used to override the explicit MOUNT endpoint in this question. Instance startup, control-file mounting and opening a database are three separate stages.

sources.title: Creating a CDB and immutable PDB seed

mnemonic.anchor: Oracle starts the instance and mounts the CDB, opening its control files but not opening the database data files and online redo logs for normal operation.

text: Which two are true about upgrading Oracle Grid Infrastructure? (Choose two.)

options.text: A direct upgrade can be performed only from the immediately preceding Oracle Grid Infrastructure version.
The newer version is installed in a separate Oracle Grid Infrastructure home on the same server as the existing version.
An existing Oracle base can be used.
The upgrade process will automatically install all mandatory patches for the current version of Oracle Grid Infrastructure.
Existing Oracle Database instances must be shut down before starting the upgrade.
Only the grid user can perform the upgrade.

explanation:
B and C are the two generally correct statements offered. Grid Infrastructure upgrades use an out-of-place home: the new software is installed separately from the currently active GI home. The supported upgrade procedure then switches cluster resources and active version state under the release's rolling-upgrade rules.

Option B is true because the new Grid home is a separate installation on the relevant server. Option C is true: the existing Oracle base can be retained when it meets the ownership, layout and installation requirements.

Option A is false: supported direct upgrade paths can include more than the immediately preceding release; consult the exact source-release and patch-level matrix. Option D is false: installing a new release does not automatically obtain and apply every mandatory patch for the environment. Downloaded patches, supplied installation options and README instructions still matter.

Option E is not universal. Rolling Grid Infrastructure upgrades are designed to preserve database availability across the cluster. Individual-node resources may be stopped or relocated as that node is processed, but every database instance need not be shut down before the upgrade starts. Option F is false: the software owner performs installer work, and privileged configuration/root-upgrade scripts require the appropriate root execution mechanism.

Plan upgrade prerequisites per node, identify the source/target compatibility and patch requirements, and distinguish software installation from privileged configuration. The original choose-three count forced acceptance of an overbroad shutdown statement. The count has been corrected to two rather than teaching that rolling GI upgrades always require an initial whole-database outage.
original_text: Which three are true about upgrading Oracle Grid Infrastructure? (Choose three.)

mnemonic.anchor: B and C are the two generally correct statements offered.

text:
A database is configured in ARCHIVELOG mode. A full RMAN backup exists but no control file backup to trace has been taken. A media failure has occurred.

In which scenario is incomplete recovery required? (Choose one.)

options.text: after losing a SYSAUX tablespace data file
after losing all members of an INACTIVE online redo log group
after losing all members of the CURRENT online redo log group
after losing all copies of the control file
after losing an UNDO tablespace that is in use

explanation:
C is the intended redo-loss scenario, provided the lost current redo contains changes needed for recovery and no alternate copy is available. Incomplete recovery stops before missing required redo; it cannot reconstruct changes whose only redo records have been destroyed. A subsequent OPEN RESETLOGS establishes the new incarnation.

Option A does not inherently require incomplete recovery. A lost SYSAUX data file can normally be restored and completely recovered using its backup and the required archived and online redo. Option B is not inherently a point-in-time recovery case: an INACTIVE group is no longer needed for instance recovery, and supported clearing/recreation procedures depend on its archival status and backup requirements.

Option C is the usual incomplete-recovery case under the stated normal assumption. Option D is not defensible merely because no backup to trace exists. A binary control-file backup may be included in the RMAN backups or autobackups. Even without either kind of control-file backup, Oracle documents manually issuing CREATE CONTROLFILE; complete recovery can still be possible with the required intact online redo. Restoring a backup control file and opening RESETLOGS does not itself prove that committed data was lost.

Option E also permits complete media recovery of the restored active undo file when the required redo exists. Therefore the original request for two necessarily correct scenarios was defective and has been reduced to one with this caveat. A practical recovery decision must inventory actual backups, control-file copies, and all required redo before choosing a recovery endpoint.
original_text: A database is configured in ARCHIVELOG mode. A full RMAN backup exists but no control file backup to trace has been taken. A media failure has occurred. In which two scenarios is incomplete recovery required? (Choose two.)

sources.title: User-managed control-file and redo-log recovery scenarios
Complete recovery of CDBs, PDBs and application containers

review_note: Original choose-two key CD was defective: no trace control-file backup does not rule out a binary backup or manual CREATE CONTROLFILE and complete recovery. C assumes unrecoverable required current redo and no surviving alternate copy.

mnemonic.anchor: C is the intended redo-loss scenario, provided the lost current redo contains changes needed for recovery and no alternate copy is available.

text: Which two are true about instance recovery? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is not possible if an archived log is missing.
It is performed automatically after the database is opened; however, blocks requiring recovery are not available until they are recovered.

Setting FAST_START_MTTR_TARGET to a lower value reduces instance recovery time by causing dirty buffers to be written to disk more frequently, thereby reducing the number of I/Os needed during instance recovery.
It is performed by the Recovery Writer (RVWR) background process.

Setting FAST_START_MTTR_TARGET to a higher value reduces instance recovery time by causing the log writer to write more frequently, thereby reducing the number of I/Os needed during instance recovery.
It is performed automatically while the database remains in MOUNT state. Then the database is opened.

explanation:
Core idea: Instance recovery restores database consistency after an instance failure. Oracle uses redo to roll forward changes after the checkpoint; undo then rolls back transactions that had not committed. FAST_START_MTTR_TARGET influences checkpointing so the amount of work after a crash is bounded.

Option analysis: A is false: missing archived logs do not always prevent instance recovery because online redo is used for crash recovery. B is false: recovery is not delayed until after the database opens. C is correct: a lower target prompts more frequent incremental checkpoint writes by DBWn, reducing expected recovery work while increasing normal I/O. D is false: RVWR is associated with flashback logging, not instance recovery. E is false: raising the MTTR target permits less aggressive checkpointing and does not shorten recovery. F is correct: cache recovery occurs while the database is mounted; the database opens before background transaction recovery completes.

Practical point: lower MTTR can improve restart time at the cost of more writes, so test the I/O impact under the real workload.

The MOUNT-state statement F describes the initial roll-forward phase. It must not be interpreted as saying every rollback action finishes before OPEN: recovery of uncommitted transactions can continue after the database opens. Option B incorrectly places the whole instance-recovery process after OPEN. A is false because crash recovery uses online redo, rather than requiring archived logs in the normal crash scenario. D names the flashback-log writer, not the instance-recovery coordinator. E reverses the tuning relationship and incorrectly describes the purpose of MTTR tuning. To investigate a real system, compare estimated recovery time and checkpoint-write pressure in V$INSTANCE_RECOVERY; a very small target can increase normal database-writer activity.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Instance recovery restores database consistency after an instance failure.

text: Which three are true about Oracle Optimizer Statistics, their use, and their collection? (Choose three.)

options.text: The number of table rows is considered when evaluating the cost of accessing a table using an index.
Index balanced B*Tree height is considered when evaluating the cost of using an index.
The Statistics Advisor can help recommend the best way to gather statistics.
Statistics collected using DBMS_STATS always yield the best optimizer result.
The Statistics Advisor generates actions for all recommendations.

explanation:
A, B and C are correct; the original choose-two count omitted a normal input to index costing. Optimizer statistics estimate the work of alternative plans. They inform cost calculations rather than providing a promise that one access method is always best.

Option A is true. The estimated number of table rows, combined with predicate selectivity, helps estimate returned rows and hence table-row access work after an index lookup. Table and index statistics interact: an index does not make table cardinality irrelevant. Option B is true. B-tree height, recorded through statistics such as BLEVEL, contributes to the estimated work of locating matching index entries. Leaf-block counts and clustering factor also influence the calculation.

Option C is true. Optimizer Statistics Advisor examines statistics-gathering practices, reports findings and recommendations, and may provide actions to improve those practices. Option D is false: DBMS_STATS is the supported collection interface, but skew, correlation, unsuitable sampling or stale statistics can still produce poor cardinality estimates and plans. Option E is too absolute: recommendations do not all have executable automatic actions.

For a practical investigation, compare object statistics before comparing execution plans:
```sql
SELECT num_rows, blocks, last_analyzed
FROM user_tables WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS';
SELECT index_name, blevel, leaf_blocks, clustering_factor
FROM user_indexes WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS';
```
Then compare estimated and actual row counts with DBMS_XPLAN after executing a representative statement. A selective predicate, a large table and a well-clustered index can favor index access; changing the estimated row count can instead favor a full scan. The original count is corrected to three.
original_text: Which two are true about Oracle Optimizer Statistics, their use, and their collection? (Choose two.)

mnemonic.anchor: A, B and C are correct; the original choose-two count omitted a normal input to index costing.

text:
A container database (CDB) contains two pluggable databases PDB1 and PDB2. The LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED database property is set to FALSE in the CDB. Data file 24 of PDB2 was deleted and you need to restore and recover it. The only RMAN backup that exists was created with the BACKUP DATABASE command while connected to CDB$ROOT.

Which three are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Data file 24 can be recovered only while connected to PDB2.
Data file 24 can be restored and recovered while connected to CDB$ROOT.
Data file 24 can be restored only while connected to CDB$ROOT.
Data file 24 can be restored only while connected to PDB2.
Data file 24 can be recovered while connected to PDB2.
Data file 24 can be recovered while connected to CDB$ROOT.

explanation:
Core idea: In a CDB, data-file numbers are unique across the CDB, so RMAN can identify a PDB data file while connected to CDB$ROOT. Recovery can also be performed from the affected PDB for files belonging to that PDB; shared undo does not force every data-file operation to use only one connection scope.

Option analysis: B is correct: the root connection can restore and recover file 24. E is correct: a connection to PDB2 can recover a data file in PDB2. F is correct: root-level RMAN can also recover a data file belonging to PDB2. A and D are false because they incorrectly make the PDB connection exclusive. C is false because the PDB connection can be used for restoration as well; root is not the only allowed connection.

Practical point: use the root when you want to orchestrate multiple PDB recoveries; connect directly to a PDB when working on its files. Keep the PDB closed or the affected file offline as required by the recovery procedure.

The decisive distinction is complete media recovery versus PDB point-in-time recovery. Shared undo places important restrictions on PDB PITR and PDB flashback, but it does not prohibit ordinary complete recovery of this deleted PDB data file through a direct PDB connection. B and F allow root-connected recovery; E allows PDB-connected recovery with the required credentials and accessible backup. A, C and D each make an unjustified exclusive-connection claim. The root-level BACKUP DATABASE includes the PDB data files; it is not a root-only backup. A useful root-connected recovery sequence is:
```text
RESTORE DATAFILE 24;
RECOVER DATAFILE 24;
```
Availability, offline/online transitions and archived-redo access must still be planned for the affected file.

sources.title: Complete recovery of CDBs, PDBs and application containers
RMAN connection and recovery scope in a CDB
RMAN database connections and container restrictions

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: In a CDB, data-file numbers are unique across the CDB, so RMAN can identify a PDB data file while connected to CDB$ROOT.

text: Which three are true about data movement between a non-CDB and a PDB using Data Pump? (Choose three.)

options.text: Tablespaces are automatically created as needed while importing full exports in either a non-CDB or a PDB.
Oracle attempts to convert conventional database users to local users when moving schemas from a non-CDB to a PDB.
A new PDB is automatically created when importing a non-CDB into a CDB.
Oracle attempts to convert common users to conventional users when moving schemas from a PDB to a non-CDB.
Moving data from a PDB to a non-CDB is only possible by using transportable tablespace export and import.
Moving data from a non-CDB to a PDB is only possible by using conventional export and import.

explanation:
A, B and D describe an ordinary privileged full or schema movement under the relevant import prerequisites. The original count of two excluded normal tablespace creation during a conventional full import. This is not a claim that every transportable import creates or relocates every file automatically.

Option A is true for a full import containing the necessary tablespace metadata, executed with the required privileges and valid destination file locations or remapping. Data Pump can execute CREATE TABLESPACE as part of importing database metadata. Missing privileges, unsuitable source paths or filtered metadata can prevent that operation; those are import prerequisites, not a general prohibition in PDBs.

Option B is true: a conventional non-CDB schema user imported into a PDB is normally created as a local user. Option D is true: a common user exported from a PDB cannot retain CDB-wide common-user scope inside a non-CDB, so the imported schema/user is conventional there.

Option C is false because connecting an import job to a CDB does not implicitly create the desired PDB. Create the destination PDB and use its service first. Option E is false because conventional Data Pump movement is available from PDB to non-CDB. Option F is false because appropriate transportable workflows also support movement into a PDB.

In practice, inspect the proposed metadata using an import SQLFILE, verify destination tablespaces and paths, and connect to the intended PDB service. Use REMAP_TABLESPACE or REMAP_DATAFILE when appropriate. Moving schema metadata and rows is different from cloning a complete PDB or retaining the original common-user scope.
original_text: Which two are true about data movement between a non-CDB and a PDB using Data Pump? (Choose two.)
review_note: A is also true for an ordinary privileged full import when tablespace DDL and usable file locations are present. Original count two is not exhaustive under that normal interpretation; transportable and restricted import variants have different prerequisites.

keywords: convert conventional database users to local users
convert common users to conventional users
mnemonic.anchor: A, B and D describe an ordinary privileged full or schema movement under the relevant import prerequisites.

text: Which three methods can be used for heap table data migration after upgrading a database? (Choose three.)

options.text: using Database Replay
using SQL Developer
using Oracle Data Pump
using operating system file copy utilities
using Database Upgrade Assistant
using the CREATE TABLE AS SELECT SQL statement

explanation:
Core idea: Heap-table data migration moves rows into a new or reorganized table structure. It can be done with logical tools or SQL that reads source rows and writes them to a destination table.

Option analysis: B is correct: SQL Developer can move table data between database connections. C is correct: Data Pump exports and imports logical table data and metadata. F is correct: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT copies query results into a new heap table. A is false: Database Replay captures and replays workload, not table contents. D is false: copying operating-system files moves physical database files, not selected heap rows as a logical migration. E is false: DBUA upgrades the database, not application table data.

Practical example: use Data Pump for controlled schema migration, or CTAS when a query-based transformation is required; verify constraints, indexes, grants, and dependencies afterward.

Takeaway: choose a row-level migration method rather than a workload replay, file copy, or database-upgrade tool.

B, C and F operate at the table/data level: SQL Developer provides supported migration/copy facilities, Data Pump exports and imports rows with relevant metadata, and CREATE TABLE AS SELECT materializes query results. A replays a workload to test behavior and does not migrate the source heap table as a data-movement tool. D copies physical files, whose contents require a valid physical-database transport/recovery workflow rather than arbitrary heap-table migration. E upgrades an existing database, not a chosen table's rows into a replacement heap. For example:
```sql
CREATE TABLE orders_copy AS SELECT * FROM orders;
```
CTAS is not a complete schema clone: independently verify indexes, constraints, grants, triggers, partitioning and statistics. Choose Data Pump when preserving supported metadata is an important part of the migration.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Heap-table data migration moves rows into a new or reorganized table structure.

text: Which two are true about Oracle instance recovery? (Choose two.)

options.text: Recovery begins from the beginning of the CURRENT redo log group.
Recovery begins from the last checkpoint position that was calculated by the Database Writer before instance failure.
Recovery begins from the start of any ACTIVE redo log group or the start of the CURRENT log group if no other group is ACTIVE.
Recovery reads redo until the end of the redo thread. SMON rolls back any dead transactions, and then the database is opened.
Recovery begins from the last checkpoint position that was recorded in the control file by the checkpoint process (CKPT).
Recovery reads redo until the end of the redo thread, and then opens the database. SMON then rolls back any dead transactions.

explanation:
Core idea: Instance recovery starts from a checkpoint and applies redo records needed to bring data files forward after an instance failure. It does not restart from the beginning of the current log by default; the checkpoint SCN limits the work.

Option analysis: E is correct: the checkpoint position is recorded in the control file by checkpoint processing, and recovery uses that metadata as its starting point. F is correct: Oracle applies redo through the end of the redo thread and opens the database; SMON then rolls back transactions that were uncommitted at failure. A is false because redo recovery does not invariably start at the beginning of the current group. B is false because DBWn does not calculate and retain the recovery start point as stated. C is false: starting at the beginning of an ACTIVE or CURRENT group is not the general checkpoint rule. D incorrectly places rollback before the database opens.

Practical point: checkpoints reduce crash-recovery work by advancing the recoverable position while the database runs.

The redo checkpoint position is an RBA/SCN location, not necessarily the beginning of a redo-log group. Therefore A and C are false. B assigns checkpoint bookkeeping to DBWR rather than CKPT. E identifies the recorded checkpoint as the roll-forward starting position. F correctly allows the database to open after redo application, with transaction rollback continuing afterward; D incorrectly makes rollback of every dead transaction a prerequisite for opening. For example, a large uncommitted update may produce substantial post-open rollback after a crash even though committed data is already available. This is different from restoring a backup and applying archived redo after media failure: normal instance recovery uses the intact current database files and online redo thread.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Instance recovery starts from a checkpoint and applies redo records needed to bring data files forward after an instance failure.

text:
Examine this configuration:

1. The ORCL database data files are in Automatic Storage Management (Oracle ASM) disk group +DATA.
2. ORCL uses disk group +FRA for the Fast Recovery Area.
3. LISTENER is the listener for ORCL.
4. The database, listener, ASM instance, and ASM disk groups are managed by Oracle Restart.
5. All components are currently shut down.

You execute this command:

```text
$ srvctl start database -d ORCL
```

What is the outcome?

options.text: The ORCL database, the Oracle ASM instances, the +DATA and +FRA disk groups, and the LISTENER are started.
Only the ORCL database instance is started.
Only the ORCL database and the ASM instances are started.
Only the ORCL database instance, the Oracle ASM instance, and the +DATA and +FRA disk groups are started.
Only the ORCL database instance and the +DATA and +FRA disk groups are started.

explanation:
Core idea: Oracle Restart tracks resources and their dependencies. Starting a database through SRVCTL lets Restart start required resources first, including ASM and disk groups when the database depends on them. ASM itself has a weak dependency on the configured listener.

Option analysis: A is correct for the stated configured dependencies: the database, ASM instance, +DATA and +FRA disk groups, and listener are started in dependency order. B is false because the database cannot access its ASM files until dependencies are available. C and E omit required ASM or disk-group resources. D omits the listener, which Oracle Restart attempts to start before ASM when configured as the ASM listener dependency.

Practical example: use SRVCTL rather than starting the database manually so Oracle Restart can honor the resource configuration. If the database was added while ASM was down, verify that disk-group dependencies were explicitly registered; otherwise the expected start chain may not exist.

Takeaway: SRVCTL's result depends on the saved Oracle Restart dependency configuration.

A assumes the registered resources and dependencies are valid and startup succeeds. The database has hard dependencies on its required ASM disk groups; their startup entails making the ASM instance available and mounting +DATA and +FRA. Oracle Restart also has a weak listener dependency: it attempts to start LISTENER when starting the database, but listener failure does not by itself prevent the local database instance from starting. B, C, D and E omit resources that Oracle Restart attempts to start under this normal dependency configuration. Thus “A” is the expected successful outcome, rather than a guarantee that listener failure is fatal. Contrast SRVCTL with a bare local SQL*Plus STARTUP, which does not provide the same resource-management request.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Oracle Restart tracks resources and their dependencies.

text: Which two are true about the Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM)? (Choose two.)

options.text: It analyzes a period of time corresponding to the 12 hours of activity.
It runs automatically after each AWR snapshot.
A DBA can run it manually.
Results are written to the alert log.
It analyzes a period of time corresponding to the last day of activity.

explanation:
Core idea: ADDM analyzes database performance using AWR snapshots and reports findings with likely causes and recommended actions. Its automatic task is part of the performance self-diagnostics workflow, and a DBA can also create a manual analysis for a selected interval.

Option analysis: B is correct: ADDM runs automatically after AWR snapshots are taken. C is correct: DBAs can run ADDM manually for a chosen snapshot range. A is false: the automatic analysis is not defined as a fixed 12-hour window. D is false: findings are available through advisor reports and views, not simply written to the alert log as the answer. E is false: ADDM does not always analyze the entire last day; the interval is tied to the selected snapshots.

Practical example: after a slow period, identify its start and end snapshots, review the ADDM findings, and investigate the highest-impact cause before changing configuration.

Takeaway: ADDM diagnoses workload intervals; it does not replace verifying the reported issue in the live system.

B refers to automatic ADDM analysis following AWR snapshots under the normal management configuration; C allows a DBA-requested analysis of a selected snapshot interval. A and E incorrectly hard-code twelve-hour and day-long intervals: the analysis scope is defined by the relevant snapshot pair. D confuses an ADDM report and its repository findings with the alert log. For a practical diagnosis, choose snapshots bracketing the actual slowdown and compare database time contributors with a healthy interval. ADDM may identify expensive SQL, I/O or contention; implementing a recommendation still requires checking workload context and measuring the outcome. Snapshot frequency and retention are configurable, so do not infer the analysis period merely from the calendar day.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: ADDM analyzes database performance using AWR snapshots and reports findings with likely causes and recommended actions.

text: Which four are true about a Recovery Manager (RMAN) duplication without a TARGET connection? (Choose four.)

options.text: The NOREDO clause must be used if the backups of the database being duplicated were taken when the database was in NOARCHIVELOG mode.
The UNDO TABLESPACE clause is always required when no connection exists to the TARGET instance.
RMAN 'pushes' the backups of the database to be duplicated over the network to the auxiliary instance.
The NOREDO clause can be used if the backups of the database being duplicated were taken when the database was in ARCHIVELOG mode.
RMAN SBT-based backups of the database to be duplicated can be used by the auxiliary instance.
The UNDO TABLESPACE clause is always required when no connection exists to the recovery catalog and the TARGET database is closed.
The UNDO TABLESPACE clause is always required when no connection exists to the recovery catalog and the TARGET database is opened.
RMAN disk-based backups of the database to be duplicated can be used by the auxiliary instance.

explanation:
Core idea: Backup-based RMAN duplication without a TARGET connection uses existing backup pieces accessible to the auxiliary instance. Because RMAN cannot query the source, the files and metadata needed for duplication must be available through the backup location and auxiliary configuration.

Option analysis: A is correct: a NOARCHIVELOG source backup is consistent and has no archived redo to apply, so NOREDO is required. D is correct: NOREDO may also be chosen for an ARCHIVELOG source when the duplicate should not apply redo. E and H are correct: accessible SBT or disk backups can be used by the auxiliary. B is false: an UNDO TABLESPACE clause is not universally required. C is false: backup-based duplication reads accessible backups; it does not automatically push them from a connected TARGET. F and G are false because their blanket conditions about catalog connection and target open state do not apply in every duplication configuration.

Practical point: stage backup pieces where auxiliary channels can read them and test the complete restore path before relying on it.

The absence of a TARGET connection distinguishes this backup-based workflow from active duplication; it does not itself prohibit SBT. E requires usable media-manager configuration and the appropriate backup metadata, usually through the recovery catalog in the SBT/no-TARGET workflow. H covers accessible disk backups. A and D concern NOREDO: a consistent NOARCHIVELOG backup needs no redo application, and an appropriate consistent ARCHIVELOG backup can also be duplicated with NOREDO. B, F and G overstate UNDO TABLESPACE as universally mandatory; its necessity depends on catalog availability, source metadata and whether a subset is duplicated. C describes network transfer associated with active duplication rather than this backup-based case. Always validate the exact command's connection, backup-location and subset prerequisites together.

sources.title: RMAN duplication: new-CDB and existing-CDB workflows

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Backup-based RMAN duplication without a TARGET connection uses existing backup pieces accessible to the auxiliary instance.

text: Which three are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Virtual Private Database (VPD) policies on objects in an application root are automatically synchronized with all application PDBs contained in the application container.
Application-common TSDP policies are always container specific.
Application-common Transparent Security Data Protection (TSDP) policies can be created only within an application install/patch BEGIN-END block.
Application-common Oracle Label Security (OLS) policies cannot be created in an application root outside an install/patch BEGIN-END block.
Fine-grained auditing (FGA) policies in an application root are automatically synchronized to all application PDBs contained in the application container.
Application-common OLS policies can be created in an application root inside an install/patch BEGIN-END block.
Unified auditing can be automatically synchronized to all application PDBs in an application container.

explanation:
B, D and G follow the feature-specific application-container restrictions. Security policies must not all be treated like a single automatically synchronized category of application object.

Option B is true: Transparent Sensitive Data Protection policies are container specific. Their scope and management are not transformed into universally synchronized common policy state merely by operating in an application container. Option C is false: Oracle specifically restricts TSDP policy operations inside application installation/patch blocks rather than requiring that block.

Option D is logically true but potentially misleading. Oracle Label Security policies cannot be created in an application root outside an install/patch block, because policy creation in the application root is not supported at all. Option F is therefore also false: moving the same operation inside the block does not make it valid. Oracle documents ORA-42900 for creating an OLS policy in an application root, with the action to create the policy in an application PDB instead.

Option G is true for supported common unified-audit policy synchronization to application PDBs. Options A and E incorrectly assume automatic synchronization of the stated VPD and FGA policies merely because their objects reside in an application root.

In a practical deployment, identify separately where the application object is defined, where its data is stored, where the security policy is created and whether that policy type supports common synchronization. Test a representative authorized and unauthorized access in each application PDB after synchronization. A successful application install does not prove that every security policy has propagated or that its container scope matches the intended access controls.

D must be read carefully: it is true that these OLS policies cannot be created outside an application install/patch block, but the inverse is not true. Oracle also rejects OLS policy creation in an application root inside such a block; F is consequently false. The documented error is ORA-42900, whose remedy is to create the policy in the application PDB rather than in the application root. B describes TSDP's container-local scope; C incorrectly requires the application-install block, where this operation is restricted. A and E incorrectly equate all security policies with synchronized application objects. G covers supported common unified-audit policy synchronization. Security-policy scope must be checked per feature, even when all the features protect the same application table.

sources.title: TSDP policies in a multitenant environment

mnemonic.anchor: B, D and G follow the feature-specific application-container restrictions.

text: Which three are true about Automatic Workload Repository (AWR)? (Choose three.)

options.text: By default, AWR snapshots are taken every 60 minutes.
Its collection level is determined by the value of the STATISTICS_LEVEL database parameter.
By default, AWR snapshots are retained for 7 days.
The taking of AWR snapshots can be disabled.
AWR data is stored in the SYSTEM tablespace.

explanation:
Core idea: AWR captures workload and performance statistics for later diagnosis. Its snapshot schedule, retention, and collection level are configurable, so distinguish defaults from settings an administrator can change.

Option analysis: A is correct: the default snapshot interval is 60 minutes. B is correct: STATISTICS_LEVEL controls the level of statistics collected for AWR and related features. D is correct: automatic snapshots can be disabled by setting the interval to zero. C is false: the default retention is eight days, not seven. E is false: AWR data is stored primarily in SYSAUX, not SYSTEM.

Practical example: retain snapshots long enough to cover business cycles, but account for SYSAUX growth and licensing/feature requirements when changing AWR collection.

Takeaway: know the default hourly/eight-day behavior, and remember both interval and retention can be configured.

A and B describe the normal automatic collection framework. D is possible by disabling the automatic snapshot interval; STATISTICS_LEVEL=BASIC also disables important automatic management/statistics facilities and should not be used casually as a space-saving shortcut. C is false because the documented default retention is eight days rather than seven. E is false because AWR's persistent repository uses SYSAUX, not SYSTEM. Inspect the actual settings rather than relying on defaults:
```sql
SELECT snap_interval, retention FROM dba_hist_wr_control;
```
For a licensed, appropriately authorized investigation, select an interval containing the performance problem and compare it with a representative healthy workload. Increasing snapshot frequency improves time resolution but increases repository work and storage; retention is an independent setting.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: AWR captures workload and performance statistics for later diagnosis.

text: Which two are true about automatic block repair? (Choose two.)

options.text: Automatic block repair can repair blocks with no standby database if DB_BLOCK_CHECKING = TRUE.
Real-Time Query must be enabled on a physical standby database for automatic block repair to be done on that physical standby database.
Real-Time Query must be enabled on a primary database for automatic block repair to be done on any of its physical standby databases.
It is not possible for media corrupt blocks.
Real-Time Query must be enabled on a physical standby database for automatic block repair to be done on its primary database.

explanation:
Core idea: Automatic block repair can replace a corrupted block by retrieving a good copy from a Data Guard partner. It is a media-recovery capability, distinct from block checking, which detects corruption but does not itself provide a replacement block.

Option analysis: B and E are correct: Real-Time Query on a physical standby is required for the automatic repair direction described, whether the standby is the target of repair or supplies a good block to its primary. A is false: DB_BLOCK_CHECKING can detect certain logical corruptions but cannot repair blocks without a good source. C is false because Real-Time Query is needed on the standby, not the primary, for this feature. D is false: media-corrupt blocks are precisely among the corruption scenarios automatic block repair can address when a suitable partner copy is available.

Practical point: maintain a usable physical standby and verify its apply/query configuration; block repair depends on a valid counterpart block.

B and E both require the Active Data Guard real-time-query physical standby used in automatic block repair. In the primary-to-standby direction or the standby-to-primary direction, the partner must have an available good block and the configured communication must succeed. C incorrectly places real-time-query mode on the primary. D reverses the purpose of the feature: it addresses supported physical/media block corruptions, not every possible logical inconsistency. A substitutes local block checking for a repair source; detecting corruption does not create a healthy replacement copy. For a practical incident, verify standby open mode, redo apply state and alert-log repair diagnostics, and distinguish automatic repair from explicitly requested RMAN block media recovery. Later 19c updates extend some corruption-repair scenarios; check the installed Release Update and current high-availability guidance before treating the real-time-query requirement as universal across all 19c updates.

sources.title: Active Data Guard automatic block media recovery

review_note: BE follows the core 19c Backup/Recovery and Data Guard guides real-time-query requirement. More recent 19c high-availability guidance describes additional mounted-standby repair cases, so check actual Release Update rather than treating B as timeless.

keywords: done on that physical standby database
mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Automatic block repair can replace a corrupted block by retrieving a good copy from a Data Guard partner.

text:
Oracle Managed Files (OMF) is enabled in a CDB and this command is successfully executed:

```text
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE app1
AS APPLICATION CONTAINER
ADMIN USER admin1 IDENTIFIED BY app_123 ROLES=(CONNECT);
```

Which three are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Application PDBs that are subsequently created in the APP1 application container will be cloned from APP1$SEED.
An application seed PDB is created for APP1.
An application root PDB is created for APP1.
A default service is created for the application root APP1.
Application PDBs that are subsequently created in the APP1 application container will be cloned from PDB$SEED.
APP1 can never be unplugged.

explanation:
Core idea: Creating a PDB with AS APPLICATION CONTAINER creates an application root. An application seed is an optional, separately created seed used to accelerate later application-PDB provisioning.

Option analysis: C, D, and E are correct: APP1 becomes an application root, receives a default service, and future application PDBs use the ordinary PDB$SEED unless an application seed is explicitly created. A is false because APP1$SEED is not automatically created by the shown statement. B is false for the same reason: an application seed requires an additional creation step. F is false: an application root can be unplugged subject to the usual PDB and application-container rules.

Practical example: create an application seed only after preparing a baseline application PDB; then future clones can use that tailored seed instead of the generic PDB seed.

Takeaway: AS APPLICATION CONTAINER creates the root, not an application seed.

The single AS APPLICATION CONTAINER clause creates an application root, not an application seed. C and D therefore follow immediately. E describes the default source for subsequently created application PDBs while no application seed has been created; if an application seed is explicitly created later, the source behavior changes. A presupposes APP1$SEED and B incorrectly claims it is created by this statement. F is false because supported unplug/plug workflows exist for application containers subject to their restrictions. A useful inspection is:
```sql
SELECT name, application_root, application_seed
FROM v$pdbs;
```
OMF supplies file naming/placement management; it does not implicitly request a seed or copy future application PDBs into existence.

sources.title: Application objects, container maps and application administration

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Creating a PDB with AS APPLICATION CONTAINER creates an application root.

text: Which two are true about RMAN encryption? (Choose two.)

options.text: RMAN encryption keys are stored in a database keystore.
RMAN can encrypt the Oracle Database password file.
Dual-mode encrypted backups can be restored only if both the password and the keystore used for encryption are available.
The SET ENCRYPTION command overrides encryption settings specified by the CONFIGURE ENCRYPTION command.
Password encryption can be persistently configured using the CONFIGURE ENCRYPTION command.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN supports transparent keystore-based encryption, password-based encryption, and dual-mode encryption. The mode determines which recovery secret is needed, while command-level encryption settings can override configured defaults for a backup operation.

Option analysis: A is correct for transparent encryption: its keys are protected in the database keystore; this should not be generalized to password-only mode. D is correct: SET ENCRYPTION at the command/session level takes precedence over persistent CONFIGURE settings. B is false: RMAN backup encryption does not encrypt the Oracle password file as a separate backup payload. C is false: dual-mode backups can be restored using the password or the keystore, not necessarily both together. E is false: password encryption is set for a backup operation rather than persistently through CONFIGURE ENCRYPTION.

Practical point: test a restore using the actual mode and key material before a disaster; an encrypted backup is useful only if its password or wallet remains available.

Key nuance: option A is phrased broadly; the keystore statement applies specifically to transparent encryption.

A is accurate for transparent RMAN encryption and the keystore component of dual-mode encryption. It is not a universal requirement for password-only encrypted backups, whose recovery can use the password without the original keystore. D concerns precedence: session SET ENCRYPTION can override persistent CONFIGURE settings for the backup operation. B is false because the password file is not a supported RMAN-encrypted database backup object. C is false because dual mode permits either the appropriate keystore or the password, rather than requiring both. E is false because password encryption is configured for the session with SET, not persistently using CONFIGURE. Do not confuse a database encryption keystore, a database password file, an RMAN repository, and media-manager encryption keys: they serve different purposes.
review_note: A is the intended transparent-encryption statement, but is not universal for password-only encryption. AD is retained with the encryption-mode qualification made explicit.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: RMAN supports transparent keystore-based encryption, password-based encryption, and dual-mode encryption.

text: Which three are true about performing an Oracle Database install on Linux? (Choose three.)

options.text: The runfixup.sh script can install missing RPMs.
The Oracle Preinstallation RPM must be used to configure the Oracle database installation owner, the Oracle Inventory group, and an Oracle administrative privileges group.
It allows you to select the languages supported by the Oracle database server.
It can be done before installing Grid Infrastructure for a Standalone Server.
The Oracle Preinstallation RPM can be used to configure the Oracle database installation owner, the Oracle Inventory group, and an Oracle administrative privileges group.
It can be done after installing Grid Infrastructure for a Standalone Server.
The Oracle database administrator must be granted access to the root operating system account to tun root privileged scripts.

explanation:
Core idea: Oracle Database installation on Linux can be performed before or after standalone Grid Infrastructure, and the preinstallation RPM is a supported convenience for preparing OS prerequisites. It is recommended but not mandatory.

Option analysis: D and F are correct: installation order can be either before or after standalone GI, depending on the chosen deployment plan. E is correct: the Preinstallation RPM can create the installation owner and groups and apply prerequisite OS settings. A is false as worded: runfixup.sh addresses selected prerequisite fixes but is not a general tool that installs every missing RPM. B is false because use of the RPM is not mandatory. C is false for this question's keyed installation task; language selection is handled through product installation configuration and does not make the other answers incorrect. G is false: DBAs do not need routine root-account access; privileged scripts are run through root or the supported sudo workflow.

Practical point: verify groups, packages, kernel settings, and root-script handling against the release installation guide.

D and F express possible installation order, rather than recommending that every production deployment install database software before GI. E describes the RPM's convenience; B incorrectly makes that convenience mandatory. A is false because fixup scripts do not substitute for installing missing operating-system packages. C confuses server capabilities and database character-set/globalization configuration with installer-language selection. G is false: an authorized administrator or configured root/sudo execution mechanism can run privileged scripts without granting the DBA unrestricted root account access. Before installation, independently validate supported OS packages, kernel settings, groups and filesystem ownership. Installing software into an Oracle home is also distinct from configuring ASM and creating a database that uses ASM storage.

sources.title: Oracle Database installation and image-based installation

mnemonic.anchor: It is recommended but not mandatory.

text: Which three are true about Recovery Manager (RMAN) in Oracle Database 19c and later releases? (Choose three.)

options.text: It is only possible for RMAN to connect to a pluggable database as a target if an RMAN Virtual Private Catalog is used.
It is always possible for RMAN to connect to a pluggable database as a target if any RMAN Catalog is used.
A Virtual Private Catalog used to register a container database must be created in a pluggable database.
A Virtual Private Catalog used to register a container database can be created in a pluggable database.
It is always possible for RMAN to connect to a pluggable database as a target.
A Virtual Private Catalog used to register a container database can be created in a non-container database.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN can target a PDB directly, while a virtual private catalog (VPC) limits a catalog user's metadata view. The catalog's host database and the target CDB are separate design choices.

Option analysis: D, E, and F are correct: a VPC can be created in a PDB; RMAN can connect to a PDB as target in supported 19c configurations; and the catalog may be hosted in a non-CDB. A is false because a VPC is not the only way to connect RMAN to a PDB. B is false because “always” ignores privilege, connection, and catalog configuration requirements. C is false because a VPC for a CDB is not required to reside in a PDB. The location of the catalog schema does not change which database RMAN is targeting.

Practical example: grant the catalog user access to the registered target and connect RMAN to the intended PDB service; confirm the target identity before running backup commands.

D and F describe possible catalog database locations under the 19c compatibility/edition requirements, not a claim that any obsolete catalog release is acceptable. E means supported RMAN target connections directly to a PDB are available; credentials, network service and operation-specific restrictions still apply. A is false because such a connection does not require a virtual private catalog. B overstates “any” catalog: catalog compatibility and registration/access restrictions matter. C incorrectly restricts catalog hosting to a PDB. A virtual private catalog limits the metadata and registered databases a catalog user can see; it does not turn otherwise unsupported RMAN operations into supported PDB-level operations. In particular, backup and recovery command scope still depends on whether the connection targets the root or a PDB.

sources.title: Creating and managing the recovery catalog
RMAN database connections and container restrictions

keywords: can be created in a pluggable database
mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: RMAN can target a PDB directly, while a virtual private catalog (VPC) limits a catalog user's metadata view.

text: Which three are true in Oracle 19c and later releases? (Choose three.)

options.text: If the password file location changes, then the new location is used automatically by the Oracle Server.
Schema Only accounts can be granted administrator privileges.
All the Oracle-supplied accounts are Schema Only accounts.
Privilege Analysis is included in Oracle Enterprise Edition and no longer requires Database Vault.
Unified Auditing can be configured to audit only events that are issued indirectly by an audited user.
Unified Auditing can be configured to audit only events that are issued directly by an audited user.

explanation:
Core idea: 19c schema-only accounts separate ownership of objects from password-based logon. Such an account can still receive privileges; “schema only” does not mean “privilege free.” Unified Auditing also supports policies that distinguish top-level actions from actions executed indirectly.

Option analysis: B is correct: schema-only accounts may receive administrative privileges, subject to the authentication and privilege controls. D is correct: Privilege Analysis is included with Enterprise Edition in 19c and does not require Database Vault. F is correct: unified audit policy syntax can target direct, top-level events. C is false because Oracle-supplied accounts are not all schema-only. A is false as a blanket claim; password-file behavior depends on the configured location and update procedure. E is false because the supported direct/indirect distinction does not mean a policy can audit only indirect actions as stated.

Practical point: removing password authentication reduces one login path, but audit and privilege reviews are still required.

B is a documented 19c enhancement: schema-only accounts may receive supported administrative privileges even though ordinary password authentication is disabled. It does not make all Oracle-supplied accounts schema-only, so C is false. D moves Privilege Analysis into Enterprise Edition without requiring Database Vault. F is the ONLY TOPLEVEL auditing capability, distinguishing directly issued user statements from recursive SQL; E reverses the feature. A overlooks the required password-file metadata-cache handling when a location changes; changing a path is not equivalent to flushing/reloading cached server information. A practical audit policy should be tested with both a directly executed SQL statement and recursive statements caused by it so that the recorded scope matches the DBA's intention.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: 19c schema-only accounts separate ownership of objects from password-based logon.

text:
You have configured RMAN SBT channels to write backups to media.

You then take an RMAN backup by using this command:

```text
RMAN> BACKUP AS COMPRESSED BACKUPSET
  2   DATABASE
  3   KEEP UNTIL TIME 'SYSDATE + 730'
  4   RESTORE POINT 'OLD CONFIGURATION';
```

Which three are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: The restore point is a label for the system change number (SCN) that will be saved two years after the archival backup was taken.
The data file backups in the self-contained archive backup are not considered obsolete for two years regardless of the retention policy.
All archive logs created after this backup are kept for two years.
The SPFILE is included in the self-contained archival backup.
The control file is included in the self-contained archival backup.
The restore point is a label for the system change number (SCN) before the archival backup was taken.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN KEEP creates an archival backup exempt from the configured retention policy until the specified time. A self-contained archival backup includes the files and redo needed to restore it consistently, plus control-file and SPFILE copies.

Option analysis: B is correct: the data-file backup is not treated as obsolete by the ordinary retention policy during the KEEP interval. D and E are correct: RMAN includes the SPFILE and control file in a self-contained archival backup. C is false: the KEEP period does not mean every archived log created for the next two years is retained. A and F are false: the restore point is a label for the SCN at which the backup can be made consistent; Oracle captures that SCN after the data-file backup completes, not two years later or before the backup starts.

Practical use: retain the backup media and its associated archived logs, and verify the backup before relying on a long-term archive.

B applies KEEP's archival retention independently of the ordinary retention policy, for the specified interval. D and E identify the SPFILE and control-file components of a self-contained archival backup, assuming the running database uses an SPFILE. C is false because KEEP does not preserve every subsequently generated archived log for two years: it includes the archived redo needed to make the archival backup recoverable to its designated point. A and F place that restore point at the wrong time; Oracle creates the associated restore-point SCN after the data-file backup, not before it or two years in the future. SBT controls the output device through the media manager; compression and archival retention do not eliminate media-manager readability or restore-testing requirements.

text: Which three are true about server-generated alerts? (Choose three.)

options.text: Stateful alerts must be created by a DBA after resolving the problem.
Stateless alerts can be purged manually from the alert history.
Stateless alerts can be cleared manually.
Stateless alerts are automatically cleared.
Stateful alerts are purged automatically from the alert history.

explanation:
B, C and E are defensible when the question includes Enterprise Manager alert management as well as the database server alert-history lifecycle. The original choose-two count mixes these scopes without explaining their retention behavior, so it has been adjusted to three with this qualification.

Stateful alerts represent a condition with a measurable current state, such as a threshold violation. When the condition returns to normal, the alert can clear automatically and its history remains for diagnosis. Stateless alerts represent events rather than a persistent condition whose later measurement can automatically signal resolution.

Option A is false: a stateful alert is generated when the monitored condition requires it, not created by a DBA after the problem has been resolved. Option B is supported by Enterprise Manager's manual purge/clear management of stateless alert history. Option C is true in that same management context: stateless alerts can be manually cleared. Option D is false as a generic lifecycle statement because stateless events have no state transition that automatically clears them.

Option E is true for the documented automatic purging of database alert history. Oracle Database 19c describes automatic purging of alert history and the alert queue; clearing an outstanding stateful alert and later purging historical records are separate operations.

In practice, distinguish an outstanding alert, a cleared event retained in history, and an Enterprise Manager incident created from that event. The monitoring repository's retention configuration and management UI determine which historical operations are available. A clean current-alert display does not mean the underlying historical diagnostic records have already been deleted.
original_text: Which two are true about server-generated alerts? (Choose two.)
review_note: Original choose-two count excludes documented automatic alert-history purging. B/C use Enterprise Manager stateless-alert lifecycle semantics; E follows Database 19c automatic alert-history purge. Exact UI and retention depend on monitoring product/configuration.

mnemonic.anchor: B, C and E are defensible when the question includes Enterprise Manager alert management as well as the database server alert-history lifecycle.

text:
The USERS tablespace consists of data files 3 and 4 and must always be online in read/write mode.

Which two are true about using RMAN to perform an open database back up of this tablespace? (Choose two.)

options.text: Backups must be done incrementally.
Backups must be contained in backup sets.
Backups can be taken only if the database is in ARCHIVELOG mode.
Backups can be done incrementally.
The database must be registered in an RMAN catalog.
Only consistent backups can be created.

explanation:
Core idea: An open RMAN backup is inconsistent while it is being read, so Oracle must have redo available to make the restored files consistent. This is why an online backup requires ARCHIVELOG mode. RMAN can back up data files as backup sets or image copies, and can take full or incremental backups.

Option analysis: C is correct: the USERS tablespace stays online read/write, so ARCHIVELOG mode is required for recoverability. D is correct: an incremental backup is allowed, but it is not mandatory. A is false because a full backup is also possible. B is false because RMAN can create image copies as well as backup sets. E is false because a recovery catalog is optional; RMAN can use the target control file repository. F is false because an open backup is not a consistent, closed-database backup.

Practical point: ensure the archived logs covering the backup window are retained and included in the recovery plan; otherwise the online copy may not be recoverable to a consistent state.

C depends on the question's read/write-online requirement: a mounted, cleanly shut down NOARCHIVELOG database is a different case. D permits changed-block backups, whereas a nonincremental full backup is also valid. B excludes supported disk image copies; E confuses optional catalog metadata with the mandatory control-file repository. F mistakes open-file consistency for restored-database recoverability. For example:
```text
BACKUP INCREMENTAL LEVEL 0 TABLESPACE USERS;
BACKUP INCREMENTAL LEVEL 1 TABLESPACE USERS;
```
The level-zero backup supplies a base for later level-one backups. A full nonincremental backup has different incremental-parent semantics even if it reads essentially the same used blocks. Retain the redo needed to make the restored online backup consistent.

text: Which four are true about RMAN backup sets? (Choose four.)

options.text: A backup piece can belong to only one backup set.
A data file can be split into multiple sections stored in different backup sets.
A data file can be split into multiple sections stored in different backup pieces in the same backup set.
Blocks from multiple data files can be contained in one backup piece.
A backup set can contain only one backup piece.
A backup set must be written to media.
A backup set must be written to disk.
Blocks from multiple data files can be contained in one backup set.

explanation:
Core idea: A backup set is RMAN's logical container for backed-up blocks; it consists of one or more backup pieces. Multiplexing can place blocks from several input files in a piece, while a multisection backup divides one large data file into sections for parallel channels.

Option analysis: A, C, D, and H are correct: each piece belongs to one set; multisection pieces can hold different sections of one file within the same set; a piece can contain blocks from several data files; and a set can contain blocks from multiple files. B is false because sections of one multisection data-file backup are in pieces of the same set, not different sets. E is false because a set can have multiple pieces. F and G are false because backup sets can be written to disk or a media manager such as tape.

Practical takeaway: do not confuse a set, its pieces, and the file sections stored inside them.

These choices concern one backup operation's organization, not whether a later independent backup can store the same data file in another set. A multisection backup divides a large file into nonoverlapping block ranges and allows channels to process sections in parallel. Distinct section pieces belong to that file's multisection backup set. Multiplexing instead combines input from different files; its supported interactions and channel settings must be checked separately rather than assuming every technique is combined in every piece. Inspect LIST BACKUP and the backup-set/piece views when planning a restore, and retain every required piece: a backup-set record alone is not a restorable copy of missing pieces.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: A backup set is RMAN's logical container for backed-up blocks; it consists of one or more backup pieces.

text: Which two are true about creating RMAN backups for an Oracle container database? (Choose two.)

options.text: Tablespaces from different PDBs with identical names must be backed up by connecting RMAN separately to each PDB to back up the tablespaces.
The BACKUP DATABASE command will create a pluggable database (PDB) backup when RMAN is connected to a PDB.
SPFILE backups can be created while connected to an application root PDB.
The BACKUP DATABASE PLUS ARCHIVELOG command will back up archive logs when RMAN is connected to a PDB.
The BACKUP PLUGGABLE DATABASE command can be used to back up CDB$ROOT.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN backup scope depends on the target container. Connected to a PDB, BACKUP DATABASE backs up that PDB. Connected to CDB$ROOT, RMAN can back up PDBs or the root using the corresponding command form.

Option analysis: B is correct: a PDB target connection with BACKUP DATABASE backs up that PDB. The bank also selects E, but Oracle 19c syntax makes this answer questionable: BACKUP PLUGGABLE DATABASE names PDBs, while a root-only backup is documented as BACKUP DATABASE ROOT. A is false because data-file numbers are unique across the CDB, so root-level RMAN can address PDB data files without reconnecting to each PDB. C is false because an application-root connection is not the general way to back up the CDB SPFILE. D is false: a PDB connection cannot back up CDB archived redo logs with PLUS ARCHIVELOG.

Practical point: confirm the target connection and command scope before running a backup. Review option E against the exact exam wording because its syntax conflicts with the Oracle 19c reference.

The defensible documented root-only form is:
```text
BACKUP DATABASE ROOT;
```
For repeated tablespace names, root-connected RMAN can use PDB-qualified tablespace names such as PDB1:USERS, or unique data-file numbers. Thus A is not required. A root-level SPFILE is a CDB-wide resource, so do not infer that an application-root backup scope automatically grants every CDB backup operation. There is insufficient documentation here to certify the exact E spelling as a supported alias; this item remains ambiguous rather than presenting its inherited key as settled. Test exact command parsing and connection restrictions in a disposable 19c CDB before relying on either disputed command in an operational script.

sources.title: RMAN backup scope, archival backups and output

review_note: B is documented. The retained intended second answer E names root as a PDB; the official 19c reference documents BACKUP DATABASE ROOT. C also requires exact application-root connection restrictions. Do not treat BE as an official verified key.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: RMAN backup scope depends on the target container.

text: Which three can be done using Oracle Database Configuration Assistant (DBCA) starting from Oracle Database 19c? (Choose three.)

options.text: cloning a remote container database in interactive mode
cloning a remote pluggable database in silent mode
relocating a remote pluggable database in interactive mode
relocating a remote container database in silent mode
cloning a remote container database in silent mode
relocating a remote pluggable database in silent mode
relocating a remote container database in interactive mode

explanation:
B, E and F are the documented silent-mode capabilities. Oracle 19c added DBCA support for duplicating an entire remote database and for relocating a PDB in silent mode; remote PDB cloning is also supported. The original BCF key incorrectly treated interactive relocation as the listed enhancement and excluded whole-database silent duplication.

Option B is true: DBCA's remote-PDB creation/clone workflow can connect to the source and create the destination PDB in silent mode. Option E is true: the createDuplicateDB command supports duplicating a remote database, including the supported CDB case. This is a separate whole-database workflow from createPluggableDatabase. Option F is true: relocatePDB is the 19c silent-mode remote-PDB relocation operation.

Option A is not the documented remote-CDB interactive capability in this feature list. Option C incorrectly assigns the new remote-PDB relocation capability to interactive mode. Options D and G change the unit of relocation from a PDB to an entire remote CDB; they are not the documented relocatePDB operation.

The relevant command families can be inspected without supplying credentials:
```text
dbca -help -createDuplicateDB
dbca -help -createPluggableDatabase
dbca -help -relocatePDB
```
Clone means creating another database/PDB while retaining the source. Relocation moves the supported PDB to a different CDB. Before either workflow, check connectivity, administrative privileges, archive/undo prerequisites, file destinations and source/target compatibility. “Remote CDB” must not be dismissed merely because a different option discusses PDB relocation: DBCA has distinct supported operations for these different scopes.
