text:
Examine these queries and their output:

```text
SQL> select pdb_name, name, pdb_restore_point, clean_pdb_restore_point
  2  from v$restore_point natural join dba_pdbs;

PDB_NAME   NAME       PDB_RESTORE_POINT CLEAN_PDB_RESTORE_POINT
---------- ---------- ----------------- -----------------------
PDB1       R1         YES               NO

SQL> select property_name, property_value
  2  from database_properties where property_name like '%UNDO%';

PROPERTY_NAME                  PROPERTY_VALUE
------------------------------ ------------------------------
LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED             FALSE
```

An online RMAN backup of the CDB was taken an hour before Restore Point R1 was created.
You want to recover PDB1 to Restore Point R1.

How do you achieve this?

options.text: Execute FLASHBACK PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB1 TO RESTORE POINT R1 by using RMAN while connected to PDB1.
Execute FLASHBACK PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB1 TO RESTORE POINT R1 by using SQL while connected to PDB1.
Execute FLASHBACK PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB1 TO RESTORE POINT R1 by using SQL while connected to CDB$ROOT.
Execute FLASHBACK PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB1 TO RESTORE POINT R1 by using RMAN while connected to CDB$ROOT.
This cannot be done due to the lack of a clean restore point.

explanation:
E is the intended answer only if “this” means the FLASHBACK PLUGGABLE DATABASE methods offered in A through D. It is too broad as a claim that PDB1 cannot be recovered to the corresponding time or SCN by any method.

The query establishes shared undo (LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED=FALSE) and an ordinary, non-clean PDB restore point. A clean PDB restore point is created with the PDB closed and no outstanding transactions. The supported shared-undo PDB flashback workflow requires such a clean point; choosing RMAN instead of SQL or changing the connection does not turn R1 into one.

Options A and B additionally attempt a direct PDB-level operation despite shared-undo connection restrictions. Options C and D use the root but still retain the non-clean restore-point problem. Therefore none of A through D is a valid way to perform the requested PDB flashback in the shown configuration.

However, complete absence of a clean restore point is not a general prohibition on backup-based PDB point-in-time recovery. With the backup and required archived redo, RMAN can perform PDB PITR using an auxiliary instance and undo recovery as necessary. The backup taken an hour earlier may therefore be useful for that different workflow; it does not validate the four FLASHBACK commands listed here.

In practice, obtain R1's SCN and verify backup/redo coverage before planning RECOVER PLUGGABLE DATABASE to the intended endpoint from CDB$ROOT. The distinction is between undoing changes using flashback logs and restoring older files then applying redo. The bank's absolute “cannot be done” wording needs this qualification.

text: Which two are true about diagnosing Oracle Database failure situations using Data Recovery Advisor? (Choose two.)

options.text: Using the Data Recovery Advisor LIST FAILURE command always requires that the database for which failures are to be listed is in MOUNT state.
A failure can be closed only when it has been repaired.
Data Recovery Advisor can be used if a database is closed.
The Data Recovery Advisor CHANGE FAILURE command can be used only to change failure priorities.
Data Recovery Advisor can proactively check for failures.

explanation:
Core idea: Data Recovery Advisor (DRA) inspects failure information and can proactively check for problems. It can work while the database is closed because some diagnostic and recovery actions are performed from mounted or other non-open states; DRA is deprecated in Oracle Database 19c, so check support status for later releases.

Option analysis: C is correct: DRA can be used when the database is closed. E is correct: a DBA can run proactive checks to look for failures. A is false because LIST FAILURE is not universally restricted to a mounted database. B is false because a failure can be closed after it is determined to be irrelevant or otherwise resolved from DRA's perspective; “only when repaired” is too absolute. D is false because CHANGE FAILURE can alter other failure attributes, not just priority.

Practical point: use DRA reports as diagnostic guidance, then confirm the recommended repair and backup availability before executing recovery actions.

C describes diagnostic access before a database is open, not a guarantee that every possible repair runs in every instance state. E includes proactive checks initiated by validation/Health Monitor facilities. B ignores manually closing failures that are no longer relevant; D ignores CHANGE FAILURE's status-changing capability. A is false because LIST FAILURE is not restricted to one universal mount-only state. A typical historical workflow was:
```text
LIST FAILURE;
ADVISE FAILURE;
```
Inspect the recommendation and affected files before any repair. DRA's deprecation in 19c is material: study its documented historical behavior for this question, but verify the precise release/update's command availability before designing new operational automation around it.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Data Recovery Advisor (DRA) inspects failure information and can proactively check for problems.

text: Which two are true about an Oracle gold image-based installation in Oracle 18c and later releases? (Choose two.)

options.text: It can be used for both Oracle Database and Oracle Grid Infrastructure installation.
It can only install and configure Oracle Database software. The database has to be created separately.
It does not require the setup wizard.
It uses a single RPM that automatically extracts and installs the Oracle Database software.
It can be used to install and upgrade Oracle Database for single-instance and cluster configurations.

explanation:
Core idea: A gold image is a prepared Oracle software home that can be deployed across hosts. Image-based installation streamlines software installation, while database creation and configuration remain separate operations when the image installs software only.

Option analysis: A is correct: gold images can be used for Oracle Database and Grid Infrastructure software. E is correct: the image-based method supports installing or upgrading Database software for single-instance and clustered configurations. B is false because gold images also apply to GI, not only Database. C is false: image-based installation still uses Oracle's installer workflow; “gold image” does not mean no setup/install utility is needed. D is false because this is not a single RPM that extracts and installs the database software.

Practical example: maintain a patched home image, deploy it consistently to test and production hosts, and then use the appropriate tools to configure the database or cluster.

Takeaway: gold images standardize Oracle homes; they are not database-creation packages.

A software-home image contains binaries and the selected software state; it does not automatically copy every database's data files. A and E concern the supported installation/upgrade deployment mechanism. B incorrectly excludes Grid Infrastructure and unnecessarily restricts the available configuration workflow. C confuses unpacking the image with completing prerequisite checks, inventory registration and privileged configuration. D describes RPM packaging, which is a different deployment method. A practical image-based installation unpacks the appropriate image into the intended Oracle home and runs that home's setup utility with the selected GUI or silent options. Ownership, inventory, supported patch level and source-to-target upgrade compatibility remain important even when the image has already been standardized.

text: Which two are true about RMAN duplexed backup sets? (Choose two.)

options.text: They can be written only to disk.
They must be written to media.
They can be created by using the RMAN CONFIGURE command to specify duplexing before taking a backup.
They can be created only by using the COPIES option of a BACKUP command.
They can be written to media.

explanation:
Core idea: RMAN duplexing creates identical copies of a backup set. It applies to backup sets rather than image copies and supports disk or tape destinations, although one duplexing operation cannot write copies to disk and tape simultaneously.

Option analysis: C is correct: persistent duplexing can be configured with CONFIGURE before a backup. E is correct: duplexed backup sets can be written to a media destination, including disk or SBT as configured. A is false because duplexing is not disk-only. B is false if “media” means tape; tape is not mandatory. D is false because duplexing can be specified through CONFIGURE, SET, or the BACKUP COPIES clause rather than only COPIES on BACKUP.

Practical example: configure two copies for SBT, ensure the media manager has enough drives, and verify that the copies land on separate media as intended.

Takeaway: duplexing is a backup-set copy policy, not a restriction to a single device type.

C establishes a persistent backup-copy policy, while E permits the SBT/media-manager destination. Here the bank uses “media” to mean tape/SBT; literally every storage device is a medium, so B would otherwise be poorly worded. Do not infer that duplexing doubles the RMAN channel count: one allocated channel can create multiple copies subject to supported SBT/media-manager capabilities. For example:
```text
CONFIGURE DATAFILE BACKUP COPIES FOR DEVICE TYPE SBT TO 2;
BACKUP DEVICE TYPE SBT DATABASE;
```
Verify copy numbers, distinct destination media and restore accessibility. Duplexing protects against loss of one backup copy; it neither replaces redo retention nor combines disk and SBT copies within one duplexed backup-set operation.

text: Which should be tuned first when doing a performance tuning exercise for an Oracle Database environment?

options.text: SQL statements
log writer performance
general operating system health
database writer performance
database instance memory management and sizes

explanation:
Core idea: SQL statements are the direct source of database work: they drive CPU, logical and physical I/O, memory use, and concurrency. A tuning exercise therefore begins by identifying high-load or poorly performing SQL and measuring its actual impact.

Option analysis: A is correct: investigate SQL statements first because inefficient access paths or excessive work can create the observed load. B and D are false as universal first steps: LGWR and DBWR are background processes that may be symptoms or bottlenecks, but should be examined in response to evidence. C is false as the exam's starting point: general OS health matters, but the question asks the database tuning sequence. E is false as a blanket first action: memory sizing should be evaluated from workload and wait/CPU evidence, not guessed before examining SQL.

Practical example: rank SQL by elapsed time, CPU, and reads, then inspect plans and bind behavior for the top contributors.

Takeaway: start with measured SQL work, then follow the evidence to the system component limiting it.

“First” is the exam's database-tuning priority, not permission to ignore an obvious failed storage path or an overloaded host. Start with a clear response-time/throughput problem and a measured baseline, then identify the SQL responsible for the largest useful reduction in database time. Rewriting an unnecessarily repeated query can reduce CPU, reads, redo and contention together; changing a background-process or memory parameter may merely shift the symptom. Compare representative elapsed time, rows processed, execution counts and plans before and after the change. Option C's general OS health is part of diagnosis, but it is not the intended first blanket tuning target in this sequence.

text: Which three are true in Oracle 19c and later releases? (Choose three.)

options.text: Tablespaces never remain in read/write mode during transportable tablespace operations.
A transportable data pump import can leave a plugged-in tablespace in read-only mode.
A transportable data pump import can leave a plugged-in tablespace in read/write mode.
Simultaneous data pump jobs can be limited at the pluggable database (PDB) level.
Tablespaces always remain in read/write mode during transportable tablespace operations.
An ordinary data pump export of a table with encrypted columns will always encrypt the same columns when imported.

explanation:
Core idea: Transportable Data Pump imports plug tablespaces into a target database and may leave them in either read-only or read/write mode depending on the import workflow and options. Resource Manager can also enforce limits on PDB activity, including Data Pump concurrency.

Option analysis: B and C are correct: a transportable import can leave a plugged-in tablespace read-only or read/write; neither state is universal. D is correct: Data Pump jobs can be limited at PDB scope. A and E are false because “never” and “always” ignore the differing transport/import states. F is false because ordinary export/import does not unconditionally reproduce encrypted-column encryption; keystore availability, encryption mode, and import setup affect the result.

Practical example: after a transportable import, verify tablespace status before application writes, and use Resource Manager limits to protect a busy PDB from too many concurrent jobs.

Takeaway: check actual import state and PDB resource policy instead of relying on absolute statements.

The concurrency mechanism for D is specifically MAX_DATAPUMP_JOBS_PER_PDB, which limits concurrent Data Pump jobs at PDB scope; it need not be described solely as a generic Resource Manager limit. Transportable export's test mode can examine metadata without forcing the usual source read-only transition, another reason A is too absolute. For B/C, explicitly verify destination tablespace status and the selected import options rather than assuming that every plugged-in tablespace permits writes immediately. F ignores the export/import encryption parameters and key availability needed to preserve or recreate column-encryption behavior. Testing these choices on a small encrypted table and a transportable test tablespace is safer than extrapolating from an unencrypted conventional export.

text: Which three are located by using environment variables? (Choose three.)

options.text: the Optimal Flexible Architecture (OFA) compliant path to store Oracle software and configuration files.
the location of Oracle Net Services configuration files
the list of a disk group names to be mounted by an Oracle Automatic Storage Management (ASM) instance at startup
default directories for temporary files used by temporary tablespaces
the temporary disk space used by Oracle Installer during installation
the maximum number of database files that can be opened by a database instance

explanation:
Core idea: Oracle uses environment variables for software paths, network configuration, and temporary installer files. Database behavior such as ASM disk groups, temporary tablespace files, and the maximum number of data files is controlled by initialization parameters or database objects.

Option analysis: A is correct: ORACLE_BASE identifies the Oracle base used for software and configuration layout. B is correct: TNS_ADMIN can identify Oracle Net configuration files. E is correct: TMP or TMPDIR identifies temporary space used by installer processes. C is false because ASM_DISKGROUPS controls disk groups mounted at startup. D is false because database file placement/default temporary tablespace behavior is not selected by an OS environment variable. F is false because DB_FILES is an initialization parameter controlling the number of database files.

Practical example: before installation, confirm ORACLE_BASE, ORACLE_HOME, TNS_ADMIN, and TMPDIR in the installation owner's environment, while checking database parameters separately.

Takeaway: do not confuse shell environment with initialization parameters.

A identifies the Oracle base, not necessarily the complete final Oracle home; ORACLE_HOME selects a particular installed software home under the chosen layout. B overrides the usual network configuration search directory and is especially useful when multiple homes share managed tnsnames.ora/sqlnet.ora files. E must point to a suitable installer scratch area with sufficient free space and permissions. C is controlled by ASM_DISKGROUPS; F by DB_FILES. D involves database-managed tempfile destinations and SQL/database configuration rather than the installer's scratch directory. Always inspect the environment of the actual process owner: a value exported in one shell does not automatically change services, other users or already-running processes.

text: Which two are true about the automatic execution of operating system scripts when performing silent mode installation starting from Oracle Database 19c? (Choose two.)

options.text: The response file can specify the root or sudo password.
The installer will prompt for the root or sudo password.
Silent install always runs operating scripts automatically.
The response file must contain the root or sudo password.
The response file can specify the path of the sudo program.

explanation:
B and E describe the documented 19c automatic privileged-script workflow. Automatic script execution is configured separately from choosing silent mode. The root/sudo credential is requested when needed; it should not be confused with database administrative passwords that some response files can contain.

Option B is true for the documented credentialed automatic execution path: the installer prompts for the root or sudo password. Option E is true: response-file settings can identify the sudo program's path, along with the automatic-execution method and sudo user as applicable.

Option A is not the documented root/sudo-password response-file setting for this workflow. Option D is false both because the response file is not required to contain that credential and because automatic execution is optional. Option C is false: adding -silent does not alone opt into automatic root-script execution; otherwise an administrator must run the scripts through the supported manual procedure.

The nonsecret configuration concepts include:
```text
oracle.install.db.rootconfig.executeRootScript=true
oracle.install.db.rootconfig.configMethod=ROOT
```
For sudo, consult the shipped response-file template and specify the supported sudo method, path and account fields. Do not invent a plaintext root-password field based on an unrelated password field in a DBCA template.

Because detailed prompting and unattended execution depend on the installed OUI build, validate the actual 19c installer help/template and applicable update documentation before scripting production installation. The corrected BE key follows Oracle's documented workflow; it does not assert that every silent installation always prompts or that every supported privilege mechanism needs a password.
review_note: Corrected AE to BE for documented 19c automatic root-script workflow: configure execution/sudo path in response file; root/sudo credential is prompted rather than saved there. Exact unattended credential behavior varies by installer/update and must not be inferred from generic DB-account password fields.

mnemonic.anchor: B and E describe the documented 19c automatic privileged-script workflow.

text: Which three capabilities require the use of the RMAN recovery catalog? (Choose three.)

options.text: using the KEEP FOREVER clause with the BACKUP command
using RMAN stored scripts
using the REPORT SCHEMA command to list a database's current data files and tablespaces
creating customized reports about a single database's backups
creating encrypted backups
using the REPORT SCHEMA command to list a database's data files and tablespaces at times in the past

explanation:
Core idea: The control file holds a limited RMAN repository history; a recovery catalog provides additional persistent metadata and features such as stored scripts and historical database structure.

Option analysis: A is correct: KEEP FOREVER requires a recovery catalog so RMAN can retain the archival backup metadata beyond control-file record retention. B is correct: RMAN stored scripts reside in a recovery catalog. F is correct: reporting the schema as it existed at a past time requires historical catalog records. C is false because REPORT SCHEMA can show the current schema using the target control file. D may be useful with catalog data but customized reporting for one database does not inherently require the catalog. E is false because RMAN encryption can be used without a recovery catalog.

Practical example: use a catalog when managing multiple targets or needing long-lived history; back up and protect the catalog itself because it stores recovery metadata.

Takeaway: current metadata may come from the control file, while long-term scripts and history need a catalog.

A's FOREVER retention requires durable catalog metadata; ordinary finite KEEP UNTIL archival retention is a different case. B refers to RMAN stored scripts created and executed through the catalog, not operating-system files containing RMAN commands. F requires retained historical schema metadata and an appropriate past point, for example REPORT SCHEMA AT TIME. C can use present target-control-file records. D is not exclusive because control-file repository views can supply single-database backup reporting. E's encryption depends on encryption mode/key management, not on owning a recovery catalog. For a practical design, back up the catalog database and periodically resynchronize metadata; a catalog tracks backup locations but does not contain the backed-up data-file blocks.

sources.title: Creating and managing the recovery catalog

mnemonic.anchor: Option analysis: A is correct: KEEP FOREVER requires a recovery catalog so RMAN can retain the archival backup metadata beyond control-file record retention.

text: Which three are true about the tools for diagnosing Oracle Database failure situations? (Choose three.)

options.text: The ADR command-line utility (ADRCI) can package incident information to send to Oracle Support.
The Automatic Diagnostic Repository (ADR) has a separate home directory for each instance of each Oracle product that is installed and uses it.
Flashback commands help with repairing physical errors.
RMAN can always repair corrupt blocks.
The ADR can store metadata in an Oracle Database repository.
The Data Recovery Advisor uses the ADR.

explanation:
Core idea: The Automatic Diagnostic Repository (ADR) stores diagnostic files and metadata for Oracle products. ADRCI can inspect incidents and package diagnostic data; RMAN and Flashback address different classes of recovery problems.

Option analysis: A is correct: ADRCI can create an incident package for Oracle Support. B is correct: ADR uses separate homes for product instances such as database instances and listeners. F is correct according to the keyed answer: Data Recovery Advisor uses diagnostic repository information when diagnosing failures. C is false because Flashback reverses logical changes or rewinds database state; it is not a general repair for physical block corruption. D is false because RMAN cannot always repair corruption; a usable backup, archived redo, or good block source may be required. E is false: ADR is a file-based repository, not a repository stored inside an Oracle database.

Practical point: package the relevant incident promptly, then choose RMAN block/media recovery or Flashback based on the failure type.

A's incident package groups relevant traces and diagnostic context for a support case; it is not itself a database backup. B permits separate ADR homes for different database instances/listeners even on one host. F follows DRA's use of persistent diagnostic failure information; DRA is deprecated in 19c, so distinguish exam-era behavior from new tooling recommendations. C and D wrongly promise universal repair: logical rewind and physical media recovery solve different problems, and neither can manufacture missing data without a usable source. E is false because ADR is filesystem based, making diagnosis possible even when the target database cannot open. In ADRCI, inspect SHOW HOMES before choosing an incident so that diagnostics come from the affected instance.

sources.title: Data Recovery Advisor and diagnostic workflow

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: The Automatic Diagnostic Repository (ADR) stores diagnostic files and metadata for Oracle products.

text:
The HR_ROOT application container must support the execution of a query on a table shared by application local PDBs PDB1 and PDB2, and remote PDB PDB3.

Which two are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A proxy PDB must exist in the application root in the remote CDB.
A database link must exist in the local CDB root referring to the remote CDB.
PDB3's application root replica must exist in the local CDB.
A database link must exist in the remote CDB referring to the local CDB.
The HR_ROOT replica must exist in the remote CDB.
A proxy PDB must exist in the application root in the local CDB.

explanation:
E and F are correct. The application container needs a local proxy PDB and the corresponding remote application-root replica. The original three-answer key also selected B, but its explicit CDB-root location conflicts with the application-root requirement documented for this topology.

Option E is true: the remote CDB contains the HR_ROOT application-root replica associated with the remote application's participating PDB. Option F is true: the local application container contains the proxy PDB that provides the local context for the remote application objects and supports the cross-container arrangement.

Option B is false as written. For a proxy PDB inside an application container, Oracle requires the creation-time database link in that application container's root, here HR_ROOT. CDB$ROOT and an application root are different containers. A database link in the local CDB root does not satisfy the stated application-root requirement. The link may connect to the remote application root or the remote referenced application PDB, subject to the documented prerequisites.

Option A puts the proxy on the remote side rather than where the local application query needs it. Option C puts the replica in the local CDB instead of the remote CDB. Option D reverses the creation-time link direction.

In practice, establish the application-root topology, create the supported link in local HR_ROOT and create the local proxy using the appropriate FROM ... AS PROXY syntax. Verify remote privileges and application synchronization before testing a CONTAINERS query. Oracle notes that the proxy communicates directly with its referenced PDB after creation; the link is a creation-time prerequisite, not a substitute for the proxy's continuing connection mechanism.
original_text:
The HR_ROOT application container must support the execution of a query on a table shared by application local PDBs PDB1 and PDB2, and remote PDB PDB3.

Which three are true? (Choose three.)

sources.title: Application objects, container maps and application administration

review_note: Corrected BEF/count3 to EF/count2. B names the CDB root, but Oracle requires the database link in the application root for a proxy in an application container.

keywords: HR_ROOT replica must exist in the remote CDB
proxy PDB must exist in the application root in the local CDB
mnemonic.anchor: The application container needs a local proxy PDB and the corresponding remote application-root replica.

text: Which two are true about poorly performing SQL statements and their tuning in Oracle database instances? (Choose two.)

options.text: SQL statements performing many physical I/Os can always have their performance improved by creating indexes.
SQL statements doing only logical reads never require tuning because they do no physical I/O.
The solution that best optimizes one SQL statement can degrade the performance of others.
SQL statements doing joins always do more physical I/O than single table queries.
Poorly performing SQL statements can be tuned automatically by the Oracle server.

explanation:
Core idea: SQL tuning is a workload problem. A change that benefits one statement may add index-maintenance cost, consume memory, or shift resources away from other statements; automatic tools can help analyze and recommend improvements.

Option analysis: C is correct: optimizing one statement can degrade others, so test changes against representative workload, not a single query in isolation. E is correct: Oracle's automatic SQL Tuning Advisor analyzes selected high-load statements and can make recommendations. A is false because indexes do not always reduce physical I/O; they can increase work or be bypassed by the optimizer. B is false because logical reads consume CPU and buffer-cache resources and can still be excessive. D is false because joins do not inherently perform more physical I/O than single-table queries; plans and data volume determine the work.

Practical example: compare overall workload before and after an index or SQL Profile change, checking both the target SQL and write-heavy statements.

Takeaway: tune measured work and validate side effects across the workload.

A common example for C is adding an index: one selective query may become much faster while inserts and updates pay extra index maintenance, redo and locking costs. B ignores the CPU and latch/cache work of repeated logical reads; a query can be inefficient entirely from cache. D ignores data volume, join order and caching, so it has no universal physical-I/O relationship. E covers automatic analysis and supported automatic implementation where configured; it does not promise that every slow statement is rewritten or improved without DBA review. Compare plans and actual row counts for representative bind values, then measure the complete workload rather than declaring success from one faster execution.

sources.title: SQL Tuning Advisor analysis and recommendations

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: SQL tuning is a workload problem.

text: Which two are true about Rapid Home Provisioning of Oracle software? (Choose two.)

options.text: It can be used for applications and middleware.
It can be used only for Oracle Grid Infrastructure, excluding Oracle Restart.
It can be used only for Oracle Grid Infrastructure, including Oracle Restart.
It can be used for both Oracle Database and Oracle Grid Infrastructure, including Oracle Restart.
It can be used for both Oracle Database and Oracle Grid Infrastructure, excluding Oracle Restart.

explanation:
Core idea: Rapid Home Provisioning centrally deploys and manages Oracle software homes and supported application or middleware software. It can manage both Database and Grid Infrastructure homes, including Oracle Restart.

Option analysis: A is correct: RHP can provision applications and middleware. D is correct: it supports both Oracle Database and Grid Infrastructure, including Oracle Restart. B and C are false because RHP is not limited to Grid Infrastructure alone. E is false because it incorrectly excludes Oracle Restart from supported GI deployments.

Practical example: an administrator can maintain a standardized image and provision it to a standalone server or cluster, then apply a consistent patch level across the fleet. RHP manages deployment and software-home lifecycle; it does not replace planning for supported combinations, storage, networking, or database configuration.

Takeaway: RHP covers Database, Grid Infrastructure/Restart, and supported application or middleware targets.

The 19c name is Oracle Fleet Patching and Provisioning, formerly Rapid Home Provisioning. Gold images and working copies let the administrator separate the standardized source image from deployed writable Oracle homes. A and D describe the broad product scope; B/C/E introduce unsupported exclusions or “only” restrictions. Provisioning applications and middleware requires a supported image/workflow rather than assuming every arbitrary installer can run unchanged. For a practical patch rollout, prepare and validate a new image in a test environment, provision a working copy to the appropriate targets, then perform the supported switch/upgrade procedure. Image management does not remove each product's own compatibility and privileged-configuration requirements.

sources.title: Fleet Patching and Provisioning of database, GI, applications and middleware

keywords: both Oracle Database and Oracle Grid Infrastructure, including Oracle Restart
mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: Rapid Home Provisioning centrally deploys and manages Oracle software homes and supported application or middleware software.

text:
Your database is in ARCHIVELOG mode and you plan to use Flashback Database.

Which two features or parameters manage space availability in the fast recovery area? (Choose two.)

options.text: the archived log deletion policy
the backup optimization policy
the backup retention policy
using guaranteed UNDO retention
the DB_CREATE_ONLINE_LOG_DEST_n parameter setting
the DB_RECOVERY_FILE_DEST parameter setting

explanation:
Core idea: The fast recovery area (FRA) has a size and location, but space reclamation depends on whether files are still required. RMAN retention policy determines backup obsolescence, and the archived-log deletion policy determines when archived logs may be deleted.

Option analysis: A and C are correct: archived-log deletion policy and backup retention policy influence what the FRA can reclaim. B is false: backup optimization skips eligible files during a backup; it does not decide whether existing FRA contents are safe to remove. D is false: guaranteed undo retention concerns undo availability, not FRA file reclamation. E is false: DB_CREATE_ONLINE_LOG_DEST_n controls online log placement, not FRA reclaimability. F is false: DB_RECOVERY_FILE_DEST sets the FRA location (and size is set separately), but does not itself decide which files are obsolete.

Practical point: tune retention and deletion policies with restore, Data Guard, and Flashback requirements in mind before space pressure occurs.

Takeaway: location defines the FRA; retention policies govern reclaimable content.

F changes the recovery area's location; DB_RECOVERY_FILE_DEST_SIZE, which is not offered, sets its capacity. A and C influence which archived logs and backups remain needed and therefore eligible for reclamation. Flashback logs have their own retention-target and guaranteed-restore-point interactions; a guaranteed restore point can pin necessary logs and contribute to space pressure even when ordinary backups are obsolete. B avoids redundant backup work rather than expiring existing files. D protects undo history in undo tablespaces, not FRA files. In practice, inspect V$RECOVERY_FILE_DEST and V$RECOVERY_AREA_USAGE and verify the restore/Data Guard requirements before changing deletion policy merely to make a full recovery area writable again.

sources.title: RMAN backup scope, archival backups and output

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: The fast recovery area (FRA) has a size and location, but space reclamation depends on whether files are still required.

text: Which two are true about Oracle Database Configuration Assistant (DBCA)? (Choose two.)

options.text: It can be launched from both the command line and the Universal Installer (OUI) interfaces.
It can be used to change the character set of an existing database.
It can be used to convert a non-container database to a container database.
It can be used to create container databases and non-container databases.
It can only be launched from the command line interface.

explanation:
Core idea: DBCA is Oracle's graphical and command-line assistant for database creation and selected lifecycle operations. Creating a database is distinct from converting an existing non-CDB into a PDB.

Option analysis: A is correct: DBCA can be launched directly and can also be initiated through Oracle Universal Installer workflows. D is correct: DBCA supports creation of both container and non-container databases. B is false because changing an existing database character set is not a general DBCA operation. C is false: DBCA can help convert a non-CDB into a PDB, but that does not convert it into a CDB—the CDB must already exist. E is false because a graphical interface is available; it is not command-line-only.

Practical example: use DBCA to create a CDB, then use the appropriate non-CDB-to-PDB conversion process if consolidating an older database.

Takeaway: distinguish creating a CDB from plugging or converting a non-CDB into one of its PDBs.

D is a 19c capability: non-CDB creation remains supported in that release even though the architecture is deprecated and later releases differ. A includes the graphical OUI configuration path as well as explicit DBCA invocation. C's wording confuses transforming an existing non-CDB into a PDB hosted by a CDB with turning that same database into a CDB root. B is not a substitute for a supported character-set migration workflow; creating a new database with a chosen character set is different from converting an existing database. E excludes the documented graphical assistant. For a practical lifecycle operation, identify whether the target is a new CDB, new non-CDB, or new/converted PDB before choosing the DBCA command family.

sources.title: DBCA templates and silent-mode command reference

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: DBCA is Oracle's graphical and command-line assistant for database creation and selected lifecycle operations.

text: Which three are performed by Oracle Automatic Storage Management (ASM) instances? (Choose three.)

options.text: mounting disk groups
managing Allocation Units (AUs) for disk group content
managing extent allocation for Oracle database segments
acting as an I/O server to write data file blocks to ASM disks on behalf of Database Writer processes (DBWn)
managing space allocation for Oracle ASM files
acting as an I/O server to read data file blocks from ASM disks on behalf of database server processes

explanation:
Core idea: ASM manages storage at the disk-group and ASM-file level. The database instance owns database segment metadata and performs database block processing; ASM provides the storage structures used by those files.

Option analysis: A, B, and E are correct: ASM instances mount disk groups, manage allocation units, and manage space allocation for ASM files. C is false because database segment extent allocation is handled by the database instance and its tablespace management, not by ASM. D and F are false because ASM is not a block-serving I/O process that performs DBWn or server-process reads/writes on their behalf; database processes use ASM interfaces to access files.

Practical example: when an ASM disk group is full, add or rebalance storage at the ASM level; when a segment needs extents, manage the database tablespace and segment behavior.

Takeaway: ASM owns disk-group and file allocation; the database owns segment and block-level semantics.

A/B/E operate on disk-group metadata and ASM-file extents/allocation units. C instead concerns database segments and their tablespace extents; those can request more space inside an ASM-backed data file without turning the ASM instance into a table/index segment manager. D and F wrongly make a standard ASM instance the data-block I/O server for database processes. Database processes normally perform their own I/O using ASM's file extent mappings. Distinguish that ordinary architecture from separately configured Flex ASM/ASM I/O Server and proxy features rather than attributing every possible storage-service role to a standard ASM instance. Rebalancing redistributes ASM allocation units; rebuilding a table/index addresses a different database-level object.

mnemonic.anchor: Core idea: ASM manages storage at the disk-group and ASM-file level.

text:
Your CDB has two regular PDBs as well as one application container with two application PDBs and an application seed. No changes have been made to the standard PDB$SEED.

How many default temporary tablespaces can be assigned in the CDB?

options.text: six
seven
five
eight
three

explanation:
B (seven) is the intended answer if “can be assigned” means default-temporary-tablespace assignments that an administrator may change, excluding the immutable standard PDB$SEED. The question is ambiguous because D (eight) counts the existing per-container default-temporary contexts, including the standard seed. Those are different questions.

Count the assignable containers explicitly: one CDB root, two regular PDBs, one application root, two application PDBs and one application seed. That totals seven. Oracle documents that the standard PDB seed cannot be modified; its presence is not an additional freely configurable default assignment. An application seed is distinct from PDB$SEED and can be opened in the supported maintenance mode while preparing application contents.

This does not mean PDB$SEED has no TEMP tablespace or no inherited default-temporary metadata. Including it among all existing containers produces eight contexts. The original explanation incorrectly mixed this eight-container count with a claim about the unchanged seed, without separating existence from modifiability.

Option A (six) omits one of the seven configurable container roles. Options C (five) and E (three) omit multiple regular/application containers. Option D is valid for the alternate existence-based reading, which is why the item remains explicitly ambiguous rather than being presented as an official settled exam key.

In a disposable CDB, inspect each container's DATABASE_PROPERTIES default-temporary setting and temporary tablespaces through the appropriate container views. Do not try to modify the standard seed to prove the arithmetic. A clearer stem would ask either how many containers have a default-temporary context or how many default assignments are administratively modifiable.

sources.title: Creating a CDB and immutable PDB seed

review_note: Seven if “can be assigned” counts modifiable default assignments and excludes immutable standard PDB$SEED. Eight if counting existing per-container default TEMP contexts including PDB$SEED. Original wording admits both interpretations; do not claim the seed has no temporary tablespace.

mnemonic.anchor: The question is ambiguous because D (eight) counts the existing per-container default-temporary contexts, including the standard seed.
